52-solutions-have-cross-problem-function.text: 52 solutions in the repo had function names copied from entirely different problems.

absences-monotonic-lates-resettable.text: In `checkRecord`, `absences` is monotonically increasing (global count) while `consecutive_lates` resets on every non-`'L'` character (local streak), reflecting the two different rule scopes

absolute-diff-k-assumes-positive-k.text: This is a constraint of the specific LeetCode problem, not a codebase invariant. Already covered by the general no-input-validation belief.

absolute-diff-k-does-not-track-indices.text: The solution never tracks element indices; it counts qualifying pairs solely from frequency products of values.

absolute-diff-k-function-name-matches-pr.text: The exported function is named `count_number_of_pairs_with_absolute_difference_k`, matching the problem domain rather than a template artifact.

absolute-diff-k-k-zero-miscounts-self-pa.text: The function would miscount if `k == 0` because checking `v + k` would multiply `freq[v] * freq[v]` instead of counting only distinct pairs with `C(freq[v], 2)`.

abstraction-cost-predicts-convergence-st.text: Strategy convergence strength in an uncoordinated repo appears predictable from abstraction overhead: streaming (zero abstractions) converges strongest, hash-then-stream (one preprocessing step with Counter/set) converges next, sort-then-scan (ordering prerequisite plus pointer management) converges weakest — the adoption barrier gradient closely tracks the abstraction cost gradient.

justifications.label: both describe the same hierarchy from different causal angles (adoption vs. infrastructure); combining reveals abstraction cost is the measurable predictor of convergence

abstraction-overhead-explains-strategy-h.text: Non-streaming strategies require lookup abstractions (Counter, set, binary search) as load-bearing infrastructure between pipeline phases, while streaming requires none — this asymmetric abstraction overhead causally explains the strategy hierarchy: streaming dominates because it avoids the data-structure selection and initialization cost that alternatives impose on each solution author.

justifications.label: Streaming's privilege is the inverse of alternatives' abstraction burden; combining the load-bearing role of lookup abstractions with streaming's privilege reveals the causal mechanism

add-digits-constant-time.text: addDigits runs in O(1) time and space with no loops or recursion.

add-digits-no-dependencies.text: Already covered by the cross-cutting belief `solutions-use-no-external-dependencies`; a per-file version adds no value.

add-digits-output-range.text: The claim that addDigits returns a value in [0, 9] is a direct restatement of what "digital root" means — it's the definition, not a codebase invariant.

add-strings-avoids-int-conversion.text: `addStrings` converts between characters and digit values using `ord()/chr()` arithmetic (`ord(c) - 48`, `chr(d + 48)`) and never calls `int()` or `str()`, satisfying the problem's constraint against built-in integer conversion.

add-strings-carry-after-exhaustion.text: The addStrings loop continues after both strings are exhausted if carry > 0, ensuring results like "999" + "1" = "1000" are correct.

add-strings-carry-propagation.text: The `or carry` condition in carry-propagation loops is a universal pattern for multi-digit addition — not specific enough to this codebase to warrant a standalone belief.

add-strings-linear-time.text: This is correct but too generic — O(max(len(a), len(b))) is the obvious complexity for any digit-by-digit addition algorithm and doesn't represent a non-obvious insight.

add-to-array-form-k-as-carry.text: The add-to-array-form solution uses the input integer `k` as both the addend and carry accumulator via `k //= 10`, eliminating the need for a separate carry variable.

add-to-array-form-loop-terminates-on-bot.text: The addToArrayForm while loop requires both the array to be fully traversed (i < 0) and k to be zero (no remaining value or carry) before exiting.

add-to-array-form-mutates-num-in-place.text: addToArrayForm mutates and returns the input list num rather than allocating a new result list.

add-to-array-form-prepend-quadratic-wors.text: When `k` has more digits than `num`, each extra digit triggers an O(n) `list.insert(0, ...)`, making the overflow phase O(d*n) rather than the O(max(n,d)) achievable with append-and-reverse.

add-two-integers-docstring-input-range.text: The `Solution.sum` docstring documents the input constraint range `[-100, 100]` from the problem statement.

add-two-integers-returns-arithmetic-sum.text: `Solution.sum(num1, num2)` returns the arithmetic sum `num1 + num2`.

add-two-integers-sum-is-pure-no-state.text: `Solution.sum` is pure, uses no instance state, and has no side effects.

additive-then-subtractive-counting-patte.text: Grid geometry problems (surface area, island perimeter) use an "add full contribution, then subtract shared faces" strategy — computing isolated values first, then removing occlusion — as a reusable template.

adjacent-duplicate-is-early-exit.text: Restates basic control flow visible in the code (an early `return False`) — not an invariant that needs tracking

adjacent-pair-range-minus-one.text: `range(len(nums) - 1)` with `nums[i+1]` access is the repo's standard pattern for pairwise element comparison, preventing out-of-bounds reads on the last index.

adoption-barrier-gradient-explains-conve.text: The repo's multi-level convergence appears to correlate with strategy self-sufficiency: streaming, which requires no preprocessing or data structure selection, exhibits the strongest convergence, consistent with the principle that lower adoption barriers tend to produce stronger convergence pressure in an uncoordinated environment. Whether this gradient extends predictably to other paradigms (sort-then-scan, hash-then-scan) remains an observed pattern rather than a confirmed causal relationship.

justifications.label: The observation of multi-level convergence combined with the causal explanation for streaming dominance reveals adoption barrier as the universal gradient governing convergence strength

algorithmic-coherence-emerges-without-en.text: Despite zero cross-solution coordination and no consistency enforcement, solutions independently converge on two dominant paradigms (streaming and sort-then-scan), demonstrating that LeetCode's problem domain naturally constrains the algorithmic solution space.

justifications.label: Convergence without coordination reveals domain-imposed structure rather than engineered consistency

algorithmic-precision-despite-engineerin.text: The repo invests in algorithmic quality (exact arithmetic via isqrt, integer division; stdlib delegation for precision via Counter, set) while neglecting engineering quality (naming, structure, reusability), creating an asymmetry where computational correctness is high but code maintainability is low.

justifications.label: Submission-optimized engineering + stdlib-reinforced exactness shows the optimization target is judge correctness, not code quality

alias-is-identity.text: `min_time_to_remove_balloons` is a module-level alias (same function object) for `countStudents`, not a wrapper — likely exists for a test harness or problem variant that expects that name.

alien-dict-assumes-valid-order.text: The alien dictionary solution assumes `order` covers all characters in `words`; a missing character produces an unhandled `KeyError` — no input validation.

alien-dict-function-misnamed.text: The function solving LeetCode 953 (alien dictionary verification) is named `reverse_string`, which has nothing to do with its actual behavior — a naming bug, not an alias.

alien-dict-linear-time-complexity.text: The alien dictionary verification runs in O(M) time where M is the total number of characters across all words, because each character is examined at most once.

alien-dict-prefix-rule.text: The alien dictionary solution explicitly enforces the prefix rule: if all shared characters match but the first word is longer, it returns `False`.

alien-dict-rank-map-idiom.text: The alien dictionary solution builds a `{char: index}` dict from the ordering string, converting custom-alphabet comparison to integer comparison with O(1) lookups.

all-groups-equal-length-k.text: Every element returned by divideString has exactly k characters, guaranteed by the pad step preceding the slice step.

all-nines-max-unchanged.text: This is a direct consequence of `max-remap-first-non-nine` (no non-9 digit exists, so no remapping occurs) — not an independent belief.

all-nonalgorithmic-defects-invisible-at-.text: All engineering defects — whether sourced from the generation pipeline (naming errors, stale aliases) or from the isolation architecture (tooling confusion, convention drift, duplicated definitions) — are invisible at runtime because the submission-optimized architecture confines their blast radius to non-functional dimensions.

justifications.label: generation-sourced and isolation-sourced defects both confined to non-runtime dimensions

all-ones-check-idiom.text: `(m & (m + 1)) == 0` tests whether `m` is zero or all-ones up to the MSB — the complement of the `n & (n-1) == 0` power-of-two check, reusable across bit-manipulation problems.

all-short-circuits-on-first-uncovered.text: Python's `all()` short-circuiting is standard language behavior, not a codebase-specific invariant.

all-short-circuits-on-inconsistent.text: This is standard Python `all()` behavior, not a codebase-specific invariant — any Python developer would expect this

all-short-circuits-on-odd.text: This is standard Python `all()` behavior, not a codebase-specific claim.

all-solutions-pure-python-no-imports.text: All five solutions use only Python builtins and (optionally) `typing.List` or `unittest` — none import third-party libraries or non-trivial standard library modules, keeping each solution self-contained

all-solutions-reduce-to-adapted-streamin.text: Every solution in the repo is fundamentally a streaming algorithm: pure streaming solutions operate directly, while sort-then-scan and hash-then-scan solutions use preprocessing as a domain adapter that transforms the problem into one where streaming's self-sufficiency applies — making the preprocessing phase structurally optional rather than architecturally distinct.

justifications.label: Preprocessing converts problems to streaming-compatible domains (depth-4) and streaming is self-sufficient (depth-4); together they reduce the entire solution architecture to streaming with optional adapters

almost-equivalent-checks-union-of-counte.text: The almost-equivalent solution iterates over `set(freq1) | set(freq2)` so characters present in either word are checked.

almost-equivalent-early-exits-on-first-v.text: `checkAlmostEquivalent` returns False immediately upon encountering the first character whose absolute frequency difference exceeds 3.

almost-equivalent-threshold-hardcoded-3.text: The almost-equivalent solution hardcodes the allowed frequency-difference threshold as 3 rather than exposing it as a parameter.

already-increasing-returns-true.text: Obvious from the code and problem definition — not a surprising invariant.

alternating-bits-input-range-1-to-2p31-m.text: `has_alternating_bits` is specified for positive integers in the range `[1, 2^31 - 1]`.

alternating-bits-o1.text: `has_alternating_bits` runs in O(1) time and space with no loops or string conversion — pure arithmetic on two intermediate values.

alternating-bits-single-function-no-clas.text: `has_alternating_bits` is implemented without imports, classes, or persistent state.

alternating-bits-sole-public-function.text: The module containing `has_alternating_bits` exposes that function as its sole public function.

alternating-digit-sum-linear-in-digit-co.text: `sum_of_digits` runs in O(d) time and O(d) space, where d is the number of digits and is at most 10 under the problem constraints.

alternating-digit-sum-negative-input-rai.text: Passing a negative integer to `sum_of_digits` raises `ValueError` because `str(n)` includes a `-` character and `int('-')` fails.

alternating-digit-sum-uses-exponentiatio.text: `(-1) ** i` in `sum_of_digits` yields +1 for even indices and -1 for odd indices, assigning the most significant digit a positive sign.

alternating-string-count-plus-complement.text: In `canDistribute`, `count + (len(s) - count) == len(s)` always holds because every position mismatches exactly one of the two alternating target patterns.

alternating-string-length-one-returns-ze.text: For a one-character binary string, `canDistribute` always returns 0 because a single character is trivially alternating.

alternating-string-nonbinary-chars-silen.text: `canDistribute` does not validate characters; non-binary characters are silently counted as mismatches against both target patterns and can produce a wrong answer rather than an error.

alternating-string-result-at-most-half-l.text: For any valid binary string input, `canDistribute` returns a value no greater than `len(s) // 2`.

anagram-check-uses-sorted-canonical-form.text: Anagram comparison in `anagramOperations` uses `sorted(word) == sorted(other)` — O(k log k) per word but avoids the complexity of frequency-counting approaches.

anagram-comparison-target-is-last-accept.text: Each word is compared against `result[-1]` (the last *accepted* word), not the previous word in the input — when consecutive anagrams are dropped, the comparison target stays the same until a non-anagram breaks the run.

anagram-dedup-consecutive-only.text: `anagramOperations` only collapses *consecutive* anagram runs; non-adjacent anagram pairs survive (e.g., `["ab", "cd", "ba"]` returns unchanged).

anagram-mappings-duplicate-safe.text: `anagramMappings` handles duplicate values correctly by queuing all indices per value in a `defaultdict(deque)`, with each occurrence in `nums1` consuming exactly one queued index via `pop()`.

anagram-mappings-lifo-index-order.text: When duplicates exist, `anagramMappings` assigns indices in LIFO order (last-appended index consumed first) because `deque.pop()` removes from the right.

anagram-mappings-linear-time.text: Redundant — O(n) time/space for a hash-map-based lookup is the obvious complexity and doesn't encode a non-trivial invariant.

anagram-mappings-no-input-validation.text: Too generic — all LeetCode solutions in this repo trust input constraints; this doesn't encode a codebase-specific invariant.

anagram-mappings-precondition-violation-.text: Violating the anagram precondition in anagramMappings surfaces as an unhandled IndexError raised by deque.pop() on an empty deque.

anagram-operations-is-pure-no-input-muta.text: `anagramOperations` does not mutate the input list and returns a new list.

anagram-operations-iterates-from-second-.text: `anagramOperations` iterates over `words[1:]`, starting comparisons from the second word.

anagram-operations-keeps-first-word-in-c.text: `anagramOperations` keeps the first word of each consecutive anagram run and drops subsequent anagrams in that run.

anagram-operations-seeds-result-with-fir.text: `anagramOperations` initializes its result list with `words[0]` before iterating over the remaining words.

anagram-ops-crashes-on-empty.text: `anagramOperations([])` raises `IndexError` because `words[0]` is accessed unconditionally with no length check.

anchor-tracking-pattern-shared.text: The "last-seen non-zero" anchor-tracking idiom appears in both `max_captured_forts` and `countHillValley` — skip irrelevant elements, compare the current significant value to the previous one.

ap-integer-division-exact.text: In `missing-number-in-arithmetic-progression/solution.py`, the expression `(arr[-1] - arr[0]) // n` never truncates under valid inputs because the span of a valid AP is always an exact multiple of the gap count.

apples-capacity-hardcoded.text: The basket capacity of 5000 is hardcoded in `maxNumberOfApples`, not parameterized — matching the LeetCode spec but preventing reuse with different limits.

apples-complexity-dominated-by-ascending.text: `maxNumberOfApples` runs in O(n log n) time because `weight.sort()` dominates the subsequent O(n) accumulation scan.

apples-early-return-index.text: `maxNumberOfApples` returns the loop index `i` (not `i+1`) on budget overflow because `enumerate` is zero-based and `i` equals the count of previously accumulated apples before the one that broke the budget.

apples-greedy-optimality.text: Sorting ascending and taking greedily is provably optimal for maximizing item count under a weight budget when all items have equal value (1 apple = 1 unit).

apples-inline-test-class-has-eight-cases.text: The inline `TestMaxNumberOfApples` class contains eight unit test cases.

apples-mutates-input.text: `maxNumberOfApples` mutates the caller's list via `weight.sort()` rather than using `sorted()`, so callers cannot rely on original order being preserved.

apples-returns-full-length-when-all-fit.text: If the cumulative weight never exceeds 5000 during iteration, `maxNumberOfApples` returns `len(weight)`, indicating every apple fits.

apples-returns-zero-on-empty-input.text: `maxNumberOfApples` returns `0` for an empty weight list because the loop completes without adding any apples and the final return is `len(weight)`.

apply-ops-inline-tests-cover-sequential-.text: The `TestPerformOps` suite covers consecutive triples, all-same arrays, and zeros between values.

apply-ops-two-phase-pattern.text: `apply-operations-to-an-array` uses a two-phase in-place transformation: Phase 1 (pairwise doubling, left-to-right with sequential dependency) must complete before Phase 2 (zero compaction via write-pointer), and interleaving them produces incorrect results.

apply-ops-zero-pair-doubling-idempotent.text: When adjacent elements are both zero, the doubling phase sets the left element to 0 and the right element to 0, producing no observable change without a special case.

architecture-immune-to-own-engineering-d.text: The repo's architecture exhibits structural immunity to its own engineering defects: zero-coupling costs are invisible at runtime because each solution's correctness is independent, and the most prominent such cost — naming drift — serves no functional role at any layer. This means the architecture cannot be degraded by the class of inconsistencies it systematically produces; even adversarial naming errors would be absorbed without observable effect.

justifications.label: Depth-7 qualitative jump: from "defects are currently invisible" to "the architecture is structurally immune to this defect class" — a property of the system, not an observation about current state

argument-order-irrelevant.text: Trivially follows from the use of `abs()` — not a surprising invariant that needs tracking

arithmetic-progression-all-equal-handled.text: Arrays where all elements are equal are handled correctly because the expected difference is `0` and every consecutive pair also has difference `0`.

arithmetic-progression-early-exit-on-vio.text: `can_construct` returns `False` on the first consecutive pair whose difference does not match `arr[1] - arr[0]`.

arithmetic-progression-mutates-input.text: `can_construct` calls `arr.sort()`, mutating the input list in place; callers needing the original order must pass a copy.

arithmetic-progression-sort-then-scan.text: `can_construct` sorts the input then verifies constant consecutive difference in one pass — O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space beyond the sort.

arithmetic-progression-sorted-order-only.text: After sorting, the ascending order is the only candidate arrangement to check for an arithmetic progression.

arithmetic-triplets-linear-space-seen-se.text: `count_arithmetic_triplets` uses O(n) auxiliary space because the `seen` set can grow to hold all elements of `nums`.

arithmetic-triplets-requires-strictly-in.text: `count_arithmetic_triplets` relies on `nums` being strictly increasing so that `x - diff` and `x - 2*diff` appear earlier and are already in `seen` when each `x` is processed.

arithmetic-triplets-set-lookup-linear.text: `count_arithmetic_triplets` achieves O(n) time via set-based membership lookups, treating each element as the largest of a potential triplet and checking for `x - diff` and `x - 2*diff` in a `seen` set

arithmetic-triplets-three-set-ops-per-el.text: Each iteration of `count_arithmetic_triplets` performs three O(1) set operations: checking `x - diff`, checking `x - 2*diff`, and adding `x` to `seen`.

armstrong-negative-input-raises.text: Passing a negative integer to `is_armstrong` raises `ValueError` because the string representation includes a `-` character and `int('-')` fails.

armstrong-single-digit-always-true.text: All single-digit non-negative integers (0-9) are Armstrong numbers under `is_armstrong` because any digit to the 1st power equals itself.

armstrong-time-complexity.text: `is_armstrong` runs in O(log n) time by iterating once over the decimal digits with constant-time exponentiation per digit.

arranging-coins-input-range.text: The LeetCode `arranging-coins` problem constrains input `n` to `1 <= n <= 2^31 - 1`.

arranging-coins-returns-max-triangular-k.text: `arrange_coins(n)` returns the largest integer k such that k(k+1)/2 <= n.

arranging-coins-triangular-root-formula.text: The expression `(isqrt(8*n+1) - 1) // 2` is equivalent to `floor((-1 + sqrt(1 + 8n)) / 2)`.

array-equivalence-allows-different-eleme.text: Two string arrays with different element boundaries can compare as equivalent when their concatenations match, such as `["a","bc"]` and `["ab","c"]` both producing `"abc"`.

array-equivalence-uses-join-then-compare.text: `arrayStringsAreEqual` computes `"".join(word1)` and `"".join(word2)` and compares the two resulting strings for equality.

array-partition-adjacent-pairing-optimal.text: After sorting, pairing adjacent elements `(nums[0], nums[1])`, `(nums[2], nums[3])`, ... maximizes the sum of pair minimums; any other pairing yields a sum less than or equal to this one.

array-partition-empty-input-returns-zero.text: For an empty input list, `sum([])` returns 0, so `array_pair_sum([])` returns 0 without raising an error.

array-partition-linear-after-sort.text: Too granular — the O(n) slice-sum after an O(n log n) sort is obvious from the two-line implementation and doesn't encode a constraint that could break things if violated.

array-partition-mutates-input.text: `nums.sort()` mutates the caller's list in-place rather than using `sorted()` to preserve the original.

array-partition-no-validation.text: `array_pair_sum` assumes even-length input and performs no length or type checking; odd-length input silently produces a wrong answer.

array-partition-sort-greedy.text: `array_pair_sum` uses sort + even-index sum as its greedy strategy; no dynamic programming or enumeration.

array-strings-are-equal-does-not-mutate-.text: `arrayStringsAreEqual` does not modify `word1` or `word2`; it only reads them through `str.join`.

array-transform-degenerate-input-returns.text: For empty or single-element input lists, the inner loop never executes and `new == arr` on the first check, so the input is returned unchanged.

array-transform-endpoints-immutable.text: The first and last elements of the array are never modified; only indices 1 through len-2 are candidates for change.

array-transform-extrema-adjust-by-one.text: In each round, strict local minima are incremented by 1 and strict local maxima are decremented by 1; non-extrema and endpoints stay unchanged.

array-transform-fixed-point-termination.text: The `while True` loop terminates because each round moves local minima up and local maxima down, monotonically narrowing values toward their neighbors until `new == arr`.

array-transform-no-mutation.text: The input list is copied on entry (`arr[:]`), so the caller's original list is never modified — contrasting with array-partition and assign-cookies which mutate in-place.

array-transform-simultaneous-update.text: All comparisons in a single round use the pre-round snapshot (`arr`), not the in-progress mutations (`new`), making updates simultaneous rather than sequential.

array-transform-strict-comparison.text: Only strict local minima/maxima trigger adjustments; elements equal to a neighbor are left unchanged, meaning plateaus are inherently stable.

ascending-check-uses-sentinel-minus-one.text: `areNumbersAscending` initializes `prev = -1`, relying on the constraint that all numbers are positive integers (1–200); any other sentinel could break the first comparison

ascending-isdigit-accepts-leading-zeros.text: `str.isdigit()` in `areNumbersAscending` would accept a token like "007" and `int()` would parse it as 7, but LeetCode constraints exclude leading zeros.

ascending-short-circuits-on-first-non-as.text: `areNumbersAscending` returns `False` on the first numeric token that is not strictly greater than the previous one and does not scan the remainder of the sentence.

ascending-strict-monotonicity-equality-f.text: `areNumbersAscending` returns `False` for equal consecutive numeric tokens because the comparison is `num <= prev`.

ascending-subarray-empty-input-crashes.text: Passing an empty list raises `IndexError` on `nums[0]`; the function relies on the LeetCode guarantee that `nums` is non-empty rather than handling this edge case.

ascending-subarray-function-name-is-wron.text: The function is named `concatenated_binary` but implements maximum ascending subarray sum; this is a copy-paste naming bug that doesn't affect correctness since tests import by name.

ascending-subarray-initializes-accumulat.text: Both max_sum and current_sum are initialized to nums[0] before the loop begins.

ascending-subarray-iterates-from-index-o.text: The loop starts at index 1 and compares nums[i] to nums[i-1].

ascending-subarray-resets-to-current.text: On a non-ascending step, `current_sum` resets to the current element (not zero), because the current element is always the start of the next potential ascending subarray.

ascending-subarray-single-pass-linear-ti.text: The algorithm makes one pass over the array with O(n) time and O(1) space using two scalar accumulators.

ascending-subarray-updates-max-after-eac.text: After each iteration, max_sum is updated to max(max_sum, current_sum).

ascending-subarray-uses-strict-inequalit.text: The ascending condition is strictly greater-than (`>`), not `>=`, so equal adjacent elements reset the running sum — matching the LeetCode specification.

ascending-subarray-uses-typing-list-impo.text: The only import is typing.List, used for type annotations.

ascii-32-detects-case-pairs.text: `abs(ord(a) - ord(b)) == 32` is true if and only if `a` and `b` are the same English letter in different cases, given inputs restricted to `[a-zA-Z]`, because ASCII lower and upper variants of every letter differ by exactly 32.

assign-cookies-empty-lists-return-zero.text: If either input list is empty, the while-loop body never executes and `find_content_children` returns 0.

assign-cookies-greedy-optimal.text: The greedy strategy (smallest sufficient cookie to least greedy child) produces a provably optimal assignment; no DP or exhaustive search needed.

assign-cookies-linear-after-sort.text: Restates the obvious time complexity of a two-pointer scan; not an invariant that could be violated or that informs how to work in the code.

assign-cookies-mutates-inputs.text: `find_content_children` mutates both input lists via in-place `.sort()`; callers cannot assume list order is preserved.

assign-cookies-returns-satisfied-child-c.text: `find_content_children` returns the `child` pointer, whose final value equals the number of satisfied children because it advances only on successful matches.

assign-cookies-zero-extra-space.text: The two-pointer algorithm uses O(1) auxiliary space beyond the in-place sort — no heaps, hash maps, or copied arrays.

assumes-square-grid.text: `projectionArea` uses a single `n = len(grid)` for both dimensions, relying on the LeetCode constraint that the grid is always n × n; non-square grids would produce incorrect results

average-even-divisible-accumulators-trac.text: The function maintains `total` as the sum of elements divisible by 6 and `count` as the number of such elements.

average-even-divisible-returns-int.text: `average_even_divisible_by_three` returns an integer (floor average), never a float.

average-of-levels-float-division-safe.text: Division by zero in `level_sum / level_size` is impossible because the while-loop condition guarantees the queue, and therefore `level_size`, is non-empty.

average-of-levels-o-n-time-o-w-space.text: `averageOfLevels` runs in O(n) time and O(w) space, where w is the maximum width of the tree.

average-of-levels-returns-one-mean-per-l.text: `averageOfLevels` returns a `List[float]` where element i is the arithmetic mean of all node values at depth i, without rounding.

average-of-levels-uses-deque-popleft.text: The BFS queue is a `collections.deque`, and the solution uses `popleft` for O(1) dequeue operations.

average-salary-divisor-assumes-length-gt.text: The expression `len(salary) - 2` in the average-salary solution would produce a ZeroDivisionError if called with fewer than 3 elements; correctness relies on the problem's length guarantee.

average-salary-method-returns-float.text: The `Solution.average` method returns a float computed as `(total - min - max) / (n - 2)`.

average-salary-no-input-validation.text: Subsumed by the cross-cutting belief `leetcode-solutions-omit-input-validation` — this is a repo-wide pattern, not specific to one solution.

average-salary-scalar-only-no-mutation.text: The average-salary solution uses only scalar variables (sum, min, max, length) and does not allocate intermediate lists or mutate the input.

average-salary-single-pass-arithmetic.text: The average-salary solution computes the trimmed mean algebraically via `(sum - min - max) / (n - 2)` using three linear scans, avoiding O(n log n) sorting entirely.

average-salary-unique-values-invariant.text: Correctness of the average-salary solution depends on all salary values being unique; duplicate min or max values would cause only one copy to be subtracted, producing a wrong answer.

ba-substring-check-linear-time.text: The all-a's-before-all-b's solution runs in O(n) time by delegating the forbidden-substring search to CPython's built-in `str.__contains__`.

ba-substring-empty-string-returns-true.text: For an empty string, `"ba" not in s` returns True, so `checkIfAllAsAppearsBeforeAllBs` returns True.

ba-substring-equivalence.text: `"ba" not in s` is equivalent to "every 'a' precedes every 'b'" when the input contains only 'a' and 'b' — the only way to violate the ordering is a b-to-a transition, which is exactly the substring "ba".

ba-substring-method-single-expression.text: `checkIfAllAsAppearsBeforeAllBs` is a single-expression method with no loops, state, or intermediate data structures.

backspace-compare-read-only.text: The backspace-string-compare algorithm does not modify either input string.

backspace-compare-reverse-two-pointer-o1.text: The backspace-string-compare solution uses reverse traversal with a skip counter instead of a stack, achieving O(1) auxiliary space and O(n+m) time for comparing two backspace-processed strings.

backspace-compare-single-pass.text: Largely redundant with `backspace-compare-reverse-two-pointer-o1-space` which already captures the O(n+m) time and O(1) space characteristics.

backspace-compare-three-exit-conditions.text: `backspaceCompare` returns True only when both pointers are exhausted, and False if one is exhausted or surviving characters differ.

balanced-binary-tree-type-annotation-inc.text: The `TreeNode` constructor uses `TreeNode | None` syntax while function signatures use `Optional[TreeNode]`.

balanced-strings-balance-range-bounded-b.text: In `find_special_integer`, the `balance` variable is always within the range `[-len(s), len(s)]` during iteration.

balanced-strings-function-name-mismatch.text: `find_special_integer` in `split-a-string-in-balanced-strings/solution.py` does not match the problem it solves — it's a template artifact that was never renamed, suggesting other solutions may share this issue.

balanced-strings-r-positive-l-negative-c.text: `find_special_integer` assigns +1 to 'R' and -1 to 'L', and swapping this convention would produce identical results because only zero-crossings matter.

balanced-strings-returns-max-balanced-su.text: `find_special_integer` returns the maximum number of non-overlapping balanced substrings into which the input string can be split.

balanced-substring-always-even-result.text: `longestBalancedSubstring` always returns an even integer (including 0) because `best` is updated as `2 * min(zeros, ones)`, and updates occur only when processing `'1'` characters.

balanced-substring-definition-zeros-then.text: A balanced substring in this problem consists of some number of '0's immediately followed by the same number of '1's.

balanced-substring-empty-input-returns-z.text: longestBalancedSubstring returns 0 for an empty input string because the loop body never executes.

balanced-substring-reset-on-zero-after-o.text: Both `zeros` and `ones` counters reset to zero when a `'0'` follows a `'1'`, which prevents stale zero-counts from inflating results across non-contiguous balanced segments.

balanced-substring-single-pass-counter.text: `longestBalancedSubstring` uses a single-pass O(n) time, O(1) space counter technique — tracking running counts of consecutive zeros and ones — rather than checking all substrings or using groupby.

balanced-substring-zeros-frozen-after-fi.text: Once a '1' appears in a run, the zeros counter remains frozen until a subsequent '0' triggers the reset.

balanced-tree-short-circuit-propagation.text: The balanced-binary-tree solution achieves O(n) time by short-circuiting: once any subtree returns `-1` (unbalanced), the value propagates upward immediately without recursing into sibling subtrees.

balloon-counter-built-one-pass.text: max_number_of_balloons builds Counter(text) in a single O(n) pass over the input string.

balloon-counter-keys-bounded-26.text: The Counter used by max_number_of_balloons has at most 26 keys because the input consists of lowercase English letters.

balloon-five-count-lookups.text: max_number_of_balloons performs exactly five count lookups for b, a, l, o, and n after building the frequency map.

balloon-hardcoded-target-not-generalizab.text: The five-argument `min(...)` in `max_number_of_balloons` encodes the word "balloon" directly; changing the target word requires rewriting the return expression rather than parameterizing.

balloon-needs-double-l-and-o.text: The `// 2` divisor in `max_number_of_balloons` is applied to exactly `l` and `o` counts because "balloon" contains two of each; all other target characters (`b`, `a`, `n`) appear once.

banned-set-conversion-for-o1-lookup.text: `mostCommonWord` converts the `banned` list to a `set` before filtering, ensuring O(1) amortized membership checks during the counting pass.

bare-function-vs-solution-class-inconsis.text: Some solutions use a `Solution` class with methods (e.g., `reverseVowels`, `maximumWealth`, `countPoints`) while others use bare functions (e.g., `judgeCircle`, `reverse_words_in_string`) — the repo is not consistent about which convention to use.

base7-digits-lsb-first.text: Digits in convert_to_base7 are accumulated least-significant-first via repeated `% 7` and `//= 7`, then reversed at the end — the standard accumulate-then-reverse idiom that avoids O(n) prepend costs.

base7-no-dependencies.text: Trivially observable from the source file; zero imports is not an invariant that would break anything if violated.

base7-remainders-in-valid-digit-range.text: Remainders collected by `% 7` in `convert_to_base7` are always in `[0, 6]`, the valid base-7 digits.

base7-sign-magnitude.text: Negative inputs in convert_to_base7 are handled by converting to absolute value and prepending `"-"`, avoiding Python's floor-division behavior on negative numbers which would complicate digit extraction.

base7-sign-reattachment-order.text: The minus sign is appended to the end of the LSB-first digit list so that reversal places it at the front of the base-7 string.

base7-while-loop-terminates.text: The `while num:` loop in `convert_to_base7` terminates because `num` is non-negative and `num //= 7` strictly decreases a positive integer toward zero.

base7-zero-special-case.text: `convert_to_base7` handles input 0 via an explicit early return; without this guard, the `while num:` loop would never execute and the function would return an empty string.

baseline-then-upgrade-allocation.text: distribute-money allocates $1 to every child first, reducing the problem to distributing `remaining` in increments of $7 — separating feasibility from optimization.

best-poker-hand-assumes-exactly-five-car.text: `best_poker_hand` assumes exactly 5 cards and performs no length validation.

best-poker-hand-assumes-rank-suit-domain.text: `best_poker_hand` assumes ranks are integers in `[1, 13]` and suits are single characters from `{'a', 'b', 'c', 'd'}`.

best-poker-hand-four-five-kind-returns-t.text: `best_poker_hand` returns `"Three of a Kind "` for hands with four or five cards of the same rank because it checks only `max_freq >= 3`.

best-poker-hand-high-card-condition.text: `best_poker_hand` returns `"High Card "` when no flush is present and the maximum rank frequency is 1.

bfs-guarantees-manhattan-order.text: BFS from a center cell on a grid with 4-directional edges produces cells in non-decreasing Manhattan distance order, because every edge has weight 1 and BFS explores layer by layer.

bfs-level-snapshot-pattern.text: `averageOfLevels` partitions BFS into discrete levels by snapshotting `len(queue)` before each inner loop, not by using sentinels or multiple queues.

bigram-collects-third-word-after-match.text: When `words[i] == first` and `words[i+1] == second`, `findOcurrences` appends `words[i+2]` to the result list.

bigram-empty-input-degrades-gracefully.text: When `text` has fewer than 3 words, `range(len(words) - 2)` produces an empty range and the result is `[]` — no special-case code needed

bigram-exact-string-equality.text: `findOcurrences` matches bigram words using exact case-sensitive string equality.

bigram-index-bound-prevents-oob.text: `findOcurrences` uses `range(len(words) - 2)` so that `words[i+2]` is always in-bounds — no try/except or sentinel values needed

bigram-linear-time.text: O(n) single-pass complexity is trivially obvious from the list comprehension — not a useful invariant to track

bigram-linear-time-single-pass.text: `findOcurrences` scans valid word indices once with O(1) work per position, giving O(n) time over n words.

bigram-no-match-empty-result.text: If no occurrence of the bigram has a following word, `findOcurrences` returns an empty list.

bigram-overlap-naturally-handled.text: Overlapping bigram matches are collected independently — a word can serve as `second` in one match and `first` in the next because each index `i` is checked without regard to prior matches

bigram-splits-text-on-whitespace.text: `Solution.findOcurrences` tokenizes `text` with `text.split()` into a list of words before scanning for the bigram.

bin-count-for-popcount.text: The repo uses `bin(n).count('1')` as the standard Python popcount idiom; no bit-manipulation tricks or `int.bit_count()` (Python 3.10+) are used

binary-gap-assumes-positive-int-up-to-1e.text: `binary_gap` assumes a positive integer input `n` with `1 <= n <= 10^9`.

binary-gap-bit-scan-pattern.text: `binary_gap` uses `n & 1` / `n >>= 1` right-shift scanning rather than `bin()` string conversion — the same bit-scanning idiom appears in `number-of-1-bits/solution.py`.

binary-gap-measures-adjacent-ones-only.text: `binary_gap` measures distances between consecutive `1` bits only — `last_one` is updated on every `1` bit, so it never computes gaps between non-adjacent set bits.

binary-gap-negative-input-infinite-loop.text: Passing a negative integer to `binary_gap` causes an infinite loop because Python's arbitrary-precision right-shift of a negative number never reaches `0`.

binary-gap-no-dependencies.text: Trivially true of most solutions in the repo — not specific enough to warrant its own belief.

binary-gap-returns-zero-for-fewer-than-t.text: `binary_gap` returns `0` when the binary representation of `n` contains fewer than two `1` bits.

binary-gap-tracks-position-from-lsb.text: `binary_gap` tracks `pos` as a 0-indexed bit position starting from the least significant bit and increments it on each shift.

binary-linked-list-empty-returns-zero.text: Passing None as head to min_operations returns 0 because the while loop never executes.

binary-prefix-divisible-by-5-empty-input.text: An empty `nums` list returns an empty result list without error.

binary-prefix-divisible-by-5-method-sign.text: The file defines `Solution.prefixesDivBy5(self, nums: List[int]) -> List[bool]` as its sole method.

binary-prefix-divisible-by-5-output-leng.text: The returned boolean list has the same length as the input `nums`.

binary-prefix-divisible-by-5-remainder-b.text: The `remainder` variable is always in `[0, 4]` because `% 5` is applied on every iteration.

binary-search-closed-interval-style.text: The binary search implementation uses closed-interval bounds `[left, right]` with `while left <= right`, where both endpoints are inclusive candidates — not the half-open `[left, right)` alternative.

binary-search-empty-array-returns-negati.text: For an empty `nums` array, `right` becomes `-1`, the loop does not execute, and the method returns `-1`.

binary-search-log-n-constant-space.text: The implementation runs in O(log n) time and O(1) auxiliary space with no recursion or auxiliary data structures.

binary-search-method-signature.text: The file defines a `Solution.search(nums, target) -> int` method as its sole public method.

binary-search-on-derived-quantities-patt.text: Binary searching on a derived monotonic function (like missing-count) rather than on array values directly is a recurring technique in this repo, applicable to problems like kth-missing-positive and first-bad-version.

binary-search-on-value-pattern.text: `is_perfect_square` binary-searches the range `[1, num]` for a value whose square equals `num`, achieving O(log n) time and O(1) space with no library calls.

binary-search-oracle-pattern.text: `guessNumber` uses standard binary search but replaces array-index comparison with a ternary oracle function (`guess()`), making it a search over an implicit sorted sequence.

binary-search-returns-negative-one-on-mi.text: `search()` returns `-1` when the target is not present in the array.

binary-search-variants-share-convergence.text: All binary search solutions share the same convergence loop structure (narrow [lo, hi] until they meet) but vary along three independent dimensions: what is searched (raw values vs. derived monotonic functions), bias direction (leftmost vs. rightmost match), and post-loop extraction (lo, hi, or result variable).

justifications.label: the four patterns are orthogonal specializations of one template — search-target and bias are independent choices, and recognizing the shared structure reveals that any new binary search problem maps to a point in this 2D design space

binary-string-at-most-one-segment-runs-l.text: The `"01" not in s` check runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space via Python's built-in substring search.

binary-string-empty-input-returns-true-w.text: An empty string passed to the implementation returns `True` because `"01"` is not found, although this input is outside the problem contract.

binary-string-segment-depends-on-no-lead.text: The `"01" not in s` check for at-most-one-segment-of-ones is only correct because the problem guarantees no leading zeros; without that constraint, `"011"` (a valid single segment) would be incorrectly rejected.

binary-string-single-zero-returns-true.text: For input `"0"`, both implementations return `True` because `"01"` is absent and zero segments of ones satisfy the at-most-one condition.

binary-tree-paths-appends-only-at-leaves.text: `results.append(path)` is called only when the current node has no children.

binary-tree-paths-arrow-delimited-no-tra.text: Path strings use `->` between values with no leading or trailing separator.

binary-tree-paths-caller-prepends-child-.text: Each recursive call adds the child's value to the path string before descending, so `dfs` never prepends its own node's value.

binary-tree-paths-leaf-requires-both-chi.text: A node is treated as a leaf only when both `left` and `right` are `None`; single-child nodes are internal.

binary-tree-paths-left-before-right-orde.text: Paths are output in left-subtree-first order because `node.left` is visited before `node.right` in every call.

binary-tree-paths-returns-root-to-leaf-s.text: `binary_tree_paths` returns a list of root-to-leaf path strings joined by `->`.

binary-tree-tilt-abs-nonnegative.text: Each node's tilt contribution is non-negative because `abs(left_sum - right_sum)` is applied.

binary-tree-tilt-findtilt-delegates-to-s.text: `findTilt` initializes `total_tilt = 0` and delegates traversal to the nested `subtree_sum(root)` closure.

binary-tree-tilt-leaf-node-zero-contribu.text: Leaf nodes contribute 0 to the total tilt because both left and right subtree sums are 0.

binary-tree-tilt-null-subtree-sum-zero.text: `subtree_sum(None)` returns 0, so null children contribute nothing to subtree sums or tilts.

binary-watch-brute-force-enumeration.text: `readBinaryWatch` evaluates all 720 (h, m) candidates via nested `range(12) × range(60)` and filters by popcount match; there is no combinatorial generation or pruning.

binary-watch-deterministic-order.text: `readBinaryWatch` output is ordered hours ascending, then minutes ascending within each hour, as a direct consequence of nested `range()` iteration order.

binary-watch-hour-minute-ranges-via-loop.text: `readBinaryWatch` restricts hours to 0-11 and minutes to 0-59 solely through the `range(12)` and `range(60)` loop bounds.

binary-watch-max-lit-leds-ten.text: The binary watch has a maximum possible popcount of 10 from 4 hour LEDs and 6 minute LEDs, so `turnedOn` greater than 10 yields an empty list.

binary-watch-no-validation.text: Trivially true of nearly every solution in this repo (LeetCode guarantees valid input); not a distinguishing invariant worth tracking per-solution.

binary-watch-output-format-hour-unpadded.text: Output strings use `f"{h}:{m:02d}"`, so hours have no leading zero and minutes are always two digits.

binary-watch-single-list-comprehension.text: `readBinaryWatch` is implemented as a single list comprehension with no intermediate state or mutation.

binary-watch-zero-imports.text: Minor detail — the absence of imports is not an invariant that could break anything or that a developer needs to know.

bisect-right-counts-fitting-elements.text: `bisect_right(prefix, q)` returns exactly the number of sorted elements whose cumulative sum is less than or equal to `q`, because the prefix sum array is non-decreasing for positive inputs.

bisect-right-for-strict-greater-than.text: `bisect_right` (not `bisect_left`) is required when searching for the first element strictly greater than a target in a sorted array; `bisect_left` would incorrectly return the target itself when present.

bisect-two-neighbor-sufficiency.text: After `bisect_left` on sorted `arr2`, checking only `arr2[pos]` and `arr2[pos-1]` is sufficient to determine if any element is within distance `d` of `val` — all other elements are provably farther away.

bit-position-independence-principle.text: In XOR-subset problems, each bit position contributes independently to the total sum — if any element has bit b set, exactly half of all 2^n subsets have that bit survive XOR.

bit-shift-accumulation-correctness.text: `(current << 1) | node.val` correctly builds a binary number MSB-first, equivalent to `current * 2 + node.val` — used in tree and linked-list path-to-number problems.

bit-walking-over-string-conversion.text: `even_odd_indices` walks bits via `n & 1` and `n >>= 1` rather than converting to a binary string with `bin()`, avoiding string allocation and keeping the solution at O(log n) with no dependencies.

boomerang-constant-complexity.text: O(1) complexity of a single-expression function is self-evident; not a meaningful architectural claim.

boomerang-integer-only.text: Subsumed by `cross-product-for-collinearity` which already captures the avoidance of floating-point issues.

both-reversal-variants-mutate-in-place.text: Neither `reverse_list` nor `reverse_list_recursive` creates new `ListNode` instances; they rewire existing `.next` pointers, meaning the original head's `.next` is `None` after reversal.

boundary-handling-complete-unless-degene.text: Streaming's structural boundary handling (sentinel initialization + early exit) combined with observed crash-freedom for degenerate inputs jointly establish that the streaming paradigm handles all boundary conditions without conditional logic — provided no degenerate input (single-element, empty, zero) escapes the sentinel+early-exit net.

justifications.label: boundary completeness is contingent on no degenerate input escaping the sentinel+early-exit net

bounded-group-count.text: This is a mathematical property of digit sums, not a codebase invariant — it can't be violated by a code change and doesn't guide developer behavior.

box-category-exhaustive-return.text: `boxCategory` always returns exactly one of four string literals; the if/elif chain covers all four (bulky, heavy) combinations with no unreachable or missing branch.

box-category-flag-then-branch.text: `boxCategory` separates classification into two phases: compute boolean flags (`bulky`, `heavy`) from thresholds, then map the flag pair to a string label via cascading if/elif.

box-category-hardcoded-thresholds.text: The boxCategory thresholds are hardcoded constants — 10,000 per dimension, 10^9 for volume, and 100 for mass — with no parameterization.

box-category-pure-function.text: Too generic — nearly every solution in this repo is a pure function with no imports. This doesn't capture anything specific to `boxCategory`.

box-category-pure-mapping.text: boxCategory is a pure, side-effect-free mapping from (int, int, int, int) to str with no mutable state or imports.

box-category-short-circuit-bulky.text: The `bulky` check uses `any(d >= 10_000 for d in ...)` joined with `or` to the volume check, so if any dimension is >= 10,000 the volume multiplication is never evaluated.

box-category-trailing-space.text: All `boxCategory` return values include a trailing space character, matching the LeetCode problem's expected output format — this is intentional, not a bug.

boyer-moore-constant-space.text: The Boyer-Moore implementation uses exactly two scalar variables (`candidate`, `count`) — O(1) auxiliary space regardless of input size.

boyer-moore-loop-invariant-unmatched-suf.text: After processing nums[0..i], the Boyer-Moore candidate is the majority of the unmatched suffix, with non-candidate occurrences paired and cancelled against candidate occurrences.

boyer-moore-no-verification-pass.text: `majority_element` in `majority-element/solution.py` does not include a second pass to verify the candidate; it assumes the precondition (a majority element exists) holds, and returns an arbitrary element if violated.

boyer-moore-single-pass-linear-time.text: majority_element iterates through nums exactly once, giving O(n) time with no early exits.

broken-set-disjoint-pattern.text: `canBeTypedWords` converts `brokenLetters` to a set and uses `set.isdisjoint` against each word, achieving O(n) time in total text length instead of O(n*b).

brute-force-cubic-complexity.text: Too problem-specific and obvious from the code (triple nested iteration over combinations) — not an invariant that would surprise a reader or break things if violated.

brute-force-deletion-over-analytical.text: `can_equal_frequency` uses O(n^2) brute-force simulation (try every single deletion) rather than an analytical O(n) approach, deliberately trading efficiency for correctness — this problem is notorious for edge-case bugs in analytical solutions.

brute-force-kernel.text: Noting that a solution uses brute force at n<=100 is an implementation detail, not a constraint that needs tracking

bst-inorder-no-materialized-list.text: The BST minimum-difference solution computes the answer in O(h) stack space during traversal without collecting all node values into a list first.

bst-min-diff-between-inorder-neighbors.text: The minimum absolute difference in a BST always occurs between two values adjacent in the inorder (sorted) traversal; the solution exploits this by comparing only consecutive visits rather than all pairs.

bst-min-diff-no-duplicate-special-case.text: The BST minimum-difference solution does not special-case duplicate values; if duplicates exist, `node.val - self.prev` yields 0, which is correctly the minimum.

bst-min-diff-requires-at-least-two-nodes.text: The BST minimum-difference solution requires at least two nodes; with only one node, `self.min_diff` remains `inf` and `int(float('inf'))` can raise `OverflowError` in some Python versions.

bst-min-diff-updates-min-diff-during-ino.text: During the inorder traversal, the BST minimum-difference solution computes `node.val - self.prev` for every node after the first visited node and updates `self.min_diff` when the difference is smaller.

bst-property-assumed-not-validated.text: `minDiffInBST` assumes its input is a valid BST without checking; a non-BST tree produces incorrect (possibly negative) differences silently.

bst-pruning-correctness.text: `range_sum_bst` prunes the left subtree when `root.val < low` and the right subtree when `root.val > high`; this is correct only if the input is a valid BST — feeding a non-BST tree silently produces wrong results

buddy-strings-cross-match-invariant.text: The final correctness check requires that the two differing positions cross-match (`s[i] == goal[j]` and `s[j] == goal[i]`), not merely that they differ — this is the necessary and sufficient condition for a single-swap solution.

buddy-strings-early-exit-on-third-diff.text: The diff-collection loop returns `False` immediately upon finding a 3rd mismatch, bounding the `diffs` list to at most length 2 and guaranteeing safe index access in the final check.

buddy-strings-equal-case-bypasses-diff-l.text: When `s == goal`, `buddyStrings` returns before entering the diff-collection loop, so the equal and unequal code paths are mutually exclusive.

buddy-strings-equal-case-duplicate-check.text: When `s == goal`, `buddyStrings` returns `True` only if `s` contains a duplicate character (`len(s) != len(set(s))`), because swapping two copies of the same character is the only valid "swap that produces the same string."

buddy-strings-length-mismatch-first-reje.text: `buddyStrings` returns `False` immediately when `len(s) != len(goal)`, before any other case handling.

buddy-strings-lockstep-diff-index-collec.text: In the unequal-strings case, `buddyStrings` iterates over both strings in lockstep and records indices where characters differ.

buddy-strings-no-imports.text: Same as binary-watch: absence of imports is not a meaningful invariant.

build-array-arbitrary-precision-no-overf.text: The encoding `original + n * new_value` does not overflow in Python because integers are arbitrary precision, though separation still relies on values being less than `n`.

build-array-encode-order-safety.text: The `% n` in `nums[nums[i]] % n` during the encode pass ensures correctness regardless of whether `nums[nums[i]]` has already been encoded earlier in the same loop iteration.

build-array-imports-typing-list.text: `build-array-from-permutation/solution.py` imports `typing.List` for type hints and has no other imports.

build-array-in-place-modular-encoding.text: `buildArray` encodes two values per slot as `original + n * new_value`, recoverable via `% n` (original) and `// n` (new value), achieving the O(1) extra space follow-up challenge.

build-array-mutates-input.text: `buildArray` mutates and returns the input `nums` list rather than allocating a separate output array — callers lose access to the original values after the call.

build-array-permutation-precondition.text: The modular encoding algorithm is only correct when `nums` is a valid zero-based permutation (all values in `[0, n)`, each appearing exactly once); invalid input produces silently wrong results.

build-array-two-pass-encode-decode.text: The solution uses two passes: an encode pass adding `n * new_value`, then a decode pass integer-dividing each element by `n`.

build-helper-pop-zero-bug-in-13-files.text: The `_build` helper used `list.pop(0)` with O(n²) behavior, and the bug existed independently in 13 files.

build-helper-uses-list-pop-zero.text: `_build` constructs trees via BFS using `queue.pop(0)`, which is O(n) per pop on a Python list, making tree construction O(n^2) — acceptable for small test inputs but not optimal

build-tree-bfs-from-level-order.text: Tree solutions use a `build_tree` utility that constructs a `TreeNode` tree from a level-order list (LeetCode's serialization format) via BFS queue traversal, with `None` representing absent nodes.

build-tree-is-shared-infra.text: `TreeNode` and `build_tree` defined in `sum-of-root-to-leaf-binary-numbers/solution.py` are imported by hundreds of test files across the repository, making that file load-bearing shared infrastructure despite being a solution file.

build-tree-level-order.text: `_build_tree(values)` constructs a tree from a level-order (BFS) list where `None` represents absent children, matching LeetCode's standard serialization format; it is used across tree-problem test suites

build-tree-level-order-convention.text: `build_tree` constructs trees from level-order lists (LeetCode's serialization format) using BFS, where `None` entries represent missing nodes — this is the standard tree construction interface across the repo.

build-tree-levelorder-serialization.text: `build_tree` constructs trees level-by-level using a queue, matching LeetCode's standard level-order serialization format where `None` marks absent nodes.

build-tree-odd-length-guard.text: In build_tree, the inner `if i < len(vals)` guard before assigning the right child is necessary to avoid an IndexError when the input list ends on a left child (odd length greater than 1).

build-tree-uses-bfs.text: Test helper implementation detail — how build_tree works internally is not an architectural invariant that would break things if violated.

build-tree-uses-leetcode-level-order.text: `_build_tree` constructs trees from LeetCode's standard level-order serialization format (BFS order with `None` for missing nodes), making test cases directly copy-pasteable from problem examples.

build-tree-uses-level-order.text: `build_tree` deserializes LeetCode's bracket/level-order format using a FIFO queue (`list.pop(0)`), assigning left then right children per node; `None` entries represent absent children.

bus-stops-clockwise-complement.text: The counterclockwise distance is computed as `sum(distance) - clockwise` rather than by iterating the reverse path — a complement trick that avoids modular wrap-around logic.

bus-stops-no-input-validation.text: Duplicates the same pattern as `diet-plan-no-input-validation`. The repo-wide convention of trusting LeetCode constraints should be captured once as a cross-cutting belief, not per-problem.

bus-stops-same-stop-zero.text: This is a direct consequence of the swap normalization and slice semantics (`distance[s:s]` is empty) — not an independent invariant worth tracking separately.

bus-stops-swap-normalization.text: The solution normalizes `start > destination` by swapping, guaranteeing `start <= destination` so that `distance[start:destination]` captures the clockwise path without wrap-around indexing.

bus-stops-total-recomputed-per-call.text: distanceBetweenBusStops recomputes sum(distance) on every call instead of caching the route total.

busy-student-empty-input-returns-zero.text: busyStudent returns 0 for empty startTime and endTime lists because sum of an empty generator is 0.

busy-student-linear-constant-space.text: busyStudent runs in O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space by using a generator expression that never materializes an intermediate list.

busy-student-uses-chained-comparison.text: busyStudent uses Python's chained comparison `s <= queryTime <= e`, equivalent to `s <= queryTime and queryTime <= e`, to test interval membership.

busyStudent-inclusive-boundaries.text: `busyStudent` uses `s <= queryTime <= e` (inclusive on both ends), meaning a student is counted as busy when queryTime equals exactly startTime or endTime.

buy-sell-stock-assumes-nonempty-input.text: Redundant — this is an instance of the repo-wide pattern that all solutions trust LeetCode's input guarantees. Not worth a separate belief.

buy-sell-stock-returns-zero-for-no-profi.text: When no profitable transaction exists (monotonically decreasing prices), `maxProfit` returns `0`, never a negative number.

buy-sell-stock-single-pass-greedy.text: `maxProfit` runs in O(n) time and O(1) space by tracking the running minimum price — a Kadane's-style greedy pattern.

buy-sell-stock-single-transaction-only.text: `maxProfit` finds the best single buy-sell pair; it is not the unlimited-transactions variant (LeetCode #122).

calpoints-c-operation-pops-last-score.text: In `calPoints`, the `"C"` operation invalidates the last score by popping the top of the stack.

calpoints-d-operation-pushes-double-top.text: In `calPoints`, the `"D"` operation pushes twice the current top score onto the stack.

calpoints-integer-string-pushes-parsed-i.text: In `calPoints`, a non-operator operation string is converted with `int(op)` and pushed onto the stack.

calpoints-linear-time.text: `calPoints` runs in O(n) time and O(n) space, where n is the number of operations.

calpoints-no-input-validation.text: `calPoints` assumes all inputs are valid per the LeetCode contract and raises unhandled `IndexError` or `ValueError` on malformed input.

calpoints-plus-operation-pushes-sum-top-.text: In `calPoints`, the `"+"` operation pushes the sum of the top two scores onto the stack.

calpoints-returns-sum-of-remaining-stack.text: After processing all operations, `calPoints` returns `sum(stack)`, where the stack contains all still-valid scores.

calpoints-stack-only.text: `calPoints` uses a single list as a stack, accessing only `[-1]` and `[-2]` — never arbitrary indexes.

calpoints-strip-defensive.text: The `op.strip()` call in `calPoints` is a defensive guard against whitespace that LeetCode inputs never contain.

camelcase-solution-methods-snakecase-hel.text: Solution class methods use camelCase to match LeetCode's interface signatures, while standalone helper functions and local utilities use Python's snake_case convention.

can-construct-is-pure.text: All LeetCode solutions in this repo are pure functions with no side effects; this is the default, not a distinctive invariant.

can-construct-true-for-repeated-substrin.text: can_construct returns True when the input string is constructed by concatenating multiple copies of a substring.

can-equal-frequency-candidate-via-slicin.text: For each index i, can_equal_frequency builds the candidate shortened string as word[:i] + word[i+1:].

can-equal-frequency-nonempty-candidate-d.text: Because LeetCode guarantees len(word) >= 2, every candidate string after one deletion has at least one character, so Counter is never called on an empty string in can_equal_frequency.

can-equal-frequency-short-circuits-on-su.text: can_equal_frequency returns True immediately upon finding any single deletion that yields uniform character frequencies.

can-place-flowers-boundary-as-empty.text: Array boundaries are treated as empty plots: index 0 has no left constraint and the last index has no right constraint, handled by short-circuit `or` guards rather than sentinel padding.

can-place-flowers-early-exit-when-n-sati.text: The loop checks `if n <= 0: return True` at the top of each iteration, short-circuiting once all flowers are placed.

can-place-flowers-greedy-is-optimal.text: Greedy left-to-right placement is provably optimal: planting at the earliest valid slot never reduces the number of remaining valid slots compared to any alternative placement order.

can-place-flowers-handles-n-zero.text: Returning `True` for `n=0` is a trivial edge case, not an invariant that would break things if violated.

can-place-flowers-mutates-input.text: `canPlaceFlowers` modifies the `flowerbed` list in place by setting planted positions to `1`; callers who need the original must copy first.

can-place-flowers-time-o-n-space-o1.text: `canPlaceFlowers` runs in O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space while modifying the flowerbed in place.

canbeincreasing-first-violation-tests-ad.text: At the first violation nums[i] <= nums[i-1], canBeIncreasing tests removing index i or index i-1 by calling is_increasing_skip on each.

candies-empty-input-returns-zero.text: An empty `cost` list causes `minimumCost` to return 0 because summing over an empty enumeration yields 0.

candies-example-one-to-six-returns-sixte.text: For `cost = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]`, `minimumCost` returns 16 after sorting descending and skipping indices 2 and 5.

candies-small-inputs-never-skip-elements.text: For `cost` lists with fewer than three elements, `minimumCost` skips no elements because no index reaches `i % 3 == 2`.

canformarray-bounds-check-before-value.text: The inner loop checks `i >= len(arr)` before comparing `arr[i] != val`, preventing an out-of-bounds access when a piece would extend past the end of `arr`.

canformarray-distinctness-required.text: The `{p[0]: p for p in pieces}` lookup strategy is only correct because the problem guarantees all integers across all pieces are distinct; duplicate first elements would silently overwrite entries.

canformarray-first-element-keyed-lookup.text: `canFormArray` indexes pieces by their first element into a dict, enabling O(1) lookup at each position in `arr` — a pattern that recurs in problems with distinctness constraints.

canformarray-linear-time.text: `canFormArray` runs in O(n) time where n = len(arr), visiting each element exactly once via a greedy left-to-right scan with hash-map lookups.

canformarray-no-piece-usage-validation.text: canFormArray does not explicitly verify that every piece was used; full traversal of arr implies piece coverage because the pieces' distinct elements are a subset of arr.

canonical-form-frequency-counting-patter.text: Multiple solutions (domino pairs, good pairs, similar strings) reduce pair/group-counting problems to: canonicalize each element, count frequencies, then derive the answer from counts — avoiding O(n^2) pairwise comparison.

canonical-pipeline-has-exactly-two-insta.text: The preprocess-then-stream pipeline has exactly two concrete forms — hash-then-stream (Counter/set for membership and frequency queries) and sort-then-stream (sorted order for positional queries) — matching the two preprocessing paradigms one-to-one with a single shared consumption phase.

justifications.label: The canonical pipeline and the preprocessing partition are the same dichotomy viewed from different angles — one structural, one problem-theoretic

cantypewords-brokenletters-distinct-lowe.text: canBeTypedWords receives brokenLetters as distinct lowercase letters per problem constraints, and set(brokenLetters) deduplicates them regardless.

cantypewords-sum-generator-counts-boolea.text: canBeTypedWords uses sum over a generator of isdisjoint boolean results to count typable words without an intermediate list or explicit counter.

cantypewords-test-coverage-seven-cases.text: The inline TestSolution class for canBeTypedWords contains seven test cases covering the three LeetCode examples, no broken letters, a single untypable word, single-character words, and all letters broken.

cantypewords-text-lowercase-spaces-only.text: canBeTypedWords assumes text is non-empty and contains only lowercase letters and spaces, with words separated by single spaces.

capitalize-title-no-builtin-titlecase.text: The solution manually constructs title case (`w[0].upper() + w[1:].lower()`) rather than using `str.title()` or `str.capitalize()`, because the length-based conditional requires a branch regardless.

capitalize-title-single-pass.text: Single-pass O(n) processing is obvious from the generator expression; not a surprising or breakable invariant.

capitalize-title-split-preserves-contrac.text: This restates standard `str.split()` behavior, not a codebase invariant.

capitalize-title-threshold-is-2.text: Words of length `<= 2` are fully lowercased; words of length `>= 3` are title-cased. The boundary is at exactly 3 characters.

capitalize-title-uses-generator-expressi.text: The solution uses a generator expression inside `str.join` to stream transformed words rather than building an intermediate list.

carfleet-alias-is-dead-code.text: `carFleet = projectionArea` in the projection-area solution is a stale alias from the automated solution generation pipeline; it is never called by tests and is unrelated to the problem

ceiling-div-integer-idiom.text: The codebase uses `(n + d - 1) // d` (here `(sum + 1) // 2`) as the standard integer ceiling division idiom, avoiding floating-point precision issues from `math.ceil`.

cell-range-builtin-only-pure-function.text: cell_range is stateless and side-effect-free, depending only on the Python builtins ord, chr, range, and int.

cell-range-column-major-by-nesting.text: `cell_range` output order is column-major (all rows for column A before column B) enforced structurally by the loop nesting order, not by a post-hoc sort.

cell-range-empty-on-inverted-bounds.text: If the start column/row exceeds the end column/row, `cell_range` returns an empty list because `range()` produces no values — no explicit guard needed.

cell-range-no-validation.text: Too common across all solutions in this repo to be worth tracking per-function; LeetCode solutions universally trust input constraints.

cell-range-pure-function.text: Same as above — nearly every solution is a pure function with no imports. Not distinctive.

cell-range-single-char-columns.text: `cell_range` parses the input string by fixed character positions (s[0], s[1], s[3], s[4]), so it only handles single-letter columns (A-Z) and single-digit rows (1-9).

century-leap-year-rule-tested.text: The `day-of-the-year` test suite covers both the century non-leap case (1900) and the 400-year leap case (2000), exercising the two most commonly missed leap-year edge cases.

century-non-leap-returns-28.text: Same issue — restates the well-known Gregorian calendar rule rather than capturing a non-obvious property of the code

chars-pool-shared-readonly-across-words.text: The `chars_count` Counter is built once and reused read-only for every word check; the character pool resets between words rather than being consumed.

chebyshev-distance-for-8dir-grid.text: The minimum steps between two points on an 8-directional grid equals Chebyshev distance `max(|dx|, |dy|)`, not Manhattan distance `|dx| + |dy|`; diagonal moves close both axes simultaneously.

check-double-even-guard.text: The `x % 2 == 0` guard is required for correctness; without it, odd numbers would falsely match via integer division truncation (e.g., `7 // 2 = 3`)

check-double-has-eight-unit-tests.text: `TestCheckIfExist` contains eight unit tests covering positive match, no match, zero handling, negative numbers, minimum-length arrays, and a later double.

check-double-imports-only-unittest.text: `check-if-n-and-its-double-exist/solution.py` imports only `unittest` from the standard library and has no external dependencies.

check-double-insert-after-lookup.text: `checkIfExist` inserts each element into `seen` only after checking for its double/half, which prevents self-matching at the same index

check-double-linear-complexity.text: `checkIfExist` runs in O(n) time and O(n) space via single-pass iteration with hash set lookups

check-double-returns-true-on-first-match.text: `checkIfExist` returns `True` immediately on the first matching pair and returns `False` only after the array is exhausted.

check-double-zero-pair.text: Two zeros in the input correctly return `True` because the second zero finds `2 * 0 = 0` already in `seen` from the first zero

children-visited-left-to-right.text: Subsumed by `preorder-reversed-children-for-left-to-right` which captures both the mechanism and the outcome — keeping a separate belief for just the outcome is redundant.

chips-empty-input-returns-zero.text: An empty `position` list returns `min(0, 0) = 0`; the function does not explicitly guard against empty input.

chips-odd-count-computed-by-modulo-sum.text: The chips solution computes the odd-position count as `sum(p % 2 for p in position)`.

chips-parity-reduction.text: Moving chips by any even distance is free, so `min_cost_to_move_chips` reduces to `min(count_odd, count_even)` — move the smaller parity group across the boundary at cost 1 each.

chips-solution-runs-in-linear-time-const.text: The chips solution computes the answer in O(n) time and O(1) space with a single pass over the input.

chr-arithmetic-maps-1-to-a.text: `chr(ord("a") + num - 1)` maps integer 1 to `'a'` and integer 26 to `'z'` — the standard idiom for 1-based alphabet mapping in this repo.

circular-comparison-count-equals-n.text: Subsumed by `sorted-rotated-at-most-one-break` which already captures the key insight including the `n` comparisons detail.

circular-distance-formula-no-modulo.text: The circular distance between two indices in an array of size n is computed as `min(abs(i - j), n - abs(i - j))` without modular arithmetic — a recurring idiom across circular-array problems in this repo.

circular-distance-idiom-min-diff-n-minus.text: The `min(diff, N - diff)` idiom for shortest arc on a modular ring appears across multiple solutions including `minimum-time-to-type-word-using-special-typewriter`, `distance-between-bus-stops`, and (without wrap) `single-row-keyboard`.

circular-sentence-adjacent-space-neighbo.text: For each space at index `i`, `is_circular` compares `sentence[i-1]` and `sentence[i+1]` to verify the boundary between adjacent words.

circular-sentence-assumes-single-spaces.text: The circular-sentence algorithm assumes exactly one space between words; multiple consecutive spaces would make the flanking-character comparison return false.

circular-sentence-no-split.text: `is_circular` checks circularity by scanning for spaces as word boundaries rather than calling `str.split()`, achieving O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

circular-sentence-nonempty-assumed.text: `is_circular` accesses `sentence[0]` and `sentence[-1]` unconditionally; an empty string raises `IndexError`.

circular-sentence-single-word-first-last.text: For a single-word sentence, `is_circular` returns true exactly when the first and last characters match, since there are no spaces for adjacent-boundary checks.

circular-sentence-space-boundary-invaria.text: The circular-sentence algorithm assumes spaces never appear at position 0 or `len(sentence)-1`; indexing `sentence[i-1]` and `sentence[i+1]` around spaces would produce wrong results or IndexError if this invariant is violated.

circular-sentence-wrap-check-separate.text: The wrap-around condition (`sentence[0] != sentence[-1]`) is checked as an independent early-exit before the space-boundary loop, not unified into the main scan.

climbing-stairs-base-case-returns-n.text: For `n <= 2`, `climbStairs` returns `n` directly as the base case.

climbing-stairs-constant-space.text: The climbing-stairs solution uses two rolling variables (`a`, `b`) with tuple swap instead of an O(n) DP array, achieving O(1) auxiliary space.

climbing-stairs-is-fibonacci.text: `climbStairs(n)` computes the (n+1)th Fibonacci number — the problem is isomorphic to Fibonacci computation with base cases fib(1)=1, fib(2)=2.

climbing-stairs-loop-invariant.text: At the start of each loop iteration `i`, variable `a` equals ways(`i-2`) and variable `b` equals ways(`i-1`).

climbing-stairs-loop-runs-n-minus-2-iter.text: The iterative loop runs from 3 through `n` inclusive, executing exactly `n - 2` iterations for `n >= 3`.

climbing-stairs-no-input-validation.text: `climbStairs` does not guard against `n <= 0`; passing 0 returns 0, and negative values return the negative input — both incorrect but outside the LeetCode contract `1 <= n <= 45`.

clock-times-enumerate-over-case-logic.text: `count_valid_times` iterates over all 24 hours and 60 minutes (84 total iterations) and pattern-matches, rather than building conditional case tables per digit position.

clock-times-hour-minute-independence.text: `count_valid_times` exploits the independence of hour and minute wildcards, computing `matching_hours * matching_minutes` instead of enumerating all 1440 combinations.

clock-times-no-input-validation.text: Already covered by the cross-cutting belief `solutions-trust-leetcode-constraints`. Redundant as a per-solution belief.

clock-times-zero-external-deps.text: Having no external dependencies is the norm for LeetCode solutions in this repo, not a distinguishing property of this file. Too trivial to track as a belief.

clockwise-rotation-formula.text: `mat[n-1-j][i]` maps a source position to a 90° clockwise rotation of an n×n matrix; confusing this with counterclockwise (`mat[j][n-1-i]`) would produce incorrect results.

closed-form-preferred-over-simulation.text: When a mathematical closed-form exists (e.g., triangular number formula for arranging-coins), the repo uses it with exact integer arithmetic (`math.isqrt`) rather than iterative simulation or binary search.

closed-form-reduction-eliminates-iterati.text: Multiple solutions reduce seemingly iterative problems to O(1) closed-form mathematical expressions — arithmetic series, algebraic identities, or combinatorial formulas — bypassing simulation or accumulation entirely.

justifications.label: each solution discovers that the iteration has a closed-form equivalent (Gauss sum, series formula, steady-state identity, combinatorial count), collapsing O(n) or O(k) work to O(1)

closed-interval-overlap-formula.text: The event conflict solution uses `a <= d and c <= b` (closed-interval overlap), meaning events sharing only a boundary moment are reported as conflicting; using `<` instead of `<=` would change this semantic.

closest-to-zero-linear-time.text: Redundant — a single-pass linear scan is the obvious approach and doesn't encode a surprising invariant.

closest-to-zero-no-empty-guard.text: Too generic — identical to the repo-wide pattern of trusting LeetCode constraints; not specific enough to be actionable.

closest-to-zero-positive-tiebreak.text: When two numbers have equal absolute value, the closest-to-zero solver returns the positive one via the `num > best` guard in the update predicate.

closest-value-bst-ordering-assumed.text: The directional pruning (`left if target < node.val else right`) is only correct for valid BSTs; a non-BST input silently produces wrong results with no validation.
