form-smallest-number-set-intersection-li.text: The `smallest_number_with_at_least_one_digit_from_each_array` function runs in O(n+m) time, dominated by set construction and intersection of `nums1` and `nums2`.

format-range-single-vs-arrow.text: `_format_range(a, b)` returns `"a"` when endpoints are equal and `"a->b"` otherwise; it is only ever called with `a <= b`, guaranteed by the gap-detection guards.

four-rotations-are-exhaustive.text: Checking 0°, 90°, 180°, 270° covers all distinct rotations of a square matrix because the rotation group is cyclic of order 4 (Z₄); 360° ≡ 0° so no further checks are needed.

frequency-map-pair-counting-avoids-quadr.text: Pair-counting solutions (e.g., absolute-difference-k) use `Counter` to reduce O(n^2) index enumeration to O(n) frequency multiplication — checking only `v + k` (not `v - k`) to prevent double-counting.

frequency-ratio-bottleneck-pattern.text: "How many X can I build from Y" problems use the pattern: count supply and demand per character, take `min(supply // demand)` across all required characters. Used by `rearrange-characters-to-make-target-string` and `maximum-number-of-balloons`.

frequency-sort-key-orders-ascending-freq.text: The sort key `(freq[x], -x)` orders elements primarily by ascending frequency and secondarily by descending numeric value.

frequency-sort-output-is-permutation-of-.text: The `num_sub` function returns a permutation of the input; it never filters or adds elements.

frequency-sort-uses-composite-tuple-key.text: The sort key `(freq[x], -x)` encodes both criteria in a single tuple, relying on Python's lexicographic tuple comparison rather than chaining separate sorts.

front-projection-sums-row-maxima.text: The front (xz) projection area equals the sum of the maximum height in each row.

frozenset-as-grouping-key.text: `frozenset(word)` is used as a hashable dictionary/Counter key to group strings by their distinct character sets, enabling O(n) grouping instead of O(n^2) pairwise comparison for set-equality predicates.

function-misnaming-is-systematic.text: At least two solutions (`sort_array` in chips problem, `max_difference` alias in candies problem) have names unrelated to their purpose, suggesting the repo's code generation or scaffolding pipeline systematically produces misnamed functions.

function-name-mismatch-min-operations-su.text: In the digit-splitting solution, the function is named `min_operations` (likely from a LeetCode template) but computes a minimum *sum*, not a count of operations.

function-name-mismatches-are-systematic.text: Solutions sometimes have function names unrelated to the problem they solve (e.g., `max_tasks` for "count even digit sum", `balanced_string` for "count negatives in matrix") — this is a recurring artifact of the code generation pipeline, not a one-off typo.

function-name-mismatches-behavior.text: `get_max_occurrences` in `greatest-english-letter-in-upper-and-lower-case/solution.py` does not count occurrences — it finds the greatest letter appearing in both cases; the name is likely a repo-wide template artifact.

function-name-mismatches-exist.text: Some solutions have function names that don't match the LeetCode problem's expected method name (e.g., `canDistribute` instead of `minOperations`), likely from copy-paste during problem setup.

fused-reverse-invert.text: `flipAndInvertImage` performs horizontal flip and bit inversion in a single two-pointer pass per row via simultaneous swap-and-XOR, not two separate passes.

gap-formula-excludes-endpoints.text: The expression `i - first_seen[c] - 1` counts characters strictly between positions `first_seen[c]` and `i`, excluding both boundary characters.

gauss-sum-for-range-problems.text: The closed-form sum `n*(n+1)//2` is a recurring idiom across this repo for problems involving missing or duplicate numbers in a 1-to-n range, avoiding a second pass to compute the expected sum.

gcd-determines-valid-partition.text: A deck of cards can be partitioned into equal-sized groups of matching values if and only if the GCD of all value frequencies is >= 2 — the solution computes this in a single `reduce(gcd, counts)` fold.

gcd-of-extremes-not-pairwise.text: `findGCD` computes `gcd(min(nums), max(nums))` — the GCD of only the smallest and largest elements, not a pairwise reduction across all elements.

gcd-reduces-common-factor-counting.text: `common_factors(a, b)` converts the two-variable problem into divisor-counting on `gcd(a, b)`, since the set of common factors of (a, b) equals the set of divisors of gcd(a, b)

gcd-strings-commutativity-check.text: `str1 + str2 == str2 + str1` is both necessary and sufficient for the existence of a common divisor string — this is the key mathematical insight (related to the Fine and Wilf theorem)

gcd-strings-length-determines-answer.text: When a common divisor exists, its length equals `gcd(len(str1), len(str2))` and the answer is simply `str1[:that_length]`

gcd-strings-linear-time.text: O(n+m) complexity from string concatenation comparison is straightforward and not an invariant that would break if violated

gcd-strings-no-exceptions.text: Redundant with the cross-cutting `leetcode-solutions-skip-input-validation` belief — every solution in the repo follows this pattern

gcd-strings-returns-empty-on-mismatch.text: If `str1 + str2` is not equal to `str2 + str1`, `gcdOfStrings` returns an empty string.

gcd-strings-uses-math-gcd.text: The solution imports `math.gcd` and uses it to compute the length of the common divisor string.

generate-string-constant-branching-linea.text: `generateTheString` has O(1) branching logic, while the string construction is O(n) due to allocation.

generated-array-base-cases-zero-one.text: The array is initialized with base cases `nums[0] = 0` and `nums[1] = 1` before the loop from index 2 to `n`.

generated-array-n0-guard-required.text: The `n == 0` early return is necessary; without it, `nums[1] = 1` raises IndexError on a length-1 list

generated-array-no-external-deps.text: Trivially obvious from looking at the file — "uses no imports" is not an invariant that guides development decisions

generated-array-odd-index-sums-adjacent-.text: For odd index `i >= 3`, `nums[i]` is assigned `nums[i // 2] + nums[i // 2 + 1]`.

generated-array-recurrence-correctness.text: For odd index `i >= 3`, `nums[i // 2 + 1]` is always in bounds because `i // 2 + 1 <= i` and the array has length `n + 1`

generated-array-single-pass-dp.text: The solution computes all values in one forward pass because every dependency index (`i // 2`, `i // 2 + 1`) is strictly less than the current index for `i >= 2`

generation-errors-amplified-by-isolation.text: The automated generation pipeline introduces systematic naming errors (mismatched function names, stale aliases), and the per-problem isolation architecture ensures these errors are never detected or corrected — the pipeline creates defects and the architecture hides them, forming a defect-accumulation cycle with no corrective feedback loop.

justifications.label: connects the defect-source (generation pipeline) to the defect-concealment mechanism (isolation); the combination reveals an open-loop system with no error correction

generation-errors-remain-invisible.text: Naming errors introduced by the automated generation pipeline remain invisible at runtime because the submission-optimized architecture isolates each solution — but this containment depends on the test harness correctly routing to the intended function despite the naming drift.

justifications.label: generation errors are contained by isolation until a misnamed export breaks the test harness routing boundary

generation-pipeline-is-naming-error-root.text: The automated code generation pipeline is the root cause of systematic naming errors across the repo — it produces both misnamed functions (names carried from unrelated problems via copy-paste templates) and vestigial aliases (dead references from prior solution scaffolding), creating a class of defects that is structurally different from manual typos because it affects function identity rather than spelling.

justifications.label: Root cause identification — naming errors are a systematic pipeline artifact, not random human error

generator-boolean-counting-pattern.text: The repo uses `sum(predicate(x) for x in iterable)` as an idiom for counting matches, exploiting Python's `True == 1` / `False == 0` arithmetic to avoid materializing a filtered list.

generator-inside-min-pattern.text: Multiple solutions use generator expressions (lazy, O(1) auxiliary space) inside `min()` rather than list comprehensions — a recurring idiom across the repo for single-pass optimization problems.

generator-over-list-for-aggregation.text: `maximumWealth` uses `max(sum(row) for row in accounts)` with a generator expression (not a list comprehension), achieving O(1) auxiliary space by avoiding materialization of intermediate results.

generator-sum-counting-idiom.text: Multiple solutions use `sum(1 for ... if ...)` or `sum(... for ...)` as the standard idiom for counting matches — O(1) auxiliary space, no intermediate list allocation.

generator-sum-counting-pattern.text: Solutions use `sum(1 for x in seq if cond)` as the standard counting idiom rather than `len([...])` or manual accumulators — avoids intermediate list allocation.

get-min-distance-does-not-use-start-as-i.text: get_min_distance uses start only inside abs(i - start) and never as an index into nums, so it does not bounds-check start.

get-min-distance-returns-minimum-absolut.text: get_min_distance returns the minimum absolute index distance between start and any index whose value equals target.

get-min-distance-runs-linear-time.text: get_min_distance runs in O(n) time via a single pass over nums.

get-target-copy-optional-import-unused.text: `typing.Optional` is imported in `solution.py` but is not referenced in any type annotation.

get-target-copy-preorder-dfs.text: `getTargetCopy` performs pre-order DFS, checking the current original node before recursing into the left and then right subtrees.

get-target-copy-worst-case-o-n-time-o-h-.text: `getTargetCopy` runs in O(n) time and O(h) recursion stack space in the worst case, where `h` is the tree height.

getheight-sentinel-neg1.text: `getHeight` in balanced-binary-tree returns exactly `-1` as a sentinel for any unbalanced subtree and never any other negative value; non-negative returns represent actual heights.

getheight-traverses-postorder.text: `getHeight` processes the left subtree, then the right subtree, then the current node (post-order traversal).

getlucky-convergence-by-k3.text: For valid inputs (up to 1000 lowercase letters), `getLucky` stabilizes to a single digit by the third transform at most, making k > 3 effectively a no-op.

getlucky-first-sum-on-string.text: `getLucky` computes the first digit-sum directly from the concatenated numeric string, avoiding conversion to a potentially thousands-of-digits integer; subsequent sums operate on small integers.

getlucky-imports-unittest-only.text: The solution file imports only unittest from the standard library.

getlucky-k-minus-one-loop.text: The transform loop in `getLucky` runs `k - 1` iterations because the initial sum on `num_str` counts as the first of `k` total transforms.

getlucky-k-zero-performs-one-sum.text: Calling getLucky with k=0 still performs one digit-sum because the initial sum on num_str is unconditional.

getlucky-max-input-first-sum-bound.text: For the maximum input of 1000 'z' characters, the first digit-sum is at most 18,000.

getlucky-testgetlucky-has-seven-tests.text: The inline TestGetLucky class contains seven unit tests.

goal-parser-al-token-to-al.text: The solution replaces every substring `(al)` with `al`.

goal-parser-empty-parens-to-o.text: The solution replaces every substring `()` with `o`.

goal-parser-g-token-unchanged.text: The token `G` passes through both `str.replace` calls unchanged.

goal-parser-linear-complexity.text: O(n) time/space for two sequential string scans is the obvious complexity — not an invariant a developer needs to be warned about

goal-parser-num-ways-misnomer.text: `num_ways` is named incorrectly; it returns a transformed string, not a count — the name likely comes from copy-paste from another problem template

goal-parser-replace-order-safe.text: The two `str.replace()` calls are order-independent because `"()"` and `"(al)"` are non-overlapping substrings in any valid Goal Parser input

goat-latin-assumes-nonempty-words.text: The function accesses `word[0]` without a length check, relying on the LeetCode guarantee that the input contains no empty tokens from splitting

goat-latin-consonant-rotation-preserves-.text: When moving a consonant to the end of a word, the original casing of that character is preserved — no `.lower()` or `.upper()` is applied

goat-latin-consonant-rule-rotates-then-a.text: For a word starting with a consonant, `to_goat_latin` moves the first character to the end, then appends `ma` and `i` copies of `a`.

goat-latin-index-is-1-based.text: `enumerate(sentence.split(), 1)` produces 1-based indices, meaning the first word gets exactly one trailing `"a"` — an off-by-one here would silently produce wrong answers

goat-latin-vowel-check-is-case-insensiti.text: The vowel set includes both upper and lowercase variants (`"aeiouAEIOU"`), so the first-character check works regardless of word casing

goat-latin-vowel-rule-appends-ma.text: For a word starting with a vowel, `to_goat_latin` appends `ma` and then `i` copies of `a`, where `i` is the word's 1-based position.

goat-latin-vowel-set-o1-membership.text: The vowel set `aeiouAEIOU` is stored as a Python set for O(1) membership testing.

good-pairs-defaultdict-int-tracks-prior-.text: `Solution.numIdenticalPairs` uses `collections.defaultdict(int)` to track prior occurrence counts for each value.

good-pairs-defaultdict-zero.text: This is standard Python behavior of `defaultdict(int)`, not a codebase-specific claim.

good-pairs-empty-input-returns-zero.text: For an empty `nums` list, `Solution.numIdenticalPairs` returns 0 because the loop never executes.

good-pairs-implicit-i-less-than-j.text: `Solution.numIdenticalPairs` adds `seen[num]` to `count` before incrementing `seen[num]`, so each counted pair has a previously seen index as `i` and the current index as `j`, satisfying `i < j`.

good-triplets-empty-range-handles-small-.text: When `len(arr) < 3`, `range(n - 2)` produces an empty range, so `countGoodTriplets` returns 0 without error — no special-casing needed.

good-triplets-loop-bounds-guarantee-room.text: The loop bounds `range(n - 2)`, `range(i + 1, n - 1)`, and `range(j + 1, n)` ensure each loop has enough remaining elements for a valid triplet.

good-triplets-pruning-order-skips-innerm.text: The `a`-constraint is checked between the second and third loops: a failed `(i, j)` pair skips all `k` iterations, while `b` and `c` constraints are only checked in the innermost loop.

good-triplets-pure-function.text: `countGoodTriplets` does not mutate the input array and has no side effects.

good-triplets-short-circuits-c-check.text: Inside the innermost loop of `countGoodTriplets`, the `b`-constraint is checked before the `c`-constraint, so the `c` computation is skipped if the `b` check fails.

good-triplets-valid-triplet-three-constr.text: `countGoodTriplets` counts a triplet `(i, j, k)` only when all three absolute-difference conditions `|arr[i]-arr[j]| <= a`, `|arr[j]-arr[k]| <= b`, and `|arr[i]-arr[k]| <= c` hold.

good-triplets-worst-case-cubic-time.text: The worst-case time complexity of `countGoodTriplets` is O(n^3), with early pruning reducing work when the `a`-constraint fails.

graph-path-exists-batch-no-early-exit.text: All edges are processed via `union` before the single `find(source) == find(destination)` query — the algorithm does not short-circuit if source and destination merge mid-loop.

graph-path-exists-initializes-parent-sel.text: The solver initializes `parent[i] = i` and `rank[i] = 0` for every node `i` in `0..n-1`.

graph-path-exists-near-linear-complexity.text: The graph connectivity solver runs in O(n + E*alpha(n)) time using union by rank plus path splitting, where E is the number of edges.

graph-path-exists-no-bounds-checking.text: The Union-Find implementation does not bounds-check `source`, `destination`, or edge endpoints, so out-of-range indices raise `IndexError`.

graph-path-exists-same-root-query.text: The graph connectivity solver returns `True` exactly when `find(source) == find(destination)` after all edges are unioned.

greatest-letter-checks-both-case-variant.text: For each uppercase letter c in the descending alphabet scan, the function checks whether both c and c.lower() are present in the input set.

greatest-letter-empty-input-returns-empt.text: An empty input string returns the empty string through the normal fallback path without special-case handling.

greatest-letter-returns-uppercase-or-emp.text: The return value is always either a single uppercase ASCII letter or the empty string, never lowercase and never multi-character.

greedy-algorithms-provably-optimal.text: Greedy strategies across the repo are accompanied by explicit correctness arguments — prefix-free code uniqueness, leftmost-digit positional weight, exchange arguments — not treated as heuristics.

justifications.label: Each greedy choice has a structural proof that no lookahead can improve it

greedy-consecutive-triples-sufficiency.text: After sorting descending, only consecutive triples need checking for the largest-perimeter-triangle problem; non-adjacent triples can never produce a larger valid perimeter than the first valid consecutive triple.

greedy-early-exit-correctness.text: In `max_number_after_remove_digit`, removing the first occurrence of `digit` that is immediately followed by a strictly larger digit always yields the lexicographically maximum result.

greedy-flip-negatives-first.text: The k-negations algorithm sorts to place negatives first and greedily flips them; this is optimal because flipping a negative yields +2|x| gain versus flipping a positive which yields -2|x| loss.

greedy-optimality-requires-nonnegative-d.text: Greedy algorithms in the repo are provably optimal across their problem domains, but this universal optimality claim is contingent on non-negative input values — at least one greedy sort-then-pair strategy (max_product_difference) is correct only for positive inputs, where magnitude ordering coincides with value ordering.

justifications.label: The positive-input-only constraint on one greedy solution gates the universal optimality claim

greedy-output-stack-pattern.text: Multiple solutions use a "greedy output stack" pattern — building output character-by-character, appending or skipping based on a bounded lookback window into the result so far (e.g., fancy-string checks last 2, decrypt-string peeks ahead 2).

greedy-scan-correct-for-prefix-free-code.text: The greedy left-to-right scan in the 1-bit/2-bit characters problem produces the unique valid decoding because `{0, 10, 11}` is a prefix-free code — no backtracking or DP is needed.

greedy-single-fork-for-one-deletion.text: Valid Palindrome II handles the "at most one deletion" constraint by forking exactly once on the first mismatch (try skipping left or right), with no backtracking, keeping total work at O(n).

greedy-single-pass-virtual-state-pattern.text: `min_operations` (array increasing) tracks a virtual `prev` value instead of mutating the input array, keeping the function pure while achieving O(n) time and O(1) space.

greedy-skip-optimality.text: Skipping 3 positions on each `'X'` produces the minimum move count because covering the leftmost uncovered `'X'` first maximizes coverage reach and never wastes a move.

greedy-sort-descending-skip-every-third.text: `minimumCost` sorts candy prices descending and sums elements where `i % 3 != 2`, skipping every third element as the free candy — the canonical greedy for "buy 2 get 1 free" minimization.

greedy-sort-mutates-input.text: `maximum-units-on-a-truck/solution.py` uses `boxTypes.sort()` which mutates the caller's list in-place rather than using `sorted()` for a non-destructive copy.

greedy-sort-then-scan-pattern.text: Multiple solutions (array-partition, assign-cookies) share the same structural pattern: sort the input, then make a single linear pass to extract the answer — a recurring idiom for greedy problems in this repo.

greedy-stack-extends-streaming-to-output.text: The greedy output stack extends single-pass streaming from scalar accumulation to structured output construction: the stack serves as a bounded accumulator enabling per-element include/revise/skip decisions while maintaining output invariants — generalizing streaming's extend-or-reset pattern from scalar state to sequence-building state.

justifications.label: Connects an orphan greedy pattern to the streaming paradigm via accumulator generalization

greedy-three-chars-always-sufficient.text: When replacing `?` to avoid consecutive repeats, trying candidates from `'abc'` always yields a valid choice because a position has at most 2 neighbors and 3 candidates guarantees one is conflict-free (pigeonhole principle).

greedy-with-early-exit-maximizes-pruning.text: Greedy algorithms in the repo are systematically paired with early-exit conditions — returning on first violation, terminating on deadlock detection, short-circuiting on zero — so that provably-optimal local choices combine with aggressive pruning to minimize both time complexity and actual executed instructions.

justifications.label: Greedy correctness guarantees that the first answer found is optimal, and early-exit exploits that guarantee to stop immediately — the combination is more powerful than either alone because greedy without early-exit still does unnecessary work, and early-exit without greedy might return a suboptimal answer

metadata.retract_reason: research: abandoned — The antecedents describe two independent patterns observed in completely disjoint problem sets with no overlapping solutions. The claim that greedy algorithms are 'systematically paired' with early-exit conditions is not just overstated — it's fabricated from unrelated observations. Softening would still assert a relationship (e.g., 'sometimes co-occur') that has zero evidential support. The synergy argument ('greedy without early-exit still does unnecessary work') is a theoretical observation, not something derived from the codebase evidence. No amount of rewording fixes a derivation whose antecedents share no common ground.

greedy-with-post-hoc-correction.text: The distribute-money solution computes an optimistic greedy answer then applies two corrections for constraint violations (surplus absorption and $4 avoidance), a pattern idiomatic for LeetCode distribution problems.

greedy-zero-crossing-optimal-for-balance.text: Splitting at every zero-crossing of the balance counter provably maximizes the number of balanced substrings; deferring a split can never create more splits later.

grid-as-strings-idiom.text: String-grid problems in this repo index directly into strings with `strs[i][j]` rather than converting to a 2D array, avoiding allocation at the cost of assuming uniform string length.

group-contribution-sweep-pattern.text: `countTriplets` uses a "left * current * right" sweep over Counter groups to count valid triplets in O(n) time, maintaining the invariant `left + c + right == len(nums)` at every iteration.

groupby-for-consecutive-runs.text: Solutions involving consecutive identical characters (e.g., decomposable substrings) use `itertools.groupby` for run-length encoding rather than manual loop-and-counter approaches.

guard-clause-then-expression-pattern.text: Easy-difficulty solutions follow a guard-clause-then-expression pattern: validate the input constraint up front, then return the entire transformation as a single expression.

guess-api-inverted-semantics.text: `guess()` returns `-1` when the guess is too high (not too low), which is the opposite of what a standard comparison function would return — the branching logic must account for this inversion.

guess-number-halves-search-space-per-ite.text: Each loop iteration of guessNumber halves the search interval, giving O(log n) time complexity.

guess-number-initializes-low-one-high-n.text: The guessNumber binary search initializes its search bounds as low = 1 and high = n.

guess-number-return-minus-one-unreachabl.text: The return -1 at the end of guessNumber is unreachable under the problem guarantee that a valid picked number exists in the range [1, n].

guess-number-uses-o-1-space.text: guessNumber maintains only low, high, and mid variables, giving O(1) auxiliary space complexity.

halves-alike-assumes-even-length.text: Subsumed by the cross-cutting belief `solutions-trust-leetcode-input-constraints`; not worth tracking per-solution.

halves-alike-case-insensitive-via-prebui.text: The halves-alike solution handles mixed-case vowel matching by storing all 10 case variants (`"aeiouAEIOU"`) in a set, avoiding a `.lower()` call on the input string.

halves-alike-empty-string-returns-true.text: Passing an empty string to determine_if_string_halves_are_alike returns True because both halves contain zero vowels.

halves-alike-is-o-n-time.text: Trivially obvious from a single-pass algorithm over the input string; not a useful belief to track.

halves-alike-linear-time-constant-aux-sp.text: The determine-if-string-halves-are-alike solution runs in O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space because it scans each half once and uses a fixed 10-element vowel set.

halves-alike-no-even-length-validation.text: The determine-if-string-halves-are-alike function does not validate that the input string length is even; for odd-length strings, the second half receives the extra character.

halves-alike-no-imports.text: The absence of imports is trivial and not an invariant that would break anything if changed.

hamming-distance-return-range-0-to-31.text: For valid non-negative 32-bit integer inputs, hammingDistance returns a value in the inclusive range [0, 31].

hamming-distance-single-expression-pipel.text: hammingDistance is implemented as a single expression pipeline: XOR the inputs, convert the result to a binary string with bin(), and count the '1' characters.

hamming-negative-inputs-produce-incorrec.text: Negative inputs to hammingDistance can produce an incorrect result because bin() on negative Python integers does not emit all leading two's-complement 1 bits.

hamming-no-input-validation.text: Absence of input validation is a repo-wide pattern (LeetCode solutions trust their inputs per problem constraints), not specific to this file. Better captured as a cross-cutting belief.

hamming-pure-builtin.text: Zero imports is the norm for simple LeetCode solutions, not a distinctive invariant worth tracking per-file.

hamming-weight-branchless-loop-body.text: The loop body of `hamming_weight` performs exactly two operations per iteration—clear the lowest set bit with `n &= n - 1` and increment `count`—with no conditional branches.

hamming-weight-count-invariant.text: At the start of each `hamming_weight` iteration, `count` equals the number of set bits already cleared from the original `n`.

hamming-weight-n12-returns-2.text: For input `n = 12` (binary `1100`), `hamming_weight` clears two set bits and returns `2`.

hamming-xor-popcount.text: `hammingDistance` computes Hamming distance as popcount of XOR (`bin(x ^ y).count('1')`); any change to either the XOR or the popcount step would break correctness.

happy-number-cycle-detected-by-pointer-c.text: is_happy detects a non-happy cycle when the slow and fast pointers become equal while the fast pointer is not 1.

happy-number-digit-square-sum-bounded-81.text: For inputs up to 2^31 - 1, the digit-square-sum computed by get_next is bounded above by 810.

happy-number-fast-starts-ahead.text: The fast pointer is initialized one step ahead (`get_next(n)`) while slow starts at `n` — this offset is critical for Floyd's algorithm to detect cycles correctly when the starting value itself is part of a cycle.

happy-number-floyds-o1-space.text: `is_happy` uses Floyd's cycle detection (tortoise and hare) with O(1) space rather than a hash set, making it the same pattern used in `linked-list-cycle`.

happy-number-get-next-fixed-point.text: `get_next(1)` returns 1, making 1 a fixed point — this is what causes the fast pointer to stop when a happy number is found and is essential to the algorithm's termination condition.

happy-number-step-function-uses-divmod-1.text: get_next computes the digit-square-sum of n by repeatedly extracting digits with divmod(n, 10) and adding digit * digit.

happy-number-zero-returns-false.text: Calling is_happy(0) returns False immediately because slow = 0 and fast = get_next(0) = 0, so the pointer-collision condition exits the loop.

harmless-defect-permanence-is-equilibriu.text: The permanence of structurally harmless defects is an equilibrium property, not a system failing: the same dual locking mechanisms that stabilize the quality profile (domain attractor + self-reinforcing incentive structure) also guarantee that frozen defects remain in their harmless state — preventing both remediation (which would require engineering investment the incentive structure discourages) and escalation (which would require cross-solution coupling the isolation architecture prevents).

justifications.label: One antecedent observes the paradox (permanent yet harmless), the other provides the mechanism (doubly locked profile); combining shows permanence-of-harmlessness as a consequence of the locking, not a coincidence

has-next-is-side-effect-free.text: `StringIterator.hasNext()` only checks `_count > 0` and never modifies state or triggers parsing — verified by a dedicated test case.

hash-lookahead-greedy-correct.text: In the decrypt-string solution, the 3-char token (`XX#`) is always checked before the 1-char token, which is the only correct parse order since `#` at position `i+2` unambiguously signals a double-digit encoding.

hash-pipeline-algebraically-and-empirica.text: The hash-then-stream pipeline's universality claim is both algebraically grounded (Counter provides a complete multiset algebra covering construction, measurement, comparison, and decomposition) and empirically validated by two complementary exemplar families (palindrome problems exercising Counter's full multiset operations, Two Sum problems spanning the lookup strategy space from hash maps through sorted arrays), making it the strongest-evidenced pipeline instantiation in the taxonomy.

justifications.label: theoretical completeness (algebraic closure) confirmed by empirical coverage (dual exemplar families) establishes the hash pipeline as the best-evidenced taxonomy member

hash-pipeline-demonstrated-by-dual-exemp.text: The hash-then-stream pipeline's universal scope is demonstrated by two complementary exemplar families: palindrome problems exercise Counter's full multiset algebra for aggregate frequency-parity reduction, while Two Sum problems exercise point-lookup semantics through hash map complement queries — together covering both fundamental query modes (aggregate frequency and exact membership) of the hash preprocessing phase.

justifications.label: complementary exemplars demonstrate coverage of both aggregate and point query modes of the hash phase

hash-preprocessing-universal-first-step.text: Hash-based data structures (Counter for frequencies, set for membership) serve as the universal O(n) preprocessing layer, with nearly every lookup-heavy or frequency-dependent problem beginning with one of these two constructions before a linear scan.

justifications.label: Counter and set are complementary hash tools — Counter for "how many" and set for "is present" — and together cover the preprocessing needs of the majority of easy/medium problems

hash-set-dimension-reduction.text: For triplet-constraint problems, precomputing a hash set of valid values for one dimension (e.g., perfect squares up to n^2) reduces an O(n^3) brute force to O(n^2) by replacing the innermost loop with an O(1) set membership check.

hash-structures-prime-bucket-sizing.text: Both hash structure implementations use prime bucket counts (1009 for HashMap, 769 for HashSet) to reduce collision clustering under modular hashing compared to power-of-two sizes.

hash-structures-silent-remove.text: Both MyHashMap.remove and MyHashSet.remove are silent no-ops when the key is absent — neither raises an exception nor returns an error signal.

hashmap-fixed-1009-buckets.text: Redundant with hashmap-separate-chaining-1009-buckets which captures the same claim with more context (includes the chaining strategy and complexity).

hashmap-get-returns-negative-one.text: MyHashMap.get returns integer -1 for absent keys (LeetCode convention), not None or KeyError.

hashmap-hash-function-key-mod-1009.text: MyHashMap._hash(key) maps a key to a bucket index via key % 1009, and the mapping is deterministic and never changes.

hashmap-mutable-pair-lists.text: MyHashMap stores entries as mutable `[key, value]` lists (not tuples), enabling in-place value updates via `pair[1] = value` without remove-and-reinsert.

hashmap-no-duplicate-keys.text: MyHashMap.put scans the target bucket for an existing key before appending, guaranteeing at most one entry per key across the entire map.

hashmap-operations-touch-exactly-one-buc.text: MyHashMap.put, get, and remove all hash the key and touch exactly one bucket per operation.

hashmap-remove-is-silent-noop.text: Subsumed by hash-structures-silent-remove which covers both HashMap and HashSet in a single cross-cutting belief.

hashmap-remove-pops-matching-index.text: MyHashMap.remove(key) linearly scans the target bucket with enumerate and pops the matching [key, value] pair by index if found; otherwise it is a no-op.

hashmap-separate-chaining-1009-buckets.text: MyHashMap uses separate chaining with a fixed array of 1009 buckets (a prime), giving O(n/1009) amortized cost per operation with no dynamic resizing.

hashset-all-ops-linear-in-bucket.text: Redundant with hashset-separate-chaining-769-buckets which already states the O(n/769) complexity.

hashset-bucket-count-is-prime.text: Subsumed by hash-structures-prime-bucket-sizing which captures the cross-cutting pattern across both hash structures.

hashset-colocated-tests.text: design-hashset/solution.py contains both the MyHashSet implementation and its TestMyHashSet unittest class in the same file, following the repo's co-located test convention.

hashset-contains-uses-in-operator-on-buc.text: MyHashSet.contains(key) hashes the key and returns whether key is present in the target bucket using the in operator.

hashset-hash-function-key-mod-769.text: MyHashSet._hash(key) maps a key to a bucket index via key % 769.

hashset-no-duplicates-invariant.text: MyHashSet.add checks `key not in bucket` before appending, guaranteeing each key appears exactly once across the entire structure.

hashset-separate-chaining-769-buckets.text: MyHashSet uses separate chaining with 769 buckets (a prime), giving O(n/769) average-case per operation.

hashset-tests-cover-boundary-and-collisi.text: The inline TestMyHashSet class includes test cases for boundary values 0 and 10^6, hash collisions on 0 and 769, duplicate adds, remove-of-absent-key, and empty-set lookup.

heapify-over-repeated-push.text: Solutions prefer `heapq.heapify()` (O(n)) for initial heap construction rather than n individual `heappush` calls (O(n log n)).

height-checker-assumes-positive-heights.text: This is a direct consequence of the LeetCode constraint (heights 1-100), not an independent invariant — it would only matter if someone tried to use this function outside its problem context.

height-checker-counting-sort.text: `height_checker` uses counting sort (O(n+k), k=100) rather than comparison sort, exploiting the constraint that heights are in [1, 100].

height-checker-empty-input-returns-zero.text: An empty heights list returns 0 from height_checker because the comparison loop body never executes.

height-checker-frequency-array-size-101.text: height_checker builds a frequency array of size 101, using indices 1 through 100 for height values and leaving index 0 unused.

height-checker-j-monotonic.text: The cursor `j` only advances forward across the outer loop, so total inner `while` iterations are O(k) amortized across all elements — the nested loop is not O(n*k).

height-checker-no-sorted-array-materiali.text: The sorted order is never stored as a list; comparison happens inline by walking the frequency array with a monotonically advancing cursor `j`, fusing the sort and compare steps.

height-checker-requires-heights-in-1-to-.text: height_checker assumes all heights are in the range [1, 100]; values greater than 100 can cause IndexError and value 0 pollutes the unused index 0.

height-zero-for-none.text: The empty tree (`None`) is defined as having height 0 in balanced-binary-tree, making `max(left, right) + 1` produce height 1 for a single leaf node — a foundational invariant the recursion depends on.

hex-output-at-most-8-digits.text: The 0xFFFFFFFF mask constrains to_hex output to at most 8 hexadecimal digits (32 bits).

hex-output-lowercase.text: to_hex always returns lowercase hexadecimal characters because the hex_chars constant is "0123456789abcdef".

hex-output-no-leading-zeros.text: to_hex output never contains leading zeros because the digit-extraction loop terminates when num reaches 0.

hexspeak-no-negative-handling.text: `to_hexspeak` does not handle negative integers; `hex()` on a negative int produces `"-0x..."`, so the `[2:]` slice would retain the `x` and produce an invalid result rather than raising an error.

hexspeak-replace-order-independent.text: The two `.replace("0","O").replace("1","I")` calls in `to_hexspeak` produce the same result regardless of order, because `hex()` output contains only `0-9a-f` — no `O` or `I` characters exist before substitution.

hexspeak-returns-error-string-for-invali.text: When the converted hex string contains any character outside the valid Hexspeak set `{A,B,C,D,E,F,I,O}` after substitution, `to_hexspeak` returns the literal string `"ERROR"` rather than raising an exception.

hexspeak-string-input-contract.text: `to_hexspeak` takes `num` as a string (not int) matching the LeetCode signature, converting internally via `int(num)` with no input validation.

hexspeak-strips-0x-prefix-with-slice.text: `to_hexspeak` strips the `hex()` output's `0x` prefix using `[2:]`, which is safe for non-negative integers because Python's `hex()` always emits that prefix.

hexspeak-uppercases-hex-before-validatio.text: `to_hexspeak` calls `.upper()` on the hex digits because `hex()` returns lowercase `a`-`f`, and Hexspeak requires uppercase letters before validity checking.

hexspeak-uses-builtin-hex-function.text: `to_hexspeak` uses Python's built-in `hex()` for decimal-to-hex conversion.

hexspeak-valid-set-complete.text: The valid Hexspeak character set `{A,B,C,D,E,F,I,O}` is exactly the six hex letter-digits plus substitutions for `0→O` and `1→I`; digits `2-9` are the only rejection trigger.

highest-altitude-empty-input-returns-zer.text: An empty gain list returns 0 without error because the loop does not execute and max_alt remains initialized to 0.

highest-altitude-empty-input-safe.text: Trivially follows from the loop structure (empty list = no iterations, returns initial value 0) — not a meaningful invariant that could break.

highest-altitude-gain-array-holds-deltas.text: In Find the Highest Altitude, the gain array contains signed altitude deltas between consecutive checkpoints, not absolute altitudes.

highest-altitude-misnamed-function.text: The highest-altitude solution function is named `min_operations` despite solving a prefix-sum maximum problem — a naming bug likely from the code generation pipeline.

highest-altitude-running-altitude-is-pre.text: After processing index i, the running alt variable equals the sum of gain[0:i+1].

highest-altitude-single-pass.text: The highest-altitude solution uses a running accumulator with tracking max in O(n) time and O(1) space, rather than materializing the prefix-sum array.

highest-altitude-starts-at-zero.text: `min_operations` (the highest-altitude solver) includes altitude 0 as a candidate for the maximum by initializing `max_alt = 0`, correctly accounting for the starting point.

highest-island-naming-error.text: `substrings-of-size-three-with-distinct-characters/solution.py` has its method named `highest_island` instead of `countGoodSubstrings` — a copy-paste error from a different problem

hills-valleys-boundary-exclusion.text: The counting loop iterates indices `1` through `len(deduped) - 2`, so the first and last elements are never counted as hills or valleys — they lack a second neighbor.

hills-valleys-dedup-eliminates-plateaus.text: After deduplication, `deduped[i] != deduped[i+1]` for all valid `i`, guaranteeing every interior element is unambiguously a hill, valley, or neither — plateau cases cannot occur.

hills-valleys-does-not-mutate-input.text: `count_hills_and_valleys` never modifies the input `nums`; it builds a separate `deduped` list.

hills-valleys-empty-input-crashes-at-num.text: An empty input to `count_hills_and_valleys` crashes at `nums[0]` during deduplication; the function does not guard against empty input.

hills-valleys-hill-or-valley-strict-neig.text: `count_hills_and_valleys` counts an interior element as a hill if it is strictly greater than both neighbors and as a valley if it is strictly less than both neighbors.

hills-valleys-leetcode-constraint-length.text: The LeetCode constraints for `count_hills_and_valleys` specify `2 <= nums.length <= 100`.

hills-valleys-single-element-returns-zer.text: `count_hills_and_valleys` returns 0 for a single-element input because the deduped list has length 1 and the counting loop does not execute.

hills-valleys-two-pass-tradeoff.text: `count_hills_and_valleys` uses O(n) auxiliary space for the `deduped` list (two-pass: dedup then scan); a single-pass approach tracking `prev_different` could reduce to O(1) space.

horner-method-for-linked-list-binary.text: Binary-to-integer conversion from linked lists uses Horner's method (`result = result * 2 + node.val`), processing MSB-first in a single pass with O(1) space.

identity-not-equality.text: `getTargetCopy` uses `is` (identity) rather than `==` (equality) to locate the target node, making it correct even when the tree contains duplicate values.

image-smoother-boundary-clamping.text: Edge and corner cells are handled implicitly via `max(0, i-1)` / `min(m, i+2)` bounds rather than explicit conditional branches, allowing the window to naturally shrink at borders.

image-smoother-constant-work-per-cell.text: The inner double loop iterates at most 9 times per cell (3×3 window), making overall complexity O(m·n) rather than O(m·n·k²).

image-smoother-empty-matrix-raises-index.text: Passing an empty matrix to `imageSmoother` raises `IndexError` when `len(img[0])` is evaluated because the function has no empty-input guard.

image-smoother-floor-division-safe.text: The window always includes cell `(i,j)` itself, so `count` is always ≥1 and the `total // count` floor division never raises `ZeroDivisionError`.

image-smoother-inline-test-class-has-sev.text: The inline `TestImageSmoother` class contains seven unit test cases.

image-smoother-out-of-place.text: `imageSmoother` allocates a separate result matrix and never writes to the input, so reads always reflect original pixel values and avoid read-after-write corruption.

image-smoother-output-has-same-dimension.text: `imageSmoother` returns a new matrix with the same `m × n` dimensions as the input image.

image-smoother-uses-floor-division-for-a.text: `imageSmoother` stores `total // count` for each cell, using Python integer floor division to match the problem's floor-of-average requirement.

immunity-complete-across-all-observed-de.text: Architectural immunity covers all observed defect classes comprehensively: naming errors from the generation pipeline, convention drift from isolation, and tooling confusion from the test harness are all structurally invisible at runtime, with no observed defect class that could escalate from engineering nuisance to runtime failure.

justifications.label: Both antecedents claim immunity/invisibility from different angles; the combination claims completeness across ALL defect classes, which holds only while no export-level naming error actually breaks the test harness's import resolution

immunity-self-reinforced-by-quality-equi.text: The architecture's immunity to its own engineering defects is not merely passive but actively maintained by the quality equilibrium: defects are structurally harmless (isolation prevents functional impact), the judge-optimized selection dynamics provide no incentive to remediate them, and this combination means defects are positively stabilized by the system's own dynamics rather than merely tolerated.

justifications.label: equilibrium dynamics actively maintain immunity rather than merely permitting it

immutable-string-list-copy-for-swap.text: Python string immutability forces solutions that swap characters (e.g., `reverseVowels`) to convert to `list(s)`, perform O(1) swaps, then `"".join()` back — avoiding O(n^2) string concatenation.

imported-by-cross-refs-misleading.text: The "Imported By" lists in code exploration prompts reflect shared test harness structure across the repo, not real import edges between solution modules.

imported-by-is-test-harness-artifact.text: The "Imported By" cross-references that appear across solution files are artifacts of the shared test runner infrastructure (likely `run_tests.py` or conftest); solutions do not actually import from each other.

imported-by-list-artifact.text: The "Imported By" lists showing ~400+ test files across the repo are misleading artifacts of the analysis tooling — they reflect shared test harness structure (likely a conftest or re-export pattern), not actual direct imports of each solution module.

imported-by-list-is-misleading.text: The "Imported By" metadata on solution files lists hundreds of test files that don't actually import the solution — they share a common test harness pattern. Each solution's genuine consumer is only its own `test_solution.py`.

imported-by-list-is-test-harness-artifac.text: The large "Imported By" lists shown in file context across the repo are artifacts of a shared test runner/harness that indexes all solution modules; they do not represent actual cross-solution dependencies.

imported-by-list-misleading.text: The "Imported By" lists shown in the exploration prompt are artifacts of the repo's test infrastructure — each problem's `test_solution.py` imports its own `solution.py`, not other problems' solutions.

imported-by-lists-are-artifacts.text: The "Imported By" metadata listing hundreds of test files is a repo-wide cross-reference artifact, not actual import dependencies; each solution is only directly imported by its own `test_solution.py`.

imported-by-lists-are-misleading.text: The "Imported By" metadata across solution files inflates actual dependency counts — most listed test files share a common `from solution import Solution` pattern and don't depend on the specific module. True importers are only the co-located `test_solution.py`.

imported-by-lists-are-noisy.text: The "Imported By" metadata for solution files includes hundreds of unrelated test files due to the test harness's broad import scanning; only the co-located `test_solution.py` is a real consumer.

imported-by-lists-are-static-analysis-ar.text: The "Imported By" lists showing 300+ test files are artifacts of the repo's shared test harness / test runner discovery, not real import relationships; each solution is only directly imported by its own `test_solution.py`.

imported-by-lists-are-tooling-artifact.text: The "Imported By" lists in the dependency analysis are misleading — hundreds of test files appear as importers of each solution, but each `test_solution.py` only imports from its own directory's `solution.py`; the cross-references are an artifact of shared import patterns or broken static analysis.

imported-by-lists-misleading.text: The tooling's "Imported By" lists show hundreds of test files across the repo, but these reflect shared test infrastructure naming patterns, not actual logical dependencies on the listed solution.

imported-by-metadata-is-misleading.text: Across the repo, the "Imported By" metadata for solution files incorrectly lists hundreds of unrelated test files because they all import a local `solution.py` via the same relative path — only the test file in the same problem directory is a real consumer

imported-by-metadata-is-unreliable.text: The "Imported By" lists in the code exploration tooling are artifacts of repo-wide test infrastructure (shared conftest or runner), not real dependency relationships — only the co-located `test_solution.py` actually imports each solution.

imported-by-metadata-systematically-unre.text: The "Imported By" dependency metadata is a pure artifact of the test harness's broad import pattern, not indicative of actual code coupling between solutions.

justifications.label: The test harness imports a uniform symbol from every solution, inflating apparent coupling to ~400 dependents per file

imported-by-metadata-unreliable.text: The "Imported By" lists in code-expert analysis are artifacts of the repo's shared test harness or runner — they show every test file in the repo, not actual cross-problem imports. Each solution is only genuinely imported by its own `test_solution.py`.

in-place-grid-mutation.text: `maxValueAfterOperations` calls `row.sort()` on each row of the input grid, destroying the original ordering — callers lose their data.

in-place-mutation-return-convention.text: Multiple solutions (flood-fill, flipping-an-image) mutate the input data structure in-place and return the same reference, following LeetCode's convention where the caller already holds the reference.

in-place-mutation-with-return-convention.text: Solutions routinely mutate input data structures (arrays, linked lists, matrices) in-place and return the same reference, blending imperative mutation with functional return-value style.

justifications.label: The mutate-and-return idiom matches LeetCode's expected interface pattern

in-place-sort-mutation.text: Multiple solutions (`max_product_difference`, `maximumProduct`) mutate the caller's list via `nums.sort()` rather than using `sorted()` — callers must copy if they need the original order.

in-place-sort-mutation-pattern.text: Multiple solutions (`trimMean`, `can_attend_meetings`) mutate input arrays via `list.sort()` in-place; this is a recurring pattern in the repo where LeetCode's single-call contract makes input preservation unnecessary.

inclusive-interval-output.text: Each returned interval `[start, end]` from `largeGroupPositions` is inclusive on both ends, matching LeetCode's expected format.

inclusive-range-contract.text: `countPrimeSetBits(left, right)` treats both `left` and `right` as inclusive bounds, using `range(left, right + 1)` to match the LeetCode problem specification

inconsistency-is-invisible-because-submi.text: Engineering inconsistencies (naming drift, dual test conventions, style divergence) persist indefinitely because the submission-optimized architecture both causes them (isolation removes forcing functions) and hides them (each solution is tested in isolation, so cross-solution inconsistencies never surface as failures).

justifications.label: Isolation both generates inconsistency (no-consistency-enforcement) and conceals it (tooling unreliability) — the architecture is a self-stabilizing inconsistency trap

increasing-bst-dummy-head-pattern.text: Uses a dummy sentinel node to avoid special-casing the first insertion, the same idiom used in linked-list merge problems — build off a throwaway head and return head.right.

increasing-bst-is-destructive.text: increasingBST mutates the input tree in place; after the call, the original BST structure no longer exists — every node's .left is None and .right points to its in-order successor.

increasing-bst-linear-time.text: The algorithm visits each node exactly once via in-order traversal, giving O(n) time and O(h) stack space where h is tree height.

increasing-bst-nulls-left-pointers.text: Every visited node has .left set to None after processing; without this, the restructured tree would contain cycles or stale references.

increasing-bst-uses-instance-state.text: The mutable cursor is stored as self.current on the Solution instance, making concurrent calls on the same instance unsafe due to shared mutable state.

increment-before-test-pattern.text: The outer-parenthesis stripping algorithm increments/decrements depth *before* testing the inclusion condition, which is what makes `> 1` (for open) and `> 0` (for close) the correct thresholds — reversing the order would produce wrong results.

incremental-counting-equals-combination-.text: The single-pass idiom `count += seen[num]; seen[num] += 1` used in `numIdenticalPairs` is mathematically equivalent to summing `C(freq, 2)` for each distinct value but avoids a second pass over the frequency map.

index-bounds-over-slicing-in-divide-and-.text: Divide-and-conquer solutions recurse on index bounds `(left, right)` rather than creating sublists, avoiding O(n log n) total copying and keeping space to O(log n) stack frames.

index-pairs-brute-force-complexity.text: indexPairs runs in O(W × N × L) time where W = len(words), N = len(text), L = max word length, due to nested loops with slice comparison. No trie or Aho-Corasick; appropriate for constraints ≤ 100.

index-pairs-duplicate-words-produce-dupl.text: If the same word appears twice in the words list, each match position is reported twice in the output — no deduplication is performed.

index-pairs-sort-guarantees-order.text: Output ordering relies on Python's lexicographic list comparison in list.sort(), which sorts [i, j] pairs by i first then j.

index-pairs-wrapper-misnamed.text: has_all_codes_in_range is incorrectly named; it wraps indexPairs, not the "check if all codes in range" problem (LeetCode 1461). Likely a scaffolding artifact.

initial-window-uses-str-count.text: Implementation detail about which stdlib method initializes the first window — not an invariant that would break anything if changed.

inline-comparison-over-max-builtin.text: The repo prefers inline `if depth > max_depth` comparisons over `max_depth = max(max_depth, depth)` calls in tight loops, avoiding a function-call overhead per iteration.

inline-tests-colocated.text: Solution and unit tests are colocated in the same file, with a `unittest.TestCase` subclass defined alongside the `Solution` class.

inline-tests-colocated-with-solution.text: Some solution files (e.g., `apply-operations-to-an-array/solution.py`) bundle `unittest.TestCase` classes directly alongside the solution function, in addition to the separate `test_solution.py` file.

inline-tests-with-unittest.text: Some solution files include a `unittest.TestCase` subclass and `__main__` block alongside the solution, making them independently runnable via `python -m unittest` or direct execution.

inorder-bst-yields-sorted.text: The minimum-distance-between-bst-nodes solution relies on in-order traversal visiting BST nodes in ascending value order, reducing the problem to adjacent-pair difference comparison.

inorder-each-node-pushed-popped-once.text: Each tree node is pushed onto and popped from the stack exactly once, giving O(n) time complexity.

inorder-iterative-stack-max-o-height.text: The explicit stack used by `inorderTraversalHelper` uses O(h) auxiliary space, where h is tree height.

inorder-name-misnomer.text: The function is named `inorder` but performs string rotation; this appears to be a template artifact rather than an intentional name.

inorder-state-via-instance-vars.text: BST inorder traversal solutions in this repo use instance variables (e.g., `self.prev`, `self.min_diff`) for running state across recursive calls rather than nonlocal closures or return-value threading.

inorder-test-class-covers-seven-scenario.text: `TestInorderTraversal` contains seven unit tests covering canonical, empty, single-node, left-skewed, right-skewed, balanced, and negative-value trees.

inorder-traversal-left-root-right.text: `inorderTraversalHelper` returns node values in left-root-right inorder order.

input-immutability.text: "Does not modify the input list" is the default expectation for counting/query functions — only worth tracking if a solution *does* mutate input.

input-mutation-convention-coherent.text: The in-place mutation with return convention forms a coherent repo-wide pattern, but inconsistent mutation behavior across solutions undermines it — some solutions mutate in-place for space efficiency while others create copies for the same category of operation, with no systematic policy governing which approach to use.

justifications.label: The inconsistency belief (currently IN) gates the coherence claim, making this correctly OUT

inscribed-square-side-is-min-dimension.text: The rectangle-to-square solution (problem 1725) relies on the geometric identity that the largest square inscribable in rectangle `[l, w]` has side `min(l, w)`

integer-accumulators-precision-safe.text: Scalar streaming accumulators achieve exact results for all inputs within LeetCode's constraint bounds because Python's arbitrary-precision integers prevent overflow and the repo systematically chooses integer arithmetic over floating-point — but this precision guarantee breaks for any solution that introduces floating-point division into the accumulation chain.

justifications.label: Integer accumulators are precision-safe by Python's arbitrary-precision guarantee, gated on no float division in the accumulation path

integer-arithmetic-avoids-float-precisio.text: Solutions systematically choose integer operations — math.isqrt over math.sqrt, integer division over float division, sum comparison over average comparison — to avoid floating-point precision loss that could produce incorrect results for large inputs.

justifications.label: four independent solutions independently chose integer arithmetic to dodge the same class of bug (float precision near integer boundaries), indicating a deliberate defensive pattern

intersect-ii-counter-decrement-streams-n.text: `intersect` builds a Counter from `nums1` only, then consumes `nums2` in a single pass — only `nums1` must fit in memory, making this suitable for streaming `nums2` from disk.

intersect-ii-empty-inputs-return-empty.text: If either input list to intersect is empty, the function returns an empty result without error.

intersect-ii-linear-time.text: intersect runs in O(n + m) time by building a Counter from nums1 and then scanning nums2 once.

intersect-ii-output-follows-nums2-order.text: The output of `intersect` reflects the iteration order of `nums2`, not `nums1`, because elements are appended as `nums2` is walked.

intersect-ii-preserves-min-frequency.text: Each element appears in the output of `intersect` exactly `min(count_in_nums1, count_in_nums2)` times, enforced by a `> 0` guard that prevents the counter from going negative.

intersect-ii-works-on-unsorted-input.text: intersect works correctly on unsorted input because it uses Counter frequency accounting rather than requiring sorted arrays.

intersection-349-does-not-mutate-inputs.text: Solution.intersection does not modify nums1 or nums2; it constructs new sets from them.

intersection-349-linear-average-time.text: Solution.intersection runs in O(n + m) average time using Python set operations rather than O(n log n) sorting.

intersection-349-returns-unique-elements.text: Solution.intersection never returns duplicate values, regardless of duplicate values in nums1 or nums2.

intersection-349-set-idiom-nondeterminis.text: `Solution.intersection` (problem 349) uses Python's `set & set` operator, so output element order is nondeterministic and may vary across Python versions.

intersection-assumes-nonempty-input.text: intersection() accesses nums[0] unconditionally; passing an empty list raises IndexError. The LeetCode constraint guarantees at least one sub-array.

intersection-distinct-elements-assumed.text: The entry itself notes that duplicates within a sub-array wouldn't affect correctness since set collapse is harmless for intersection. Not an invariant that could break things.

intersection-no-mutation.text: Too obvious from the implementation (`set(nums1) & set(nums2)` constructs new sets) — not a useful invariant to track.

intersection-returns-sorted.text: intersection() always returns elements in ascending order, enforced by sorted() on the final line.

intersection-time-linear.text: O(n+m) via hash sets is the expected complexity for any set-based intersection; this is textbook, not a codebase-specific insight.

intersection-uses-in-place-narrowing.text: The result set only shrinks across iterations via &=; no element can appear in the output that wasn't in nums[0].

interval-overlap-formula.text: The `max(0, min(end1, end2) - max(start1, start2) + 1)` idiom for closed-interval overlap length appears in `days_together` and is a cross-cutting pattern used across multiple solutions in the repo.

invariant-based-testing-for-bst.text: BST-related tests verify structural properties (BST ordering, height-balance, in-order traversal matching input) rather than asserting a specific tree shape, making tests robust to multiple valid constructions.

invert-tree-double-application-is-identi.text: `invert_tree` is idempotent over two calls: `invert_tree(invert_tree(root))` restores the original tree structure.

invert-tree-mutates-in-place.text: `invert_tree` swaps child pointers on existing nodes rather than allocating new ones; the returned root is the same object as the input root.

invert-tree-postorder-recursion.text: invert_tree uses post-order recursion: it inverts both subtrees first and then swaps them at the current node.

invert-tree-recursion-depth-linear-heigh.text: invert_tree recursion depth is O(h) where h is tree height, giving O(log n) depth for balanced trees and O(n) worst-case depth for skewed trees.

invert-tree-tuple-swap-prevents-clobber.text: The simultaneous assignment `root.left, root.right = invert_tree(root.right), invert_tree(root.left)` evaluates both recursive calls before either assignment executes, preventing the bug where overwriting `root.left` first would lose the original left subtree before the right-side recursion reads it.

is-increasing-skip-logical-deletion.text: is_increasing_skip simulates deletion by skipping the target index during iteration rather than slicing or copying the array.

is-prime-covers-0-to-20.text: `is_prime` uses a hardcoded set `{2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19}` that is correct for all integers 0–20, sufficient for inputs up to `2^20 - 1` (the problem's upper bound); extending beyond 20-bit inputs would require adding primes up to the new bit width

is-prime-trial-division-bound.text: `is_prime` in prime-arrangements checks divisors only up to `int(k**0.5) + 1`, making it O(sqrt(k)) per call — sufficient for the n<=100 constraint but would need a sieve for larger inputs.

is-same-tree-complexity-min-nodes-height.text: `is_same_tree` runs in O(min(n, m)) time and O(min(h_p, h_q)) stack space for trees with node counts n, m and heights h_p, h_q.

is-same-tree-null-guards-before-value-ac.text: `is_same_tree` checks both-None and one-None cases before any `.val` access, guaranteeing no `AttributeError` on `None` nodes.

is-same-tree-read-only-no-mutation.text: `is_same_tree` performs a read-only traversal and never modifies either input tree.

is-same-tree-short-circuits-on-mismatch.text: `is_same_tree` evaluates `p.val == q.val and recurse(left) and recurse(right)` with short-circuit evaluation, bailing on the first structural or value mismatch without visiting remaining nodes.

is-vowel-lowercase-only.text: Trivially obvious from a set containing `{'a','e','i','o','u'}` — not a surprising invariant, and the LeetCode contract guarantees lowercase input anyway

isbalanced-is-pure-wrapper.text: This is an implementation detail about function decomposition, not an invariant — refactoring `isBalanced` to inline the logic would change nothing about correctness or behavior.

isbalanced-pure-wrapper-around-getheight.text: `isBalanced` contains no logic beyond converting `getHeight`'s result to a boolean; all balance checking is delegated to `getHeight`.

isdigit-filters-non-numeric-tokens.text: `areNumbersAscending` uses `str.isdigit()` to skip non-numeric words entirely; safe for ASCII-only LeetCode inputs but would accept Unicode digit characters in general Python 3

island-perimeter-boundary-guard.text: The `r > 0` and `c > 0` guards are the only bounds checks needed because the algorithm only examines up and left neighbors, never down or right.

island-perimeter-no-traversal.text: Restates the absence of a pattern rather than asserting a testable invariant; the algorithm choice is already fully captured by `island-perimeter-single-pass`.

island-perimeter-single-pass.text: The island perimeter algorithm computes the result in a single row-major scan with no auxiliary data structures, running in O(rows × cols) time and O(1) extra space.

island-perimeter-subtract-two.text: Each shared edge between two land cells removes exactly 2 from the perimeter total; checking only up and left neighbors (not all four) guarantees each adjacency is counted exactly once because the scan is top-to-bottom, left-to-right.

isolation-cascades-to-tooling-unreliabil.text: The zero-coupling isolation architecture has second-order effects beyond style inconsistency: dependency-tracking tools produce systematically misleading output because the only cross-file references are test-harness imports, not true solution dependencies.

justifications.label: Isolation makes dependency analysis impossible because there are no real dependencies to analyze

isolation-creates-undetectable-inconsist.text: Zero-coupling isolation both causes inconsistency (no forcing function for conventions) and makes it undetectable (dependency tools produce misleading metadata from the test harness), creating a feedback loop where style divergence accumulates silently and no automated tool can surface it.

justifications.label: When the same architecture that prevents consistency also breaks the tools that would detect inconsistency, the drift is self-concealing

isolation-enables-style-drift.text: The complete absence of cross-problem imports removes any forcing function for consistent conventions, directly enabling the class-vs-function divergence and method name mismatches observed across the repo.

justifications.label: Zero coupling means zero convention enforcement; each directory evolves independently

isolation-side-effects-invisible-at-runt.text: The second-order effects of per-problem isolation (tooling unreliability, undetectable naming drift, convention divergence) are invisible at runtime because each solution is executed and judged independently in the LeetCode submission context.

justifications.label: Isolation effects are architectural (cross-solution) but the execution model is per-solution — they can only surface when the test harness's cross-solution imports encounter misnamed exports

isomorphic-dual-map-bijection.text: `is_isomorphic` enforces a bijection (not just a function) by maintaining two synchronized dictionaries — `s_to_t` and `t_to_s` — updated atomically for each new character pair.

isomorphic-early-return.text: The function returns `False` at the first conflict detected during iteration; it never scans the full input when a violation exists at position `i`.

isomorphic-iterates-via-zip.text: is_isomorphic iterates over paired characters using zip(s, t), processing one position per loop iteration.

isomorphic-no-length-validation.text: `is_isomorphic` assumes `len(s) == len(t)` without validation; `zip` silently truncates to the shorter string, so unequal-length inputs produce silently wrong results rather than errors.

isomorphic-zero-dependencies.text: Having no imports is trivially observable and common across simple LeetCode solutions; not an architectural invariant worth tracking.

isqrt-over-sqrt-for-exactness.text: `isThreeDivisors` uses `math.isqrt` instead of `int(math.sqrt(n))` to avoid floating-point rounding errors in the perfect-square test; `isqrt` returns the exact integer square root.

isqrt-over-sqrt-for-large-inputs.text: Solutions needing integer square roots use `math.isqrt` instead of `int(math.sqrt(...))` to avoid floating-point precision errors, especially for inputs near 2^31-1.

isqrt-preferred-over-float-sqrt.text: `math.isqrt` is used instead of `int(math.sqrt(...))` to avoid incorrect results for large integers where float precision is insufficient (near 2^53).

iterates-only-c1-keys.text: `countWords` only iterates over `c1`'s keys, never `c2`'s — words exclusive to `words2` are never examined, which is correct since common words must appear in both arrays.

iteration-works-by-varying-prompt-contex.text: Iterative review works because each pass changes the prompt, context, and framing, activating different regions of the model's knowledge distribution.

iterative-not-recursive-tree-traversal.text: Both n-ary tree traversal solutions (preorder and postorder) use explicit stack loops rather than recursion, avoiding Python's default 1000-frame recursion limit on deep trees.

iterative-over-recursive-tree-traversal.text: Tree traversal solutions consistently use explicit stacks rather than recursion, avoiding Python's ~1000-frame recursion limit and handling arbitrarily deep trees.

iterative-reversal-O1-space.text: `reverse_list` uses exactly three local pointer variables (`prev`, `curr`, `next_node`) regardless of list length, making it O(1) auxiliary space.

jewels-stones-case-sensitive.text: Jewel matching is case-sensitive; `'a'` and `'A'` are treated as distinct jewel types, preserved by the set conversion.

jewels-stones-duplicate-safe.text: Duplicate characters in `jewels` are silently handled by set deduplication without affecting correctness, since the problem only asks about membership, not frequency.

jewels-stones-empty-inputs-return-zero.text: num_jewels_in_stones returns 0 for empty jewels or empty stones without special-case code.

jewels-stones-generator-sum-count.text: num_jewels_in_stones counts matches with `sum(s in jewel_set for s in stones)`, using a generator expression rather than an intermediate list.

jewels-stones-linear-time.text: `num_jewels_in_stones` runs in O(J + S) time and O(J) space by converting `jewels` to a set for O(1) membership testing, then iterating `stones` with a generator expression.

jewels-stones-no-deps.text: Trivially observable; not an architectural claim that would guide a developer's decisions.

join-based-equality.text: This is a single problem's algorithmic choice (join two lists and compare), not a codebase invariant — there's no reason other solutions would need to know or maintain this.

judge-circle-empty-input-returns-true.text: An empty moves string returns True because all opposing move counts are zero.

judge-circle-invalid-characters-ignored.text: Characters outside U, D, L, and R are silently ignored by judgeCircle because str.count only matches the four counted characters.

judge-circle-short-circuit.text: `judgeCircle` makes 2–4 linear passes: it checks L/R counts first and short-circuits to `False` via Python `and` before counting U/D if horizontal balance already fails.

judge-circle-uses-str-count-for-moves.text: judgeCircle computes move counts with Python str.count calls for 'L', 'R', 'U', and 'D'.

k-beauty-leading-zeros.text: Leading zeros collapsing via `int()` is standard Python behavior, not a codebase-specific invariant.

k-beauty-leading-zeros-int-conversion.text: Leading zeros in a length-k substring are handled implicitly by int() conversion (e.g., "04" becomes 4), which is correct per the problem spec.

k-beauty-no-imports.text: Zero-dependency claim is trivially observable from the import block and not an architectural invariant that could break anything.

k-beauty-returns-count-of-valid-substrin.text: divisor_substrings(num, k) returns the count of length-k contiguous substrings that are nonzero and divide num evenly.

k-beauty-single-public-function.text: divisor_substrings is the sole public function in the find-the-k-beauty-of-a-number solution file.

k-beauty-string-sliding-window.text: `divisor_substrings` uses string conversion and slicing (`str(num)[i:i+k]`) for digit extraction rather than modular arithmetic, which is the standard idiom for digit-substring problems in this repo.

k-beauty-window-count-formula.text: The sliding window iterates exactly `len(str(num)) - k + 1` times, which is the complete set of contiguous length-k substrings; if `k` exceeds the digit count, the range is empty and the function safely returns 0.

k-beauty-zero-guard-before-modulo.text: `divisor_substrings` guards `sub != 0` before computing `num % sub`, preventing `ZeroDivisionError` when substrings like `"00"` parse to zero via `int()`.

k-distant-brute-force-complexity.text: Worst-case time is O(n*k) when every element equals `key`, acceptable for the problem's n,k <= 1000 constraints.

k-distant-clamping-prevents-oob.text: `max(0, j-k)` and `min(n, j+k+1)` guarantee all generated indices stay within `[0, n)`.

k-distant-empty-input-returns-empty-list.text: If `nums` is empty, `find_k_distant_indices` returns an empty list.

k-distant-key-absent-returns-empty-list.text: If `key` does not occur in `nums`, `find_k_distant_indices` returns an empty list.

k-distant-key-position-range-expansion.text: `find_k_distant_indices` scans for every index `j` where `nums[j] == key` and adds the clamped inclusive range from `j-k` to `j+k` to a set.

k-distant-output-always-sorted.text: The return value is always in ascending order because `sorted()` is applied to the set before returning.

k-distant-uses-set-dedup.text: Overlapping ranges from multiple key positions are deduplicated via a Python `set`, avoiding interval-merging logic.

k-equals-n-returns-whole-array.text: In `largestSubarray`, when `k == len(nums)` the scan loop range is empty and the method correctly returns the entire array without special-casing.

k-length-apart-consecutive-sufficiency.text: `kLengthApart` only checks consecutive pairs of 1s; if all consecutive pairs satisfy the minimum distance, all pairs do (transitivity of minimum spacing in a linear scan).

k-length-apart-early-exit-on-violation.text: `kLengthApart` returns False immediately when it finds a pair of 1s whose gap `i - last - 1` is less than `k`, without scanning the rest of the array.

k-length-apart-gap-is-exclusive.text: The gap expression `i - last - 1` in `kLengthApart` counts elements strictly between two 1-positions, not including the endpoints — so 1s at indices 2 and 5 yield a gap of 2.

k-length-apart-linear-time.text: O(n) time / O(1) space for a single-pass scan is the obvious complexity — this is too trivial to track as a belief.

k-length-apart-sentinel-minus-one.text: `kLengthApart` initializes `last = -1` as a sentinel so the first 1 encountered never triggers a gap violation, avoiding a separate boolean flag.

k-length-apart-zero-or-one-ones-returns-.text: `kLengthApart` returns True when `nums` contains zero or one occurrence of 1, because there is no pair to violate the spacing constraint.

k-negations-alias-is-misnomer.text: The `is_univalued` alias for `largest_sum_after_k_negations` has no semantic relationship to this problem; it exists solely to satisfy the repo's test harness uniform-import convention.

k-negations-flips-negatives-while-k-posi.text: A while loop walks left to right, negating each negative element while k > 0 and decrementing k.

k-negations-in-place-mutation.text: `largest_sum_after_k_negations` mutates the input list via `sort()` and element assignment; callers that need the original array must copy before calling.

k-negations-no-imports.text: The solution uses pure stdlib Python and has no imports.

k-negations-odd-parity-noop-when-k-zero.text: The k % 2 branch is a no-op when k == 0 because 0 % 2 == 0.

k-negations-sums-after-flips.text: After the flipping loop, the algorithm computes total = sum(nums) over the partially flipped array.

keep-multiplying-no-input-mutation.text: find_final_value does not modify the input list nums; it builds a separate set for membership lookups.

keep-multiplying-original-returned-if-ab.text: find_final_value returns original unchanged when original is not present in nums, because the while loop never executes.

kelvin-is-index-zero.text: `convert_temperature` returns `[kelvin, fahrenheit]` — Kelvin at index 0, Fahrenheit at index 1; swapping breaks the LeetCode judge contract.

kernighan-bit-clear-loop.text: `hamming_weight` uses Brian Kernighan's `n &= n - 1` trick, iterating exactly k times for k set bits rather than a fixed 32 iterations

keyboard-row-case-insensitive-match.text: `find_words` lowercases each word for row lookup but returns the original-cased word — matching is case-insensitive, output is case-preserving.

keyboard-row-find-words-sole-public-func.text: keyboard-row/solution.py defines `find_words(words: list[str]) -> list[str]` as its sole public function.

keyboard-row-no-input-validation.text: Non-alphabetic characters in input words cause an unhandled `KeyError` from the `row_map` lookup; the function trusts the LeetCode constraint of alpha-only input.

keyboard-row-preserves-input-order.text: `find_words` returns matched words in their original input order.

keyboard-row-row-map-covers-26-letters.text: `row_map` maps exactly the 26 lowercase English letters to row indices 0, 1, or 2; any non-alphabetic character causes a `KeyError`.

keyboard-row-row-map-line-13.text: `row_map` is defined on line 13 of keyboard-row/solution.py.

keyboard-row-single-pass-filtering.text: `find_words` is O(n*m) where n is word count and m is max word length — one pass through each word with constant-time dict lookups and a set-size check.

keyboard-row-testfindwords-eight-tests.text: `TestFindWords` contains eight unit tests covering LeetCode examples plus single-character, all-uppercase, mixed-case, no-match, and all-match edge cases.

kids-candies-empty-input-crashes.text: Passing an empty `candies` list raises `ValueError` from `max()`; the problem constraints (`n >= 2`) prevent this under valid input.

kids-candies-gte-not-gt.text: The comparison uses `>=` (not `>`), so a kid already at the global max always returns `True` regardless of `extraCandies`.

kids-candies-linear-time.text: `kidsWithCandies` runs in O(n) time and O(n) space, making exactly two passes over the input: one for `max`, one for the comprehension.

kids-candies-no-mutation.text: `kidsWithCandies` never modifies the input `candies` list; it returns a new boolean list.

kids-candies-precompute-then-sweep.text: Redundant with `kids-candies-linear-time` — the two-pass structure is already captured by the complexity claim.

kids-candies-result-index-aligned.text: The output list has the same length as `candies` and is index-aligned with the input.
