kids-candies-solution-class-method.text: `kidsWithCandies` is implemented as a method of the `Solution` class, matching LeetCode's submission interface.

kids-candies-threshold-formula.text: `kidsWithCandies` returns True at index i iff `candies[i] + extraCandies >= max(candies)`.

kids-candies-typing-list-import.text: kids-with-the-greatest-number-of-candies/solution.py imports `List` from `typing` only for the return type annotation; there is no runtime dependency beyond the standard library.

kmp-empty-needle-returns-zero.text: When `needle` is empty, `strStr` returns 0 without special-case code — a natural consequence of `j == m` when both are 0.

kmp-first-match-semantics.text: `strStr` returns immediately on the first complete match (`j == m`), guaranteeing the leftmost occurrence index is returned.

kmp-implemented-over-builtin.text: `strStr` implements KMP (Knuth-Morris-Pratt) manually rather than using Python's built-in `str.find()`, making the O(n + m) algorithmic intent explicit.

kmp-lps-fallback-invariant.text: In the KMP implementation, the LPS array satisfies `0 <= lps[i] < i+1` for all `i`, and on mismatch the fallback `length = lps[length - 1]` guarantees forward progress — every search iteration either advances the haystack pointer or decreases the pattern pointer.

kmp-space-complexity.text: O(m) space for the LPS array is the textbook definition of KMP — not a codebase-specific claim worth tracking.

kth-distinct-early-return.text: `kth_distinct` returns immediately when the decremented local `k` reaches zero, avoiding iteration over the rest of the array.

kth-distinct-is-one-indexed.text: The parameter `k` is 1-indexed; passing `k=1` returns the first distinct string, matching LeetCode's contract.

kth-distinct-linear-time.text: `kth_distinct` is O(n) time and O(n) space: one pass to build the Counter, one pass to scan for the kth unique element.

kth-distinct-local-k-mutation.text: `kth_distinct` mutates only its local parameter `k` and leaves the input array `arr` untouched.

kth-distinct-means-count-equals-one.text: In `kth_distinct`, 'distinct' means a string with exactly one occurrence in the entire array, not unique among previously seen elements.

kth-distinct-preserves-insertion-order.text: The second pass iterates `arr` in its original order, so "kth distinct" respects the position strings first appear, not alphabetical or any other ordering.

kth-distinct-returns-empty-on-insufficie.text: `kth_distinct` returns `""` (not `None` or an exception) when fewer than `k` strings have count == 1.

kth-distinct-sole-public-function.text: `kth_distinct(arr: list[str], k: int) -> str` is the sole public function in kth-distinct-string-in-an-array/solution.py.

kth-largest-add-is-log-k.text: Each `add` call performs at most one push and one pop on a heap of size k, giving O(log k) time regardless of total stream length.

kth-largest-defensive-copy.text: The `KthLargest` constructor copies `nums` via `nums[:]` before heapifying, so the caller's list is never modified by `heapify`'s in-place rearrangement.

kth-largest-heap-may-be-smaller-than-k.text: The heap may contain fewer than k elements if fewer than k total values have been provided so far.

kth-largest-heap-size-invariant.text: After `__init__` and every `add` call, `len(self.heap) <= self.k` holds unconditionally — the bounded min-heap never grows past k elements.

kth-largest-init-complexity.text: Initialization costs O(n) for `heapify` plus O((n-k) log n) for pops, i.e., O(n log n) worst case.

kth-largest-init-pops-to-k.text: The `KthLargest` constructor heapifies a copy of `nums` and then pops elements until only `k` remain.

kth-largest-root-is-answer.text: `self.heap[0]` equals the kth largest element across all values ever provided (init + all add calls), assuming at least k values have been seen.

kth-largest-space-o-k.text: `KthLargest` uses O(k) space because it stores at most k elements in the heap.

kth-largest-uses-heapq.text: `KthLargest` uses `heapq`'s `heapify`, `heappush`, and `heappop` to maintain a min-heap.

kth-missing-binary-search-ologn.text: `findKthPositive` runs in O(log n) time via binary search on the missing-count function `arr[i] - (i + 1)`, not the naive O(n) linear scan.

kth-missing-finds-first-boundary.text: `findKthPositive` binary-searches for the first index where `arr[i] - (i + 1) >= k`.

kth-missing-formula-k-plus-left.text: The final answer `k + left` works because `left` counts how many array elements appear before the kth missing number, each shifting the answer position up by one.

kth-missing-input-preconditions.text: `findKthPositive` assumes `arr` is strictly increasing and contains only positive integers; the missing-count formula breaks with duplicates or non-positive values.

kth-missing-mid-missing-count-check.text: The binary-search loop computes `mid` and checks whether `arr[mid] - (mid + 1) < k` to decide whether to move `left` to `mid + 1`.

kth-missing-monotonic-invariant.text: The binary search is valid because `arr[i] - (i + 1)` (count of missing positives before index i) is monotonically non-decreasing for a strictly increasing array of positive integers.

kth-missing-requires-strictly-increasing.text: Redundant — this is a problem constraint, not a code invariant. The code doesn't validate it, and the monotonic-invariant belief already captures why it matters.

kth-missing-right-bound-len-arr.text: The right boundary is `len(arr)` (not `len(arr) - 1`) so the search correctly handles cases where all k missing numbers fall after every element in the array.

kth-missing-typing-unittest-imports.text: kth-missing-positive-number/solution.py imports `typing.List` and `unittest` and has no project-internal dependencies.

l-geq-w-by-construction.text: `L >= W` is enforced structurally, not by a conditional: since `w <= sqrt(area)`, `area // w >= sqrt(area) >= w` always holds.

language-causally-determines-convergence.text: Python's language-level defaults are a primary determinant of the convergence landscape: they privilege streaming by making it self-sufficient (Counter's zero-default, set's O(1) membership, arbitrary-precision integers require no external infrastructure), and this self-sufficiency aligns with the adoption-barrier gradient that makes convergence strength predictable from prerequisite count — suggesting the convergence pattern is substantially shaped by the host language's built-in semantics, not solely by the problem domain.

justifications.label: Strategy privilege (which strategy is dominant) and the adoption barrier gradient (why convergence strength varies) are both downstream of Python's defaults — combining them shows the entire convergence landscape is language-determined.

language-defaults-determine-strategy-pri.text: Python's language-level defaults — particularly Counter's zero-default for missing keys and sentinel initialization for loop state — are a primary mechanism that makes streaming self-sufficient by encoding boundary conditions into initial state, removing the need for special-case logic in loop bodies. Because streaming is the privileged default strategy (self-sufficient, covering the largest problem subset with the tightest resource bounds), these defaults help explain why streaming occupies its dominant position in the solution taxonomy: the language's built-in semantics align with the prerequisites of the strategy that needs the least external support.

justifications.label: unique contributions are defaults-encode-domain-knowledge + three-strategies-cover-taxonomy; combined, language design participates in shaping the taxonomic structure

language-produces-quality-inversion-thro.text: Python's language defaults produce the quality inversion through a specific three-step causal chain: language features determine which strategies are self-sufficient, streaming is privileged because it requires no abstractions beyond what the language provides natively, and streaming's dominance is the specific mechanism through which algorithmic quality outpaces engineering quality — making the quality inversion a downstream consequence of language design rather than developer choice.

justifications.label: Language defaults determine strategy privilege (cause), streaming is the mechanism of quality inversion (effect) — combining them traces the quality inversion's full causal chain back to Python's design decisions.

large-group-threshold-is-3.text: A group is "large" if and only if it contains 3 or more consecutive identical characters; groups of length 1 or 2 are excluded from the result.

largest-3-same-digit-empty-string-sentin.text: Initializing `result` to the empty string is correct because Python string comparison orders `000` greater than the empty string.

largest-3-same-digit-lexicographic-great.text: The solution keeps a candidate `num[i:i+3]` only when it is lexicographically greater than the current `result`.

largest-3-same-digit-loop-bound-prevents.text: The loop bound `range(len(num) - 2)` ensures `i+2 < len(num)`, so the slice `num[i:i+3]` never goes out of bounds.

largest-3-same-digit-short-input-returns.text: For input strings shorter than 3 characters, `range(len(num) - 2)` is empty and the method returns the empty string.

largest-3-same-digit-sliding-window-rang.text: The solution checks every length-3 contiguous window using a loop over `range(len(num) - 2)`.

largest-local-values-does-not-mutate-inp.text: `largest_matrix` does not modify the input grid.

largest-local-values-each-cell-max-of-3x.text: Each output cell is computed as the maximum of the 9 cells in the corresponding 3x3 block of the input grid.

largest-local-values-nested-comprehensio.text: The implementation uses a nested list comprehension with `max()` over a double `for` generator to flatten each 3x3 block into 9 values.

largest-local-values-output-dimensions-n.text: For an `n x n` input grid, `largest_matrix` returns an `(n-2) x (n-2)` matrix.

largest-local-values-undersized-input-re.text: If the input grid has fewer than 3 rows, `range(n-2)` is empty and `largest_matrix` returns an empty list.

largest-number-complexity-n-log-n-due-to.text: Total time complexity is O(n log n) because the two parity-pool sorts dominate the O(n) reconstruction loop.

largest-number-dual-pointer-oi-ei-recons.text: Reconstruction uses two counters, `oi` for the sorted odd pool and `ei` for the sorted even pool, advancing the counter matching each original digit's parity.

largest-number-parity-pool-exact-consump.text: The odd/even counters exactly consume their sorted pools because the number of odd/even digit positions in the original number equals the size of the corresponding sorted list.

largest-number-parity-pools-sorted-desce.text: The solution filters digits into odd and even sublists and sorts each sublist in descending order before reconstruction.

largest-odd-number-all-even-returns-empt.text: If no odd digit exists in `num`, `largest_odd_number` returns the empty string.

largest-odd-number-inline-test-class-nin.text: The file defines `TestLargestOddNumber` with nine test cases, including 100k-character stress cases.

largest-odd-number-oddness-int-mod.text: The function uses `int(num[i]) % 2 == 1` to test whether a digit is odd.

largest-odd-number-right-to-left-scan-fi.text: `largest_odd_number` scans `num` from the last index toward index 0 and returns immediately when it finds an odd digit.

largest-odd-number-worst-case-scan-linea.text: The right-to-left loop scans all characters in the worst case, which occurs when every digit is even.

largest-perimeter-triangle-mutates-input.text: `largest_perimeter_triangle()` sorts the input list in-place via `nums.sort()`; callers who need the original order must copy before calling.

largest-perimeter-triangle-returns-first.text: `largest_perimeter_triangle` returns immediately upon finding the first descending-sorted triple that satisfies the triangle inequality.

largest-perimeter-triangle-returns-zero-.text: When `nums` has fewer than 3 elements, `largest_perimeter_triangle` returns 0 because the scan loop body never executes.

largest-perimeter-triangle-scans-i-from-.text: `largest_perimeter_triangle` scans index `i` from 0 through `len(nums) - 3` inclusive, checking the consecutive triple at each index.

largest-squares-at-array-extremes.text: In a sorted array with negatives, the largest-magnitude elements (and thus largest squares) are always at the two ends, which is the invariant the two-pointer approach exploits

largest-subarray-is-linear.text: Obvious from the single-loop structure — not an invariant that needs to be tracked separately from reading the code.

largest-subarray-length-k-returns-slice-.text: `largestSubarray` returns the contiguous slice `nums[max_idx:max_idx + k]` after finding the index of the maximum valid starting value.

largest-subarray-length-k-runs-in-linear.text: `largestSubarray` runs in O(n) time with a single pass over valid starting indices and does not sort or use a heap.

largest-subarray-length-k-scans-start-in.text: `largestSubarray` scans candidate start indices `i` from 1 through `n - k` inclusive, considering only starts where a full length-`k` window fits.

largest-triangle-area-enumerates-all-com.text: `largestTriangleArea` uses `itertools.combinations(points, 3)` to enumerate every unordered triple of input points.

largest-triangle-area-returns-zero-for-f.text: `largestTriangleArea` returns `0.0` when given fewer than three points because `combinations` yields no triples and `max_area` remains at its initial value.

largest-triangle-area-runs-in-cubic-time.text: `largestTriangleArea` runs in O(n^3) time because it evaluates all C(n,3) triples without pruning or convex-hull optimization.

largest-twice-elif-branch-updates-second.text: The `elif n > second_max` branch updates `second_max` without changing `max_val` or `max_idx`.

largest-twice-empty-input-returns-zero-o.text: An empty list would make the method return `0` with `max_val = -1`, which is outside the problem's non-empty contract.

largest-twice-new-max-demotes-old-max-to.text: When a new maximum is encountered, the previous `max_val` is assigned to `second_max` and `max_idx` is updated.

largest-twice-single-element-returns-ind.text: For a single-element array, `second_max` remains `-1`, the dominance check passes, and the method returns index `0`.

largest-twice-single-pass-tracks-max-and.text: The solution finds the maximum and second maximum in a single enumeration of `nums`, without sorting or a second pass.

largest-unique-number-empty-list-returns.text: `largest_unique_number([])` returns `-1` because an empty `Counter` yields no items with count 1.

largest-unique-number-return-type-int-el.text: The return value is always an `int`: either an element from `nums` or the literal `-1`.

largest-unique-number-ternary-guard-avoi.text: The ternary guard `max(uniques) if uniques else -1` prevents `ValueError` from calling `max()` on an empty sequence.

largest-unique-number-unique-means-count.text: The solution treats an element as unique only when its frequency count is exactly 1, so `[3, 3]` has no unique number.

last-seen-stores-latest-index.text: `last_seen[num]` always holds the most recent index where `num` appeared — the unconditional overwrite after each check maintains this invariant, which is what makes it safe to discard older indices.

last-stone-weight-empty-heap-returns-zer.text: When all stones cancel and the heap is empty, the function returns 0 rather than raising an error.

last-stone-weight-loop-removes-at-least-.text: Each loop iteration pops two stones and pushes back at most one, so it terminates in at most n-1 iterations.

last-stone-weight-overall-complexity-n-l.text: The solution runs in O(n log n) time: O(n) heapify plus up to n-1 iterations with O(log n) heap operations.

last-stone-weight-pop-order-ensures-y-at.text: After the two pops, `y >= x` holds because the negated min-heap returns the smallest negative value, corresponding to the largest original stone, first.

latest-time-hour-digits-are-coupled.text: The tens-hour digit and ones-hour digit are coupled: `t[0]` depends on `t[1]`'s value and `t[1]` depends on resolved `t[0]`.

latest-time-left-to-right-greedy-is-opti.text: Resolving `?` digits left-to-right produces the maximum valid time because each higher-place digit dominates all lower-place digits combined.

latest-time-minute-digits-are-independen.text: Minute digits at positions 3 and 4 have fixed maxima 5 and 9 regardless of other positions because minutes range from 00 to 59.

latest-time-question-mark-in-ones-hour-a.text: When `t[1]` is `?`, `t[0]` can safely be set to `2` because `t[1]` will later resolve to at most 3.

lazy-single-pair-parsing.text: `StringIterator` parses at most one `(char, count)` pair at a time via a cursor — it never pre-processes the entire compressed string, keeping memory O(1) even for counts up to 10^9.

lc2099-function-misnamed-copypaste.text: `find-subsequence-of-length-k-with-the-largest-sum/solution.py` exports a function named `count_patterns_in_word` that actually selects a max-sum subsequence — a copy-paste naming error from another solution, suggesting batch generation of solution files.

lc2099-k-exceeds-length-returns-fewer-el.text: In `find-subsequence-of-length-k-with-the-largest-sum/solution.py`, if `k > len(nums)`, the function returns fewer than `k` elements because the `[:k]` slice takes all available elements.

lc2099-output-exactly-k-for-valid-k.text: For valid `1 <= k <= len(nums)`, the `find-subsequence-of-length-k-with-the-largest-sum` function returns exactly `k` elements.

lc2099-runs-in-on-log-n-time.text: The `find-subsequence-of-length-k-with-the-largest-sum` algorithm runs in O(n log n) time and O(n) space.

lcis-assumes-nonempty.text: `findLengthOfLCIS` initializes `max_len = 1` with no empty-array guard, returning 1 for empty input — correct only under LeetCode's `len >= 1` constraint

lcis-contiguous-not-subsequence.text: Despite the problem title saying "subsequence," `findLengthOfLCIS` finds a contiguous subarray — the problem name is historically misleading on LeetCode

lcis-inline-max-update.text: `findLengthOfLCIS` updates `max_len` only inside the increasing branch (when `cur_len` grows), not after every iteration, avoiding redundant comparisons

lcis-linear-time-constant-space.text: `findLengthOfLCIS` runs in O(n) time and O(1) space using a single pass with two integer counters.

lcis-strictly-increasing.text: `findLengthOfLCIS` breaks the streak on equal elements (uses `>`, not `>=`), so `[1, 1, 1]` returns 1

lcp-early-termination.text: `longest_common_prefix` terminates as soon as any single string diverges or ends, never examining characters past the common prefix length

lcp-empty-input-returns-empty.text: An empty input list to `longest_common_prefix` returns `""` without accessing any element

lcp-first-element-pivot.text: `longest_common_prefix` uses `strs[0]` as the reference string and checks all remaining strings against it, avoiding an upfront `min(len(s))` computation

lcp-inner-loop-slices.text: `longest_common_prefix` iterates `strs[1:]` in the inner loop, allocating a new list slice on each outer iteration; a `range(1, len(strs))` index loop would avoid this

lcp-vertical-scan.text: `longest_common_prefix` scans characters column-by-column across all strings (vertical scanning), not by comparing pairs of strings sequentially

lcp-worst-case-complexity.text: Worst-case time O(S) where S is total characters is correct but too generic — this is the trivial lower bound for any LCP algorithm and doesn't distinguish this implementation

leading-zero-collapse.text: This is standard Python `int()` behavior, not a codebase-specific invariant. Any Python developer would expect `int("007") == 7`.

leading-zero-rejection.text: Any numeric segment in `abbr` starting with `'0'` causes `validWordAbbreviation` to immediately return `False`, including standalone `0` (semantically meaningless "skip zero characters").

leaf-similar-get-leaves-is-recursive-dfs.text: `get_leaves` collects leaf values with recursive depth-first traversal, returning a single-element list for a node with no children.

leaf-similar-get-leaves-returns-left-to-.text: `get_leaves` returns leaf values in left-to-right order because it recurses into `node.left` before `node.right` and concatenates in that order.

leaf-similar-list-concatenation-log-line.text: `get_leaves` uses list concatenation, giving O(n log n) work for a balanced tree instead of optimal O(n) with append or generators.

leaf-similar-none-roots-compare-equal.text: Two `None` roots are leaf-similar because `get_leaves(None)` returns `[]` and `[] == []` is true.

leaf-tilt-is-zero.text: Mathematical consequence of the algorithm, not a codebase invariant — follows directly from the null base case returning 0. Not useful as a standalone belief.

leap-day-count-uses-y-minus-1.text: `_days_from_epoch` counts leap days for completed years `1..(y-1)`, not `1..y`, because the current year's leap day is handled separately via the `month > 2` correction

leap-year-adjustment-only-after-feb.text: `dayOfYear` adds 1 for leap years only when `month > 2`, correctly handling that Feb 29 itself is already counted by the `day` component when the date is in February.

leetcode-bank-closed-form.text: `totalMoney` computes the answer in O(1) time and space using arithmetic series formulas rather than simulating day-by-day deposits.

leetcode-bank-integer-only-arithmetic.text: The method uses only integer arithmetic with `//` and avoids floating point entirely.

leetcode-bank-remaining-days-sum-formula.text: The partial-week total is computed as `remaining_days * (full_weeks + 1) + remaining_days * (remaining_days - 1) // 2`, an arithmetic series starting at `full_weeks + 1`.

leetcode-bank-returns-zero-for-n-zero.text: Passing `n = 0` returns `0` because `full_weeks` and `remaining_days` are both `0`.

leetcode-imported-by-lists-misleading.text: The tooling's "Imported By" cross-reference lists are misleadingly large — each problem's `test_solution.py` imports only its own directory's `solution.py`, not other problems' solutions

leetcode-judge-optimized-not-reusable.text: Design decisions — no input validation, in-place mutation of arguments, per-directory duplication of data structures — collectively optimize solutions for single-run correctness on LeetCode's online judge rather than for reuse, composability, or library consumption.

justifications.label: each decision is rational for a judge environment (trusted input, single caller, no shared state) but would be a defect in reusable library code

leetcode-no-input-validation-convention.text: Solutions assume inputs satisfy LeetCode's stated constraints and perform zero validation or error handling — invalid inputs either raise unhandled exceptions or produce wrong output silently.

leetcode-pipeline-found-17-bugs.text: The LeetCode pipeline found 17 bugs across 510 AI-generated solutions through belief network analysis.

leetcode-repo-mixed-function-style.text: Solutions inconsistently use either a `Solution` class with methods or bare module-level functions — both patterns coexist in the repo

leetcode-solution-class-convention.text: Every problem directory contains a `solution.py` with a `Solution` class exposing a single public method, following LeetCode's standard interface pattern.

leetcode-solutions-assume-valid-input.text: Solutions throughout the repo omit input validation (bounds checking, type checks, empty-state guards), relying on LeetCode's guaranteed-valid-input contract. Invalid inputs may raise uncaught exceptions or produce silently wrong results.

leetcode-solutions-no-input-validation.text: Solutions across the repo perform no input validation — they trust LeetCode's guaranteed constraints and raise unhandled exceptions on malformed input.

leetcode-solutions-no-validation-convent.text: All LeetCode solutions in this repo omit input validation, trusting the caller to satisfy the problem's stated constraints; this is a deliberate convention matching LeetCode's guaranteed-valid-input contract.

leetcode-solutions-omit-input-validation.text: Solutions in this repo consistently perform no input validation (no bounds checking, type checking, or constraint verification), relying entirely on LeetCode's problem guarantees enforced by the judge.

leetcode-solutions-skip-input-validation.text: All solution functions rely on LeetCode's input constraints rather than performing their own bounds checking; invalid inputs produce undefined behavior (empty strings, IndexError, etc.)

leetcode-solutions-trust-constraints.text: Solutions in this repo perform no input validation (no bounds checks, no type checks, no empty-input guards); they rely on LeetCode's guaranteed preconditions, and invalid inputs cause raw Python exceptions (`IndexError`, `ValueError`).

leetcode-solutions-trust-input-constrain.text: Solutions in this repo universally omit input validation (null checks, range checks, format checks), relying on LeetCode's guarantee that inputs satisfy stated constraints. This is by design, not an oversight.

leetcode-solutions-trust-input-contracts.text: Across all solutions in the repo, functions perform no input validation and raise no exceptions — they trust callers to satisfy LeetCode problem constraints. Invalid inputs (empty arrays, wrong types, violated invariants) produce silent wrong results or unguarded crashes.

leetcode-solutions-trust-input-conventio.text: Solutions across the repo generally perform no input validation beyond problem-specific guards (e.g., empty-input check in destCity), trusting LeetCode's constraints for type safety, value ranges, and structural guarantees.

left-biased-binary-search-pattern.text: First-bad-version uses left-biased binary search: when `isBadVersion(mid)` is true, `right = mid` (not `mid - 1`) because `mid` itself may be the answer; when false, `left = mid + 1` since `mid` is definitively excluded.

left-leaf-root-never-counted.text: A single-node tree returns 0 from `sum_of_left_leaves` because the root is seeded with `is_left=False` — the root cannot be a "left leaf" regardless of its children.

left-mid-bias-on-even-length.text: `(left + right) // 2` selects the left-middle element for even-length ranges, producing a left-leaning balanced BST; choosing `(left + right + 1) // 2` would also be valid.

left-right-sum-answer-element-is-abs-lef.text: Each output element is `abs(left - right)`, where `left` is the sum before the current index and `right` is the sum after the current index.

left-right-sum-empty-input-returns-empty.text: An empty input list produces an empty output list because the loop body never runs.

left-right-sum-output-length-equals-inpu.text: The output list always has the same length as the input list.

left-right-sum-right-computed-before-lef.text: The right sum is computed before `left` is updated with the current element, so `left` represents the sum of elements strictly before index `i`.

left-to-right-no-backtrack.text: Subsumed by the broader `greedy-three-chars-always-sufficient` belief, which already implies single-pass resolution.

leftovers-equals-odd-frequency-count.text: The `leftovers` value returned by `count_pairs_leftovers` equals the number of distinct values in `nums` that appear an odd number of times, since each contributes exactly `count % 2 == 1`.

lemonade-change-early-return.text: The lemonade-change solution short-circuits with `False` at the first customer who can't receive correct change, skipping the rest of the queue.

lemonade-change-o-n-time-o1-space.text: The lemonade-change algorithm runs in O(n) time and O(1) space, using only the two integer counters `fives` and `tens`.

lemonade-change-returns-true-after-compl.text: The lemonade-change solution returns `True` only after processing every bill without encountering a change failure.

lemonade-change-ten-dollar-requires-five.text: For a $10 bill, the lemonade-change solution owes $5 change and returns `False` if no $5 bill is available.

lemonade-greedy-order-is-critical.text: For $20 bills, the lemonade-change solution must prefer $10+$5 over $5×3 — this ordering is required for correctness, not just an optimization.

length-of-last-word-assumes-english-lett.text: `length_of_last_word` assumes each word consists only of English letters, so punctuation is not treated as a word separator.

length-of-last-word-no-empty-guard.text: `length_of_last_word` assumes `s` contains at least one word; passing an empty or all-whitespace string raises `IndexError` from `split()[-1]`.

length-of-last-word-o-n-space.text: `length_of_last_word` runs in O(n) space because `split()` materializes the full word list, not just the last word.

length-of-last-word-rstrip-redundant.text: Too implementation-specific — documenting that a particular call is redundant is a code review comment, not a codebase invariant. It would break nothing if rstrip were removed or kept.

length-of-last-word-rstrip-redundant-wit.text: The `rstrip()` call in `length_of_last_word` is redundant with no-argument `str.split()` for trailing whitespace, though it makes the intent explicit.

length-of-last-word-runs-in-linear-time.text: `length_of_last_word` runs in O(n) time because it scans the string and materializes the split word list.

length-of-last-word-uses-no-arg-split.text: `length_of_last_word` relies on `str.split()` with no arguments, which collapses consecutive whitespace and strips leading/trailing spaces — distinct from `str.split(' ')`.

lexicographic-hhmm-is-chronological.text: Comparing `"HH:MM"` strings with `<=` produces correct chronological ordering because the format is fixed-width and zero-padded; this breaks if the input is not zero-padded (e.g., `"9:30"` instead of `"09:30"`).

lexicographic-ordering-suffices.text: Too narrow — this is a property of one specific problem's candidate set (3-char same-digit strings), not a reusable codebase invariant

lhs-counter-based-linear.text: `findLHS` runs in O(n) time and O(n) space via a single `Counter` construction and one pass over distinct keys

lhs-one-directional-check.text: `findLHS` only checks `k + 1` in the counter (never `k - 1`), ensuring each valid adjacent pair is counted exactly once without double-counting

lhs-returns-zero-for-uniform-list.text: `findLHS` returns 0 when all elements are identical, because a harmonious subsequence requires max - min == 1, not 0

lhs-subsequence-not-subarray.text: `findLHS` correctly treats the input as a subsequence problem (order-independent) by using frequency counts rather than positional logic

license-key-assumes-k-at-least-one.text: The license-key-formatting solution assumes `k >= 1`; passing `k=0` causes a `ZeroDivisionError` on the remainder calculation.

license-key-empty-input-safe.text: License-key-formatting handles all-dashes or empty input without error — the loop range is empty, `parts` stays `[]`, and `"-".join([])` returns `""`.

license-key-first-group-remainder.text: In license-key-formatting, the first group size equals `len(cleaned) % k`; all subsequent groups are exactly `k` characters.

license-key-output-has-no-edge-dashes.text: The license-key-formatting output has no leading or trailing dashes because the parts list is never padded with empty strings.

license-key-output-never-contains-lowerc.text: The license-key-formatting output never contains lowercase letters because `.upper()` is applied to the entire cleaned string before grouping.

license-key-strip-then-partition.text: The license-key-formatting solution uses the strip-then-partition pattern: destroy all existing structure (`replace` + `upper`), then rebuild from scratch — avoiding edge cases around existing group boundaries.

limited-sum-uses-accumulate-and-bisect.text: The solution imports `bisect.bisect_right`, `itertools.accumulate`, and `typing.List`, using `accumulate` to build the prefix sums and `bisect_right` for each query.

line-break-before-overflow.text: In the line-writing solution (problem 806), a new line starts *before* the character that would exceed 100 pixels; a character landing exactly at 100 does not trigger a break

line-writing-empty-string-returns-one-li.text: For an empty input string, the line-writing solution returns [1, 0] because lines is initialized to 1 and never incremented.

line-writing-greedy-no-lookahead.text: The number-of-lines solution packs characters greedily onto each line without lookahead or backtracking.

line-writing-linear-time-constant-space.text: The number-of-lines solution runs in O(n) time for string length n and uses O(1) extra space.

line-writing-widths-no-length-validation.text: The line-writing solution performs no validation that widths has 26 entries, so an accessed letter whose ordinal offset falls outside the list raises IndexError.

linear-time-complexity.text: Generic O(n+m) complexity claim for `countWords` — this is obvious from reading two-Counter-plus-iteration code and not an invariant that could be violated.

linear-time-constant-passes-min-ops.text: Time complexity of a specific one-liner is trivially derivable from reading the code and not an invariant that could be violated.

linear-time-constant-space.text: Trivial complexity observation, not an invariant a developer needs to maintain.

linear-time-guarantee.text: Complexity analysis of a well-known algorithm; not a surprising or codebase-specific fact.

linear-time-linear-space.text: Generic complexity classification, not a testable codebase claim. Every solution has some complexity; stating it per-problem doesn't add architectural value.

linear-time-no-simulation.text: `count_pairs_leftovers` avoids the O(n^2) pair-removal simulation described in the problem and instead uses O(n) frequency counting with `Counter` plus integer division.

linear-time-two-scan.text: `maxDistance` achieves O(n) time and O(1) space via two linear scans with early termination, anchoring at opposite endpoints.

linear-worst-case-constant-best-case.text: Complexity analysis of a single solution — trivially derivable from the code and not a constraint that guides future development

linked-list-cycle-empty-list-returns-fal.text: `hasCycle` returns `False` for an empty linked list because `fast` is `None` and the loop does not execute.

linked-list-cycle-make-list-no-bounds-ch.text: `make_list` in linked-list-cycle does not validate `pos` against `len(vals)`; an out-of-range positive `pos` raises `IndexError`.

linked-list-cycle-read-only.text: `hasCycle` never modifies the list — it is a purely read-only traversal, preserving the original structure.

linked-list-cycle-tests-use-vals-pos-for.text: The linked-list-cycle tests use the `(vals, pos)` format matching LeetCode's test-case specification for this problem.

linked-list-intersection-empty-head-safe.text: If either headA or headB is None, getIntersectionNode still converges and returns None rather than raising an error.

linked-list-intersection-identity-not-eq.text: `getIntersectionNode` uses `a is not b` (identity comparison), not value equality — two nodes with the same `val` at different addresses are not considered an intersection.

linked-list-intersection-no-mutation.text: getIntersectionNode does not modify the input linked lists; it only reassigns its local pointer variables.

linked-list-intersection-o1-space.text: getIntersectionNode uses exactly two pointer variables regardless of input size, achieving O(1) auxiliary space.

linked-list-two-pointer-redirect-converg.text: The two-pointer redirect trick guarantees convergence: each pointer traverses both lists (total `len(A) + len(B)` nodes), so they align at the intersection node or both reach `None` simultaneously if lists don't intersect.

list-concat-not-optimal.text: Performance characteristics of a single solution's helper function — too narrow and solution-specific to be a useful cross-cutting belief.

list-to-tree-assumes-valid-input.text: Every LeetCode solution in this repo assumes valid input per the problem contract — this isn't a distinguishing invariant.

list-to-tree-none-entries-advance-index.text: list_to_tree treats None entries as missing children but still advances the input index, maintaining level-order alignment.

listnode-default-val-zero-next-none.text: The `ListNode` constructor defaults `val` to 0 and `next` to `None`.

listnode-defined-locally-per-problem.text: `ListNode` is defined locally in each linked-list problem's `solution.py` rather than imported from a shared module — keeps solutions self-contained but means the class is duplicated across every linked-list problem in the repo.

listnode-defined-per-solution.text: `ListNode` is redefined locally in each linked-list solution file rather than imported from a shared module, keeping each problem directory self-contained.

listnode-is-shared-definition.text: Conflicts with `shared-linked-list-infra` — that belief attributes the shared `ListNode` to `merge-two-sorted-lists/solution.py` (400+ importers), while this one attributes it to `middle-of-the-linked-list/solution.py` (300+ importers). Both entries acknowledge the import counts may be artifacts of the dependency graph tool. Need to verify which file is the actual canonical source before accepting either as definitive.

listnode-shared-dependency.text: `ListNode`, `from_list`, and `to_list` defined in `remove-linked-list-elements/solution.py` are imported by hundreds of other problem directories as the repo's de facto shared linked list utilities, despite living under a single problem's directory.

log-n-time-constant-space.text: Too problem-specific; this is a standard complexity fact about binary search, not a codebase invariant a developer needs to remember.

logger-10s-boundary-inclusive.text: A message printed at timestamp `t` can be printed again at exactly `t + 10` — the comparison is `>=`, making the blocked window `[t, t+10)`.

logger-assumes-non-decreasing-timestamps.text: The logger solution assumes timestamps arrive in non-decreasing order and never handles a late message arriving before an earlier one.

logger-has-single-state-field.text: The `Logger` class has exactly one state field, `next_allowed`.

logger-no-state-change-on-reject.text: When `shouldPrintMessage` returns `False`, the `next_allowed` dict is not modified — only accepted messages update state.

logger-should-print-message-o1-per-call.text: `Logger.shouldPrintMessage` performs O(1) work per call, using a single dict lookup and comparison.

logger-stores-next-allowed-not-last-seen.text: The logger stores `timestamp + 10` (next-allowed time) rather than the last-seen timestamp, collapsing the acceptance check to a single `>=` comparison.

logger-unbounded-memory.text: The logger's `next_allowed` dict is never pruned; memory grows monotonically with the number of distinct messages over the logger's lifetime.

logger-unseen-message-always-prints.text: A never-seen message always returns `True` because `dict.get(message, 0)` returns `0`, which any non-negative timestamp satisfies.

lonely-detection-parent-perspective.text: Lonely-node detection operates from the parent's perspective (checking if exactly one child exists), which structurally excludes the root from results without special-casing.

lonely-detection-xor-logic.text: A child is appended to lonely-node results if and only if exactly one of `(left, right)` exists at the parent — a logical XOR on child presence, implemented via `if`/`elif` branches.

lonely-nodes-order-not-guaranteed.text: The order of values in the lonely-nodes result list is not guaranteed, and the test suite sorts before comparing.

lonely-nodes-preorder-visit-once.text: The lonely-nodes DFS traverses the tree in preorder (parent check, then left, then right) and visits every non-null node exactly once, yielding O(n) time complexity.

long-press-full-consumption.text: `isLongPressedName` returns `i == len(name)` to reject cases where `typed` is a valid long-press prefix of `name` but doesn't cover all characters

long-press-greedy-order.text: The `isLongPressedName` algorithm never backtracks pointer `i`; each character in `name` is matched at most once, left to right, using a greedy two-pointer approach

long-press-j0-guard.text: The `j > 0` guard in `isLongPressedName` prevents `typed[j-1]` from wrapping to the last character when `j == 0`, ensuring the first character must match `name[0]` or fail

long-press-three-case-dispatch.text: Each character in `typed` is handled by exactly one of three cases: match (advance `i`), long-press repeat (skip), or mismatch (return False immediately)

long-press-time-complexity.text: `isLongPressedName` runs in O(len(typed)) time with O(1) extra space since pointer `i` only moves forward and the loop visits each `typed` character exactly once

longest-palindrome-empty-string-returns-.text: When called with an empty string, `longestPalindrome` returns 0 because the Counter is empty and `has_odd` remains False.

longest-palindrome-linear-time.text: The `longestPalindrome` algorithm runs in O(n) time and uses O(1) auxiliary space bounded by the 52-character alphabet.

longest-palindrome-uses-collections-coun.text: `longestPalindrome` imports and uses `collections.Counter` to build the character frequency map in O(n) time.

longest-task-assumes-nonempty-sorted-log.text: The employee-longest-task solution assumes `logs` is non-empty and sorted by leave time, with no validation enforcing either precondition.

longest-task-first-starts-at-zero.text: The employee-longest-task solution treats the first task as starting at time 0, capturing its duration as `logs[0][1]` directly without explicit subtraction.

longest-task-parameter-n-unused.text: The `n` parameter in `worker_with_longest_task` exists solely to match the LeetCode signature and has no effect on the algorithm or output.

longest-task-single-pass-o1-space.text: `worker_with_longest_task` makes exactly one pass over `logs` using three scalar variables — O(n) time, O(1) space.

longest-task-tie-break-smallest-id.text: When two tasks have equal duration, `worker_with_longest_task` retains the employee with the strictly smaller ID, not the one encountered first.

lookup-abstraction-trio-covers-all-queri.text: Three lookup abstractions recur across the repo's solution patterns: Counter for frequency, multiset, and pair-counting queries; set conversion for O(1) membership and dedup checks; and binary search for convergence-based positional queries. Together these cover a broad range of query patterns encountered in the codebase, each providing efficient time complexity for its query type.

justifications.label: Three abstractions partition the query-type space with no overlap and no gaps

lookup-abstractions-enable-linear-time-a.text: The three lookup abstractions (Counter, set, binary search) are the mechanism that converts preprocessing investment into linear-time scans across both paradigms: hash preprocessing enables O(1) per-query lookups while sort preprocessing enables O(log n) binary search, and both reduce what would be O(n²) nested iteration to O(n) or O(n log n) single-pass scans.

justifications.label: The trio bridges preprocessing and scanning — without these abstractions, preprocessing would not improve asymptotic complexity of the scan phase

lookup-abstractions-instantiate-pipeline.text: The lookup abstraction trio (Counter, set, binary search) is the load-bearing joint between the pipeline's preprocessing and scanning phases — each preprocessing paradigm (hash or sort) establishes exactly the data structure one of these abstractions queries, making the lookup the mechanism that converts preprocessing investment into linear-time scan payoff across both pipeline instantiations.

justifications.label: Connects the abstract pipeline decomposition (two forms) with the concrete computational mechanism (three lookup abstractions) that makes each form work

lookup-string-as-digit-map.text: `hex_chars = "0123456789abcdef"` uses string indexing as a lightweight digit-to-character mapping, avoiding dictionaries or conditional chains.

loop-terminates-at-one.text: The width search loop always terminates because `w = 1` divides every positive integer, serving as a universal fallback.

lowercase-only-regex-fails-uppercase-inp.text: The regex `[a-z]` only replaces lowercase letters; uppercase letters or special characters survive and can cause `.split()` to produce tokens containing non-digits.

lstrip-zero-fallback-prevents-empty-key.text: The `or '0'` guard after `lstrip('0')` in `num_different_integers` ensures all-zero strings like `"000"` canonicalize to `"0"` rather than the empty string, which would silently miscount distinct integers.

lucky-numbers-at-most-one-when-distinct.text: With distinct matrix values, there can be at most one lucky number, because two elements each being row minimum and column maximum would imply a contradiction.

lucky-numbers-distinct-values-required.text: The lucky numbers solution uses `row.index(min_val)` which returns the first occurrence; correctness depends on all matrix values being distinct, as duplicates could cause incorrect column selection.

lucky-numbers-lte-equivalence.text: The `<=` vs `<` distinction on a specific line is too fine-grained and tied to an implementation detail that could change with any refactor; the distinct-values-required belief already captures the underlying constraint.

lucky-numbers-row-min-then-col-max.text: The algorithm finds row minimums first, then validates each candidate as a column maximum via a linear scan; it never independently scans columns to find maximums.

lus-constant-space.text: O(1) space for a two-line equality check is too obvious to be worth tracking as a belief.

lus-mathematical-reduction.text: Longest Uncommon Subsequence I collapses to a string equality check: if strings differ, return `max(len(a), len(b))`; if equal, return `-1` — no subsequence enumeration needed.

lus-no-external-dependencies.text: Trivial dependency fact — same as above, "uses no imports" is directly visible from the source and not architecturally significant.

majority-check-absent-target-returns-fal.text: If `target` is absent from `nums`, `is_majority_element` returns False because either the bounds check fails or `nums[first + n // 2] != target`.

majority-check-bounds-safe.text: The short-circuit `and` in `is_majority_element` guarantees `nums[first + n // 2]` is never accessed out of bounds — the left operand `first + n // 2 < n` must be true before the right operand is evaluated.

majority-check-empty-array-returns-false.text: For an empty `nums`, `is_majority_element` computes `n = 0`, `first = 0`, and `0 + 0 < 0` is False, so it returns False.

majority-check-majority-implies-n-half-i.text: If `target` is a majority element starting at index `first`, then `nums[first + n // 2]` must also equal `target`.

majority-check-no-input-validation.text: Redundant with the repo-wide pattern that LeetCode solutions trust caller preconditions — this is not specific enough to this solution to warrant its own belief.

majority-element-initializes-candidate-a.text: majority_element initializes candidate = 0 and count = 0 before scanning the input list.

mathematical-insight-replaces-brute-comp.text: Solutions leverage mathematical reasoning — closed-form formulas for arithmetic series, greedy optimality proofs for prefix-free codes and assignment problems, algebraic reductions — to replace iterative or exhaustive computation with provably correct O(1) or O(n) alternatives.

justifications.label: Both patterns achieve the same outcome (bypassing brute-force enumeration) via the same means (a mathematical argument that a simpler computation yields the same answer); they differ only in whether the shortcut is algebraic or algorithmic

mathematical-reduction-eliminates-all-ru.text: Mathematical reduction achieves the logical extreme of the space minimization strategy: by replacing iteration with closed-form computation, it eliminates both the algorithmic state (running accumulators that streaming requires) and structural state (preprocessed data structures that pipeline solutions require), collapsing the entire scan-accumulate loop to a single constant-time evaluation with zero auxiliary memory.

justifications.label: Mathematical reduction is the degenerate case of the dual space-minimization strategy where both algorithmic and structural state reduce to zero

mathematical-reduction-is-degenerate-str.text: Closed-form mathematical solutions are degenerate instances of the streaming paradigm: they reduce the "scan" to a single constant-time evaluation, eliminating not just preprocessing but iteration itself — the logical extreme of streaming's progressive elimination of computational prerequisites.

justifications.label: closed-form = streaming with zero iterations; extends streaming universality to O(1) solutions

mathematical-reduction-is-third-eliminat.text: Mathematical reduction (closed-form formulas, modular arithmetic) constitutes a third axis of the elimination principle alongside construction-based validation elimination and isolation-based coupling elimination: where construction eliminates runtime checks and isolation eliminates inter-module dependencies, mathematical reduction eliminates computational phases entirely.

justifications.label: Mathematical insight replaces computation (depth-2) and the repo's coherence comes from elimination not enforcement (depth-6); math reduction is the missing third arm — it eliminates computational phases just as construction eliminates validation and isolation eliminates coupling

mathematical-reduction-proves-streaming-.text: Closed-form mathematical solutions serve as constructive proofs of streaming's extremal minimality: by collapsing the streaming scan to a single constant-time evaluation while remaining within the paradigm (as degenerate instances), they demonstrate that the normal form admits reduction all the way to zero iteration — the theoretical minimum of the minimal strategy.

justifications.label: One antecedent shows math reduction as degenerate streaming, the other establishes streaming as the minimal normal form; together they identify math reduction as the constructive lower bound of that minimality

mathematical-reduction-unifies-simulatio.text: Closed-form algebraic formulas and modular arithmetic are two instances of the same strategy: replacing iterative simulation with direct mathematical computation, eliminating entire computational phases rather than optimizing them.

justifications.label: Both depth-1 conclusions eliminate loops/simulation via math but through different mechanisms (algebraic series vs modular structure); the shared principle is that mathematical insight makes the computation itself unnecessary

max-captured-forts-valid-pair-opposite-s.text: A valid pair in max_captured_forts consists of two non-zero values of opposite sign with only 0s between them.

max-diff-single-pass-linear.text: The algorithm is O(n) time and O(1) space with exactly one traversal of the input.

max-remap-first-non-nine.text: The max value in digit-remapping is always achieved by remapping the leftmost non-9 digit to 9, because that digit has the highest positional weight among improvable digits.

max-sum-pure-function.text: No side effects and no mutable state is the default expectation for a single-expression LeetCode solution; not a distinguishing invariant.

max-value-is-pure-linear.text: Trivially obvious — a single loop over the input with an accumulator is self-evidently O(n)/O(1). Not worth tracking as a belief.

merge-paradigm-linear-via-pointer-advanc.text: The merge problem family (merge-alternately, merge-nums, merge-two-lists) collectively demonstrates that pointer-per-input advancement achieves O(n+m) time with minimal allocation: each pointer advances monotonically, the merge is stable (equal-value ties broken by input ordering), and the output reuses existing nodes rather than allocating fresh ones.

merge-scan-extends-sort-pipeline-to-dual.text: The merge-scan pattern is the canonical extension of the sort-then-two-pointer pipeline to problems with two pre-sorted input sequences: instead of sorting a single array then scanning with converging pointers, it interleaves two already-sorted inputs using advancing pointers, preserving the pipeline's structure while accepting dual inputs.

justifications.label: merge-scan preserves sort-then-scan's structure while generalizing to dual sorted inputs

merge-scan-pattern-for-sorted-pair-proce.text: The two-pointer merge-scan pattern (maintain a pointer into each sorted sequence, advance the pointer on the smaller value, act on equality or exhaustion) is a recurring O(n+m) technique for processing paired elements from two sorted inputs — instantiated in merge-alternately (interleave by index), merge-nums (sum by matching ID), and min-common-number (return on first match).

justifications.label: Depth-1 cross-problem grouping: three solutions independently instantiate the same merge-scan template with different actions at the match/advance points

merge-similar-items-output-sorted-by-val.text: The return value of `sum_weights` is always sorted ascending by the first element (value) of each pair, enforced by `sorted()` on the final list comprehension.

merge-similar-items-self-contained-tests.text: `merge-similar-items/solution.py` includes both the solution and a `unittest.TestCase` with 7 test methods, runnable standalone via `__main__`.

merge-similar-items-sums-duplicates-with.text: `sum_weights` does not enforce uniqueness within each input list; if that precondition is violated, duplicate values within one list are summed together.

merge-similar-items-tests-cover-overlap-.text: The seven `TestSumWeights` test cases cover overlapping items, no overlap, full overlap, single elements, and boundary values up to 1000.

merge-similar-items-uses-defaultdict-acc.text: `sum_weights` uses `defaultdict(int)` to merge both lists in O(n) time before a single O(n log n) sort, rather than a two-pointer merge on pre-sorted input.

merge-stable-ordering.text: `merge_two_lists` is a stable merge: when both lists contain equal values, `list1`'s node appears first in the output due to the `<=` comparison.

merge-tail-append-remainder.text: After one list is exhausted, `merge_two_lists` attaches the remaining non-empty list in one step via `tail.next = list1 or list2`.

merge-trees-creates-new-nodes-for-overla.text: `merge_trees` allocates a new `TreeNode` for every position where both input trees have a node; it never mutates either input at overlapping positions.

merge-trees-hybrid-ownership-semantics.text: The merge-trees algorithm produces a hybrid ownership structure: overlapping positions get newly allocated nodes (independent of inputs), while non-overlapping subtrees are shared by reference with the original trees — the output's lifetime is entangled with both inputs, making it unsafe to mutate either input tree after merging.

justifications.label: Two merge-trees beliefs jointly reveal an ownership hazard invisible at the single-belief level

merge-trees-output-structure-is-union.text: The output tree's structure is the union of both input structures — every position that has a node in either input has a node in the output.

merge-trees-recursion-depth-equals-max-h.text: `merge_trees` recursion depth is bounded by the height of the taller input tree — O(log n) for balanced trees, O(n) worst case for skewed trees.

merge-trees-shares-subtrees-for-non-over.text: When one input tree is `None` at a position, `merge_trees` returns the other tree's subtree by reference — the output shares structure with the inputs for non-overlapping regions.

method-alias-for-test-harness.text: Solution classes alias the main method to a second name (e.g., `find_latest_step = countConsistentStrings`) with no semantic relationship to the algorithm — this exists purely to satisfy test infrastructure expectations

method-alias-is-shared-object.text: Implementation detail of Python class-level assignment semantics, not a codebase invariant. The important fact (why the alias exists) is captured in method-alias-is-test-harness-artifact.

method-alias-is-test-harness-artifact.text: `mincostTickets = divisorGame` in divisor-game/solution.py creates a class-level alias so the module satisfies generic `Solution` attribute lookups from other problems' test files — it has no semantic relationship to LeetCode 983.

method-alias-pattern-for-leetcode-names.text: The repo uses class-level aliasing (`correctName = wrongName`) to expose LeetCode-expected method names without wrapping overhead, as seen in `numberOfSteps = queensAttacktheKing`

method-name-mismatch-minimum-moves.text: `Solution.maximumRemovals` in `minimum-moves-to-convert-string/solution.py` is misnamed; it solves LeetCode 2027 (minimum moves to convert string), not LeetCode 1898 (maximum removals).

method-name-mismatch-pattern.text: Multiple solutions in the repo have method names from a different LeetCode problem due to copy-paste from templates (`maxSideLength` for 1413, `mctFromLeafValues` for 1228); tests likely bind to the wrong name to match.

method-name-mismatches-common.text: Multiple solutions use method names that don't match LeetCode's canonical names (e.g., `numberOfWays` for problem 806, `numberOfSets` for problem 1725, `queensAttacktheKing` for problem 1342) — a recurring pattern across the repo, not isolated typos

method-name-mismatches-exist.text: Multiple solutions use incorrect method names that don't match LeetCode's canonical names (e.g., `sortItems` instead of `freqAlphabets` for #1309, `minOperations` instead of `decrypt` for #1652) — likely copy-paste artifacts from scaffolding.

method-naming-inconsistencies.text: Multiple solutions have method names that don't match LeetCode canonical names (`possible_bipartition` for sortArrayByParityII, `maxValue` for sortEvenOdd), likely artifacts from the code generation pipeline.

middle-element-lo-le-hi.text: The `lo <= hi` condition (not `lo < hi`) in `flipAndInvertImage` is critical: it ensures the center element of odd-length rows is inverted exactly once when `lo == hi`.

middle-returns-node-not-copy.text: `middle_of_the_linked_list` returns the actual middle node object from the input list, not a copy.

min-abs-diff-empty-or-single-element-rai.text: Passing fewer than two elements to `minimumAbsDifference` causes `min()` to be called on an empty sequence, raising `ValueError`.

min-abs-diff-mutates-input.text: `minimumAbsDifference` mutates the caller's list via `arr.sort()` rather than working on a copy — standard for LeetCode solutions in this repo but relevant if the caller retains the list.

min-abs-diff-output-pairs-sorted-by-firs.text: `minimumAbsDifference` returns pairs naturally sorted ascending by their first element because the input array is sorted before collection; no separate output sort is performed.

min-abs-diff-relies-on-distinct-input.text: `minimumAbsDifference` relies on the problem's distinct-integer guarantee so that all adjacent differences after sorting are positive.

min-abs-diff-two-linear-passes.text: The `minimumAbsDifference` algorithm makes exactly two linear passes over the sorted array: one to compute the minimum adjacent difference, and one to collect all adjacent pairs matching that minimum.

min-abs-diff-two-pass.text: The two-pass structure (find min, then collect) is an implementation detail visible from a 5-second code read, not an invariant that guides other work.

min-bit-flips-method-signature.text: `minBitFlips` is an instance method on the `Solution` class with signature `(self, start: int, goal: int) -> int`.

min-bit-flips-negative-inputs-handled-by.text: Negative inputs to `minBitFlips` still produce a result because Python XOR handles negative integers via two's complement with infinite sign extension, though LeetCode constraints exclude them.

min-bit-flips-no-loops-branching-or-muta.text: `minBitFlips` is implemented without loops, branching, or mutation as `(start ^ goal)` followed by `bin(...).count('1')`.

min-common-loop-advances-at-least-one-po.text: Each iteration of the two-pointer scan in `min_common_number` advances at least one pointer, bounding the loop to at most len(nums1) + len(nums2) iterations.

min-common-number-has-no-side-effects.text: `min_common_number` has no side effects and does not mutate its input lists.

min-common-number-returns-negative-one-i.text: `min_common_number` returns -1 when no integer appears in both input lists.

min-cost-assumes-length-ge-2.text: `minCostClimbingStairs` will raise `IndexError` if `cost` has fewer than 2 elements; it relies on the LeetCode constraint `len(cost) >= 2` without validation.

min-cost-cost-range-0-to-999.text: The min cost climbing stairs problem guarantees each cost element is between 0 and 999 inclusive.

min-cost-dp-recurrence.text: The DP recurrence used in `minCostClimbingStairs` is `dp[i] = cost[i] + min(dp[i-1], dp[i-2])`.

min-cost-dp-uses-constant-space.text: `minCostClimbingStairs` uses O(1) auxiliary space via two rolling variables (`prev1`, `prev2`) instead of an O(n) DP array.

min-cost-final-answer-is-min-of-last-two.text: The final `min(prev1, prev2)` is necessary because you can reach the top (one past the last index) from either of the last two steps.

min-cost-loop-invariant.text: After processing index `i`, `prev1` holds the minimum cost to reach and pay step `i`, and `prev2` holds the same for step `i-1`.

min-cuts-colocated-tests.text: `minimum-cuts-to-divide-a-circle/solution.py` contains both the solution function and its `unittest.TestCase` in the same file, in addition to the separate `test_solution.py` — following a pattern of colocated tests for some solutions.

min-cuts-constant-time.text: A three-branch function with no loops is obviously O(1) — stating this adds no useful information for a developer working in the codebase.

min-cuts-does-not-validate-n.text: `min_cuts` does not validate that `n >= 1`; inputs outside the LeetCode constraint can produce silently wrong results.

min-cuts-even-half-odd-full.text: `min_cuts(n)` returns 0 for n=1, n//2 for even n, and n for odd n > 1 — even-numbered slices allow diameter reuse (each cut creates two boundaries) while odd-numbered slices cannot.

min-cuts-input-domain-is-one-to-one-hund.text: LeetCode constrains `min_cuts` input to `1 <= n <= 100`, and the function relies on that guarantee.

min-cuts-runs-in-constant-time.text: `min_cuts` runs in O(1) time and O(1) space with no loops, recursion, or data structures.

min-diff-bst-defines-nested-recursive-in.text: minDiffInBST defines a nested recursive inorder(node) function and invokes it on the root to perform the traversal.

min-diff-bst-linear-time-tree-height-spa.text: minDiffInBST runs in O(n) time and O(h) stack space by streaming in-order values without materializing a list.

min-diff-bst-returns-inf-below-two-nodes.text: minDiffInBST returns float('inf') when the tree has fewer than two nodes because self.prev remains None and no adjacent difference is computed.

min-digit-sum-empty-list-raises-valueerr.text: Calling sum_of_digits with an empty nums list raises ValueError from min().

min-digit-sum-mutates-local-min-value.text: The while loop destructively consumes a local min_val copy, leaving the original nums list unchanged.

min-digit-sum-uses-single-min-call.text: Solution.sum_of_digits finds the minimum element with a single min(nums) call rather than by sorting.

min-digit-sum-zero-minimum-returns-one.text: If the minimum element is 0, the digit-extraction loop is skipped and the function returns 1 because the digit sum 0 is even.

min-distance-generator-not-list.text: `get_min_distance` uses a generator expression (lazy) inside `min()`, not a list comprehension, avoiding allocation of an intermediate list — O(1) auxiliary space.

min-distance-linear-time.text: O(n) complexity is the obvious and only approach for an unsorted array with no preprocessing — not a design decision that could be violated.

min-distance-no-imports.text: Having zero imports is trivially observable from the file and not an invariant that could be unknowingly violated.

min-distance-precondition-target-exists.text: `get_min_distance` raises `ValueError` if `target` is absent from `nums` because `min()` receives an empty generator; no internal guard exists.

min-max-alternation-resets-per-round.text: The min/max alternation resets each round — pair index `i` starts at 0, so the first pair always uses `min` regardless of which operation ended the previous round.

min-max-game-does-not-mutate-input.text: `min_steps` does not mutate the input array; it builds a new array each round and reassigns the local variable.

min-max-game-iterative-simulation.text: The min max game solution uses iterative simulation, building a new half-sized array each round, rather than recursion or a mathematical shortcut.

min-max-game-linear-total-work.text: Total comparisons across all rounds is O(n) due to geometric halving (n/2 + n/4 + ... = n - 1).

min-max-game-no-input-validation.text: `min_steps` does not verify that `len(nums)` is a power of 2 or that the list is non-empty; invalid inputs produce silent wrong answers or `IndexError`.

min-max-game-returns-value-not-count.text: `min_steps` returns the last surviving element value, not the number of reduction rounds — the function name is misleading.

min-moves-length-one-or-two-returns-zero.text: For input lists of length 1 or 2, `min_moves` returns 0 because no value can be strictly between the minimum and maximum.

min-moves-no-empty-guard.text: `min_moves` calls `min()` and `max()` without guarding for empty input; an empty list raises `ValueError` — this is by design, relying on LeetCode's guarantee of non-empty input.

min-moves-precomputes-min-and-max-once.text: `min_moves` computes `min(nums)` and `max(nums)` once before the counting pass, avoiding per-element recomputation.

min-moves-pure-no-mutation.text: `min_moves` is a pure function that does not mutate `nums` or produce side effects.

min-moves-strict-inequality-excludes-bou.text: `min_moves` uses strict `<` comparisons, so elements equal to `min(nums)` or `max(nums)` are never counted — only interior values qualify.

min-moves-three-pass-linear.text: `min_moves` makes three O(n) passes (min, max, count) using a generator inside `sum()`, achieving O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

min-moves-to-seat-empty-input-returns-ze.text: Passing two empty lists to `min_moves_to_seat` returns 0 without error.

min-moves-to-seat-sorted-zip-sum.text: `min_moves_to_seat` computes total moves as `sum(abs(a - b) for a, b in zip(sorted(seats), sorted(students)))`.

min-moves-to-seat-space-complexity-on.text: `min_moves_to_seat` uses O(n) extra space for the sorted copies of `seats` and `students`.

min-moves-to-seat-time-complexity-nlogn.text: `min_moves_to_seat` runs in O(n log n) time because it sorts both input lists, and the summation pass is O(n).

min-moves-uniform-list-returns-zero.text: When all elements are identical, `min_val == max_val` makes the condition `min_val < x < max_val` unsatisfiable, correctly returning 0 without special-casing.

min-of-adjacent-groups.text: In `count_binary_substrings`, the number of valid binary substrings spanning two adjacent groups of sizes a and b is exactly `min(a, b)` — this is the mathematical invariant the O(1)-space algorithm relies on.

min-on-empty-is-unguarded.text: `max_distance` crashes with `ValueError` from `min()` on an empty generator if `k > len(nums)`; no explicit validation exists.

min-operations-is-misnamed.text: The function `min_operations` in `convert-binary-number-in-a-linked-list-to-integer/solution.py` performs binary-to-integer conversion, not any "minimum operations" computation; the name doesn't match the problem.

min-ops-equals-distinct-positives.text: `minOperations` in `make-array-zero-by-subtracting-equal-amounts/solution.py` returns `len(set(nums) - {0})` — the count of distinct positive values — because each subtraction operation eliminates exactly one distinct positive value.

min-ops-increasing-empty-input-crashes.text: `min_operations` (array increasing) accesses `nums[0]` unconditionally — passing an empty list raises an unhandled `IndexError`.

min-ops-increasing-first-element-unchang.text: `min_operations` initializes `prev = nums[0]` and starts its loop at index 1, so the first element is never modified.

min-ops-increasing-greedy-optimal.text: `min_operations` is globally optimal because setting a violating element to exactly `prev + 1` minimizes total operations; any larger target increases total operations without benefit to later elements.

min-ops-increasing-on-violation-sets-pre.text: When `nums[i] <= prev`, `min_operations` increments `prev` by 1 to `prev + 1` as the minimum valid value for the current element.

min-ops-increasing-ops-adds-prev-minus-n.text: After setting `prev += 1`, `min_operations` adds `prev - nums[i]` to `ops` to account for increments needed at that position.

min-ops-linear-time.text: O(n) time for a single-pass loop is self-evident from the code structure; not a surprising or breakable invariant.

min-recolors-function-named-min-operatio.text: The recolors solution's function is named `min_operations`, even though it computes a minimum number of recolors.

min-recolors-initial-window-uses-str-cou.text: `min_operations` initializes the first window's white count with `blocks[0:k].count('W')` rather than using the incremental add/remove logic.

min-recolors-k-exceeds-length-returns-to.text: If `k > len(blocks)`, `min_operations` returns the count of `'W'` in the entire string because the loop body never executes, producing a semantically wrong answer.

min-recolors-min-ops-monotonic-nonincrea.text: `min_ops` in `min_operations` is monotonically non-increasing, updating only when the current window's white count is lower.

min-recolors-window-always-size-k.text: In `min_operations`, the sliding window always contains exactly `k` elements, with loop index `i` as the right edge and `i - k` as the element leaving the window.

min-remap-always-leading-digit.text: The min value in digit-remapping is always achieved by remapping `s[0]` to `'0'`, regardless of what `s[0]` is — leading zeros collapse naturally via `int()`.

min-scan-is-linear.text: Trivially obvious — `min()` is always O(n). Not a claim that would surprise or help anyone working in this codebase.

min-start-value-empty-nums-returns-1.text: An empty nums list returns 1 because the loop does not execute and min_sum stays 0.

min-start-value-guarantees-prefix-sum-at.text: The algorithm guarantees that for every index i, startValue + sum(nums[0..i]) >= 1.

min-start-value-returns-max-1-1-minus-mi.text: The return expression is max(1, 1 - min_sum), producing a startValue of at least 1.

min-start-value-runs-linear-time-constan.text: The algorithm runs in O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space using two scalar accumulators.

min-start-value-solution-implements-leet.text: The solution file implements LeetCode 1413 — Minimum Value to Get Positive Step by Step Sum.

min-start-value-tracks-minimum-prefix-su.text: The algorithm accumulates running_sum and tracks the minimum prefix sum seen so far in min_sum.

min-subarray-alias-is-generic.text: The `min_subarray` alias at module level is a project-wide test harness convention, not semantically related to the individual solution.

min-subsequence-always-terminates.text: Termination follows trivially from positive elements and bounded iteration — not a useful belief to track.

min-subsequence-empty-input-returns-empt.text: Passing an empty list to `min_subsequence` returns `[]` without error, although the problem guarantees non-empty input.

min-subsequence-greedy-descending-optima.text: Sorting `nums` descending and greedily taking elements until `subseq_sum > total - subseq_sum` produces the minimum-length subsequence whose sum exceeds the complement.

min-subsequence-integer-only-threshold.text: The threshold check `subseq_sum > total - subseq_sum` uses only integer arithmetic, avoiding floating-point precision issues that would arise from `subseq_sum > total / 2`.

min-subsequence-loop-terminates-within-l.text: The `min_subsequence` loop terminates in at most `len(nums)` iterations because every element is positive, guaranteeing `subseq_sum` eventually reaches `total`.

min-subsequence-mutates-input.text: `min_subsequence` calls `nums.sort(reverse=True)` in-place, reordering the caller's list as a side effect.

min-subsequence-result-descending-order.text: `min_subsequence` returns elements in non-increasing order because they are appended in sorted-descending traversal order.

min-sum-four-digit-assumes-four-digits-n.text: `min_operations` assumes exactly four digits and performs no bounds checking, so inputs outside 1000–9999 produce incorrect results rather than validation errors.

min-sum-four-digit-constructs-numbers-wi.text: `min_operations` constructs the two 2-digit numbers as `digits[0]*10 + digits[2]` and `digits[1]*10 + digits[3]` after sorting the digits ascending.

min-sum-four-digit-extracts-digits-via-s.text: `min_operations` converts the input integer to a string, iterates each character, and casts it to `int` to extract the four individual digits.

min-sum-init-zero-is-intentional.text: In the min-start-value solution, `min_sum` is initialized to 0 (not `-inf`) so that when all prefix sums are non-negative, the result is correctly `max(1, 1 - 0) = 1` without a special case.

min-time-typewriter-greedy-optimal.text: Processing characters left-to-right with shortest-arc moves is provably optimal for the typewriter problem; no lookahead or reordering can reduce total time because the pointer must visit each character in sequence.

min-time-typewriter-no-imports.text: Trivially observable from the file; "no imports" is not a meaningful architectural invariant worth tracking across the knowledge base.

min-time-typewriter-per-char-bound.text: Each character in the typewriter problem contributes exactly `min(|target - curr|, 26 - |target - curr|) + 1` seconds, bounded to `[1, 14]`.

min-time-typewriter-result-lower-bound.text: The claim that `result >= len(word)` is a direct arithmetic consequence of per-character cost being >= 1; it's derivable on demand and not an invariant that could be violated by code changes.

min-tracking-pattern-shared.text: `maxProfit` and `maximum-difference-between-increasing-elements/solution.py` share the same min-so-far tracking pattern: maintain a running minimum, compute max delta at each position.

min-training-hours-function-signature.text: The solution exports a single function `min_training_hours(initialEnergy, initialExperience, energy, experience) -> int`.

mindepth-bfs-over-dfs.text: `minDepth` uses BFS (level-order traversal) rather than DFS so it can return immediately at the first leaf encountered, avoiding full-tree traversal on unbalanced trees.

mindepth-depth-one-indexed.text: `minDepth` uses 1-indexed depth (root = 1), so a single-node tree returns 1 and an empty tree returns 0.

mindepth-queue-entries-store-node-and-de.text: Each BFS queue entry in `minDepth` is a `(node, depth)` tuple carrying the depth alongside the node.

mindepth-single-child-not-leaf.text: A node with exactly one child is never treated as a leaf in `minDepth`; the algorithm descends into the existing subtree — the key correctness property that distinguishes minimum depth from maximum depth.

mindepth-unreachable-return.text: Dead code for linter satisfaction is a common idiom, not a codebase invariant worth tracking.

mindepth-unreachable-return-after-loop-i.text: The `return 0` after the BFS while loop in `minDepth` is dead code because every non-empty tree has a leaf and the loop always returns via the early-exit check.

mindepth-uses-deque-for-bfs-queue.text: `minDepth` uses `collections.deque` and `popleft` for O(1) BFS queue operations.

minimum-moves-convert-empty-string-retur.text: An empty input string returns 0 from Solution.maximumRemovals because the while loop body never executes.

minimum-moves-convert-pointer-overrun-sa.text: After a move, i += 3 may place the pointer past len(s), and the while i < len(s) condition safely terminates the scan.

minimum-moves-convert-single-pass-linear.text: The maximumRemovals implementation of minimum-moves-to-convert-string runs in O(n) time and O(1) space with a single left-to-right scan.

minimum-training-hours-linear-time-const.text: The minimum training hours solution runs in O(n) time and O(1) space using scalar accumulators and no auxiliary data structures.

minimumcost-mutates-input-list.text: `minimumCost` calls `cost.sort(reverse=True)` in place, reordering the caller's list as a side effect.

minus-one-means-infeasible.text: distribute-money returns -1 if and only if `money < children`, the sole condition where giving every child at least $1 is impossible.

minus-one-sentinel-is-dual-purpose.text: Subsumed by the cross-cutting belief `sentinel-return-values-match-leetcode-spec` — the dual-purpose nature is an implementation detail, not a codebase invariant.

misleading-function-names-from-generatio.text: At least two solutions have wrapper/function names unrelated to their problem (`minimizeTheDifference` for palindrome finding, `mem_sticks_crash` for graph connectivity), indicating a systematic naming issue in the code generation pipeline.

misleading-method-names-exist.text: Some solution methods have names that do not reflect their algorithm — `countStrings` counts removal steps not strings, and `dfs` performs a greedy linear scan with no recursion or backtracking.

misnamed-method-split-and-minimize.text: `largest-3-same-digit-number-in-string/solution.py` defines `split_and_minimize` but the correct LeetCode signature is `largestGoodInteger` — likely a code generation pipeline bug

misnamed-module-exports-in-test-harness.text: Some solution modules export a module-level alias (e.g., `count_balls = Solution().replaceDigits`) that does not match the actual problem — this is a code-generation artifact from the repo's test harness, not a logic error.

missing-ap-constant-sequence-returns-arr.text: When expected_diff == 0, the code short-circuits and returns arr[0] because every element is identical.

missing-ap-fallback-returns-arr0.text: The function has a defensive fallback `return arr[0]` that should be unreachable under valid inputs if expected_diff != 0.

missing-ap-recovers-common-difference-fr.text: The algorithm computes expected_diff = (arr[-1] - arr[0]) // n to recover the common difference of the original progression.

missing-ap-runs-linear-time-constant-spa.text: The algorithm runs in O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

missing-ap-scans-adjacent-pairs-for-firs.text: The algorithm scans adjacent pairs and returns arr[i] + expected_diff at the first pair whose actual difference does not match expected_diff.

missing-ap-solution-implements-leetcode-.text: The solution file implements LeetCode 1228 — Missing Number In Arithmetic Progression.

missing-char-returns-zero.text: If any character in `target` is absent from `s`, `maxNumberOfCopies` returns 0 because `Counter.__getitem__` returns 0 for missing keys, making `0 // demand` yield 0.

missing-number-gauss-sum.text: `missing-number/solution.py` uses Gauss's formula `n*(n+1)//2 - sum(nums)` for O(n) time and O(1) space, rather than XOR, hash set, or sorting approaches.
