missing-number-integer-division-is-exact.text: The expression n * (n + 1) // 2 is always exact because one of two consecutive integers is even.

missing-number-n-is-len-nums.text: The algorithm sets n = len(nums), treating the input as n elements drawn from the range [0, n].

missing-number-no-validation.text: All LeetCode solutions in this repo skip input validation; this is a repo-wide convention, not a per-file fact worth tracking individually.

missing-number-o1-space.text: Redundant with `missing-number-gauss-sum` which already implies O(1) space — no data structures are involved in a subtraction.

missing-number-requires-distinct-values-.text: The formula assumes nums contains exactly n distinct values from [0, n]; duplicates or out-of-range values silently produce a wrong answer.

missing-number-requires-exactly-one-miss.text: The formula assumes exactly one value is absent; zero or multiple missing values silently produce a wrong answer.

missing-number-runs-linear-time-constant.text: The algorithm runs in O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

missing-number-solution-implements-leetc.text: The solution file implements LeetCode #268 — Missing Number.

missing-ranges-advances-cursor-to-num-pl.text: For each input element num, find_missing_ranges advances next_expected to num + 1 after checking for a gap.

missing-ranges-cursor-not-sentinel.text: `find_missing_ranges` uses a `next_expected` cursor to detect gaps rather than mutating the input by prepending `lower-1` / appending `upper+1` — the input list is never modified or copied.

missing-ranges-empty-input-returns-full-.text: When `nums` is empty, `find_missing_ranges` returns the single formatted range `[lower, upper]` — the loop body never executes and the post-loop residual check captures the entire bound.

missing-ranges-imports-only-typing-list.text: missing-ranges/solution.py imports only List from typing and has no external or internal dependencies.

missing-ranges-linear-time.text: Subsumed by the more specific `missing-ranges-cursor-not-sentinel` belief which already captures the single-pass O(n) nature along with the mechanism.

missing-ranges-post-loop-tail-gap-check.text: After the main loop, find_missing_ranges checks whether next_expected <= upper and appends the remaining tail gap [next_expected, upper] when true.

missing-ranges-precondition-sorted-uniqu.text: `find_missing_ranges` assumes `nums` is sorted, contains unique values, and all elements fall within `[lower, upper]` — none of these preconditions are validated at runtime.

missing-ranges-single-pass-linear-time.text: find_missing_ranges processes the sorted input in a single O(n) pass with no sorting, binary search, or set construction.

missing-target-returns-neg-one.text: `shortest_distance` returns `-1` when the target string is absent from the array, not 0 or an exception — the sentinel check `result < n` distinguishes found from not-found.

mixed-api-style-class-and-function.text: Solutions inconsistently use either a `Solution` class with instance methods (matching LeetCode's expected interface) or standalone module-level functions — both styles coexist in the repo.

mixed-solution-export-conventions.text: Some solutions export a `Solution` class with a method (e.g., `largestInteger`, `largestNumberAtLeastTwiceOfOthers`), while others export a bare function (e.g., `largest_matrix`, `largest_odd_number`) — the repo has no single enforced convention

mod-6-equivalence.text: The average-even-divisible-by-three solution collapses `n % 2 == 0 and n % 3 == 0` into `n % 6 == 0` using the fact that lcm(2, 3) = 6, a number-theory simplification that recurs across solutions with coprime divisibility checks.

mod-applied-per-multiply.text: In prime-arrangements, modular reduction (`% MOD`) is applied at each multiplication step rather than once at the end, keeping intermediate values bounded — a pattern used across competitive-programming solutions in this repo.

modular-arithmetic-avoids-large-integers.text: The binary-prefix-divisible-by-5 solution tracks only the remainder modulo 5 at each step (`remainder = (remainder * 2 + bit) % 5`), never constructing the actual binary number — a pattern for constant-space streaming over unbounded numeric sequences.

modular-arithmetic-eliminates-simulation.text: Solutions for problems with circular, periodic, or wrap-around structure uniformly reduce to O(1) closed-form expressions via modular arithmetic (min-of-diff-and-complement for shortest arc, mod-then-truncate for cyclic shifts, division-and-modulo for periodic bouncing), eliminating iterative simulation entirely.

justifications.label: Three independent solutions use modular arithmetic to achieve O(1) on structurally similar circular/periodic problems — the shared technique constitutes a coherent reduction strategy complementary to algebraic closed-form reductions.

modular-digit-extraction-pattern.text: `subtract-the-product-and-sum-of-digits` extracts digits via `n % 10` / `n //= 10` loop rather than string conversion, achieving O(1) space with no string allocation

module-alias-instantiates-at-import.text: The module-level alias pattern (e.g., `sort_integers_by_the_number_of_1_bits = Solution().sortByBits`) creates a `Solution()` instance at import time and binds its method, providing a uniform snake_case entry point for the test harness.

modulo-for-circular-wraparound.text: `idx % len(array)` is the standard idiom for circular wrap-around in sorted/search problems — it handles target-greater-than-all, target-equals-last, and target-equals-interior cases without explicit conditionals.

monotonic-constant-array-is-monotonic.text: A constant array (all elements equal) returns `True` from `isMonotonic` because neither the `>` nor `<` comparisons fire, leaving both flags `True`.

monotonic-dual-flag-no-early-exit.text: `isMonotonic` tracks `increasing` and `decreasing` flags simultaneously but never short-circuits — the loop runs to completion even if both flags are `False` mid-scan, making worst-case and best-case both O(n).

monotonic-flags-initialized-true.text: Solution.isMonotonic initializes both boolean flags increasing and decreasing to True before scanning the array.

monotonic-returns-increasing-or-decreasi.text: Solution.isMonotonic returns the boolean expression increasing or decreasing after scanning adjacent pairs.

monotonic-single-pass-constant-space.text: Solution.isMonotonic uses O(n) time and O(1) extra space with no auxiliary data structures.

monotonic-solution-class-no-init.text: Solution.isMonotonic lives on a LeetCode Solution class with no __init__ method.

monotonic-vacuous-truth-short-arrays.text: Arrays of length 0 or 1 return `True` from `isMonotonic` without entering the loop — `range(0)` produces no iterations, so both flags remain `True`.

month-dict-completeness.text: The `months` dictionary maps exactly the 12 three-letter English month abbreviations to zero-padded two-digit strings `"01"` through `"12"`.

month-zero-silent-wrong-answer.text: `number_of_days` performs no input validation; passing month=0 silently returns 31 (December) via Python's negative list indexing rather than raising an error

morse-gin-zen-collision-tested.text: The test suite explicitly verifies that distinct words (`"gig"` and `"msg"`) produce identical Morse strings, confirming the deduplication behavior is non-trivial

morse-ord-indexing-pattern.text: Character-to-Morse lookup uses `ord(c) - ord('a')` to index into a 26-element list, requiring input to be strictly lowercase a-z

morse-set-comprehension-dedup.text: Uniqueness counting is done via set comprehension, making the solution O(S) time where S is total characters across all words

morse-table-is-itu-standard.text: The 26-element `morse` list in `unique-morse-code-words/solution.py` matches the ITU International Morse Code alphabet in a-z order

most-common-word-banned-assumed-lowercas.text: mostCommonWord assumes the banned list already contains lowercase strings; uppercase banned entries would never match the lowered word tokens.

most-common-word-lower-before-regex.text: mostCommonWord calls paragraph.lower() before re.findall(r'[a-z]+', ...), so the regex does not need re.IGNORECASE.

most-common-word-no-empty-guard.text: `mostCommonWord` raises `IndexError` if every word is banned or the paragraph has no alphabetic characters — there is no guard on an empty `Counter`, relying on LeetCode's guarantee of a valid answer.

most-common-word-regex-tokenization.text: `mostCommonWord` tokenizes via `re.findall(r'[a-z]+', paragraph.lower())`, which strips all punctuation and whitespace implicitly — no explicit delimiter character class is needed.

most-common-word-tie-breaking-insertion-.text: When multiple non-banned words share the highest frequency, Counter.most_common(1) returns whichever was encountered first during iteration under CPython 3.7+ dict ordering.

most-frequent-even-inline-tests.text: `most-frequent-even-element/solution.py` contains both the solution function and a `TestMostFrequentEven` unittest class in the same file, unlike the repo's typical pattern of separate `test_solution.py` files.

most-frequent-even-negative-one-sentinel.text: `most_frequent_even` returns `-1` (not `None` or an exception) when the input contains no even numbers — this is the sentinel convention for this problem.

most-frequent-even-o-n-time-o-n-space.text: most_frequent_even runs in O(n) time and O(n) space where n is the length of nums.

most-frequent-even-test-class-nine-cases.text: TestMostFrequentEven contains nine test cases covering LeetCode examples, edge cases, and two-way and four-way tie-breaking scenarios.

most-frequent-even-tiebreak-smallest.text: When multiple even elements share the highest frequency, `most_frequent_even` returns the numerically smallest via `min(counts, key=lambda x: (-counts[x], x))` — a composite sort key that maximizes count then minimizes value.

most-frequent-even-zero-is-even.text: most_frequent_even correctly classifies 0 as an even number, and an explicit test case verifies this behavior.

most-visited-only-depends-on-endpoints.text: The most-visited-sector solution's correctness relies on intermediate rounds contributing uniform visits to all sectors, so only `rounds[0]` and `rounds[-1]` determine the answer.

mostWordsFound-empty-list-raises.text: Passing an empty `sentences` list to `mostWordsFound` raises `ValueError` from `max()` because no fallback default is provided.

mostWordsFound-single-pass.text: The generator-based `mostWordsFound` iterates through sentences exactly once with O(1) auxiliary space beyond each individual split.

mostWordsFound-uses-split-no-args.text: `mostWordsFound` calls `str.split()` without a delimiter, splitting on any whitespace and stripping leading/trailing spaces — not just single spaces.

mostwordsfound-input-length-constraint.text: LeetCode 2114 constrains sentences to length between 1 and 100, and each sentence contains at least one word.

mostwordsfound-list-import-annotation-on.text: In maximum-number-of-words-found-in-sentences, List from typing is imported only for the type annotation and has no runtime effect.

mostwordsfound-single-return-expression.text: The entire mostWordsFound algorithm is a single return statement using max over a generator expression.

mountain-peak-must-be-interior.text: The valid-mountain-array solution requires the peak index to satisfy `0 < peak < n-1`, rejecting purely monotonic sequences even when both pointers converge.

move-zeroes-no-return-value.text: `moveZeroes` returns `None` and mutates the input list in-place; callers must inspect the modified list to observe results.

move-zeroes-single-pass.text: Subsumed by `move-zeroes-swap-not-overwrite` which already captures the single-pass property as part of the swap-based approach — keeping both would be redundant.

move-zeroes-stable-ordering.text: Non-zero elements maintain their original relative order after `moveZeroes` completes — the swap-based two-pointer advances the slow pointer only on non-zero encounters, preserving sequence.

move-zeroes-swap-not-overwrite.text: `moveZeroes` uses element swaps (slow/fast pointer) rather than overwriting non-zeros to front and filling zeros after, performing at most n swaps in a single pass with no second fill phase.

moving-avg-eviction-order.text: In `MovingAverage.next()`, the subtraction of the evicted element must happen before `deque.append()` because `append` on a full `maxlen` deque silently discards `_queue[0]`.

moving-avg-no-size-validation.text: Edge case behavior under invalid input (`size=0`) is not a meaningful codebase invariant — it's a consequence of trusting LeetCode constraints, which is already a repo-wide pattern.

moving-avg-o1-next.text: `MovingAverage.next()` runs in O(1) time by maintaining a running sum incrementally, avoiding O(k) re-summation of the deque on each call.

moving-avg-sum-invariant.text: `self._sum == sum(self._queue)` holds after every `next()` call in `MovingAverage`; if this invariant breaks, all subsequent averages silently return wrong values.

multi-digit-counts-supported.text: The digit-scanning loop in `_extract_next` handles arbitrarily large multi-digit counts (e.g., `1000000000`) by scanning consecutive digit characters until a non-digit or end-of-string.

multiplication-before-division-ordering.text: In `percentageLetter`, the `count * 100` multiplication happens before the `// len(s)` division — reversing the order would produce 0 for any `count < len(s)` due to integer floor division.

mutable-list-for-string-manipulation.text: Solutions that need character-level string mutation convert to `list()`, mutate in place, then `''.join()` back — the standard Python idiom since strings are immutable.

mutable-list-for-string-mutation.text: Solutions that need in-place character modification convert the input string to a `list` via `list(s)`, mutate it, then rejoin with `''.join(chars)` — this avoids O(n²) repeated string concatenation.

mutation-invisible-in-single-call-contex.text: In-place mutation of input arguments (sorting, element swaps, pointer reassignment) has no observable effect beyond the current call because LeetCode's judge invokes each solution exactly once per test case, making aliasing and input reuse irrelevant under the submission model.

justifications.label: Mutation is invisible in LeetCode's single-call model, but the documented sort-mutations would surprise any caller that reads the input after the call

n-choose-2-for-pair-counting.text: When counting unordered pairs within groups, solutions apply the combinatorial formula `n*(n-1)//2` per group rather than enumerating pairs, relying on the integer-division-is-exact invariant (one of n, n-1 is always even).

n-choose-2-pair-counting-formula.text: Pair-counting solutions use `n*(n-1)//2` per frequency group (or the incremental equivalent `count += seen[x]; seen[x] += 1`) rather than enumerating all pairs; integer division is exact because one of two consecutive integers is always even.

n100-yields-682289015.text: For n=100 (25 primes, 75 non-primes), Prime Arrangements returns 682289015, serving as a regression anchor for the full computation chain including primality counting and modular factorial.

names-serve-no-functional-role.text: Function and method names are entirely non-functional in this architecture: naming errors introduced by the generation pipeline remain permanently invisible at runtime, and naming drift across solutions never affects execution — making names purely documentary artifacts with no load-bearing role.

justifications.label: Generation errors are invisible (depth-5) because isolation prevents cross-solution name collisions, and naming drift doesn't affect execution (depth-2) because the alias convention decouples names from test harness binding; together, names have zero functional significance

naming-drift-does-not-affect-execution.text: Method name mismatches from copy-paste are invisible at runtime because the test harness imports via module-level aliases bound at the top of each solution file, not via method names on the Solution class.

justifications.label: Module-level aliases bridge naming drift unless the alias itself is misnamed

naming-drift-evidences-co-adaptation-loc.text: Naming drift serves as empirical evidence that the streaming-isolation co-adaptation lock is actively operating: drift accumulates precisely because streaming's self-sufficiency eliminates functional dependency on correct names, while isolation's zero-coupling eliminates detection mechanisms — the canonical instance of permanently frozen debt is a directly observable trace of the dynamically locked co-adaptation between the dominant paradigm and the architectural pattern.

justifications.label: naming drift is the observable trace left by the streaming-isolation lock mechanism; its persistence proves the lock holds

naming-drift-is-canonical-frozen-debt.text: Naming drift is the canonical instance of permanently frozen engineering debt: names serve no functional role at any layer of the architecture (neither runtime execution nor test harness depend on semantic correctness of names), while the isolation mechanism that freezes all engineering debt simultaneously ensures naming errors are undetectable without manual inspection — making naming the purest case of a defect that is simultaneously consequenceless and uncorrectable.

justifications.label: Depth-7 instantiation: naming concretely demonstrates both the non-functionality (depth 6) and the permanence (depth 5) that define frozen debt

naming-drift-is-definitive-immunity-proo.text: Naming drift serves as the definitive proof of architectural immunity: it is simultaneously the most pervasive engineering defect (affecting multiple solutions systematically via the generation pipeline) and the most completely harmless (names serve zero functional role at any architectural layer), demonstrating that immunity handles even the worst-case defect class — maximum surface area, zero impact.

justifications.label: One antecedent establishes naming drift as the canonical frozen defect, the other establishes immunity as a general property; combining reveals naming drift as the strongest possible evidence for that immunity (worst-case test)

naming-drift-is-domain-selection-signatu.text: Naming drift is the empirically observable signature of domain-level quality selection: the domain's fixed-point dynamics select for algorithmic investment over engineering discipline (no force pushes toward fixing names), and naming drift — simultaneously the most pervasive engineering defect and the most harmless (definitive immunity proof) — is the visible residue of that selection, making it the canonical diagnostic for identifying LeetCode-domain quality dynamics in any codebase.

justifications.label: Naming drift is what domain selection LOOKS LIKE in practice — the most informative single observable because it simultaneously demonstrates both the selection pressure (no engineering fix incentive) and its consequence (harmless persistence)

naming-drift-structurally-inevitable-at-.text: Naming drift is not merely tolerated but structurally inevitable at the streaming fixed point: because the fixed point's four-fold optimality (convergence attractor, algebraic normal form, self-sufficient paradigm, constructive minimal strategy) eliminates all naming infrastructure from the solution space (no imports, no shared interfaces, no cross-module references), naming precision has exactly zero selection pressure at the convergence attractor, guaranteeing drift accumulates monotonically.

justifications.label: The streaming fixed point eliminates all selection pressure on naming, making drift a structural inevitability rather than an accident

nearest-valid-point-fused-filter-reduce.text: `nearestValidPoint` fuses the validity filter and argmin reduction into a single O(n) pass with O(1) space — no intermediate filtered list, no sorting.

nearest-valid-point-initializes-sentinel.text: `nearestValidPoint` initializes `min_dist` to `float('inf')` and `min_idx` to `-1` before scanning.

nearest-valid-point-no-imports.text: `nearestValidPoint` has zero imports — it uses only Python builtins (`float`, `abs`, `enumerate`), making it fully self-contained.

nearest-valid-point-or-means-either-axis.text: A point is valid in `nearestValidPoint` if it shares the x-coordinate OR the y-coordinate with the query (not necessarily both) — an easy-to-misread detail of the problem contract.

nearest-valid-point-returns-first-index-.text: When multiple valid points share the minimum Manhattan distance, `nearestValidPoint` returns the smallest index because it uses strict `<` comparison (first occurrence is kept).

nearest-valid-point-returns-minus-one-wh.text: `nearestValidPoint` returns `-1` when no point shares either coordinate with the query.

nearest-valid-point-uses-manhattan-dista.text: `nearestValidPoint` measures distance as `|x - ai| + |y - bi|` (Manhattan distance).

nearest-valid-point-valid-same-location-.text: A valid point identical to `(x, y)` has Manhattan distance 0 and will always be selected.

negated-max-heap-idiom.text: Max-heap behavior is emulated by negating all values on insertion and negating again on extraction, since Python's `heapq` only provides a min-heap — a standard idiom used across heap-based solutions in this repo.

negation-marking-abs-required.text: In the negation-marking pattern, `abs()` is required when reading a cell's value (as opposed to its sign) because earlier iterations may have negated it; omitting `abs()` would produce negative indices and raise `IndexError`.

negation-marking-collect-phase-positive-.text: In the negation-marking pattern, the collect phase returns values v=i+1 for every index i where nums[i] remains positive after the mark phase.

negation-marking-idempotent-guard.text: The `if nums[idx] > 0` guard in `find_disappeared_numbers` ensures each index is negated at most once, preventing double-negation by duplicates from restoring a positive sign and producing false "missing" results.

negation-marking-linear-time-constant-sp.text: The in-place negation-marking algorithm for find_disappeared_numbers achieves O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space, excluding the output list, outperforming hash-set (O(n) space) and sorting (O(n log n) time) alternatives.

negation-marking-mutates-input.text: `find_disappeared_numbers` destructively modifies the input array via in-place sign flipping; callers cannot reuse `nums` after the call.

negation-marking-requires-1-to-n-range.text: The in-place negation-marking technique only works when values are guaranteed in `[1, n]`, since each value `v` maps to index `v - 1`; values outside this range would cause out-of-bounds access.

negation-trick-requires-integers.text: The tiebreaker `-x` only produces correct descending order for numeric types; applying this pattern to strings or other non-numeric types would fail.

negative-input-causes-nontermination.text: `hamming_weight` has no guard against negative inputs; on Python's arbitrary-precision integers, `n &= n - 1` on a negative value never reaches zero, causing an infinite loop

negative-one-sentinel.text: Standard LeetCode convention for "not found" return values — not a codebase-specific invariant worth tracking.

negative-one-sentinel-for-max-tracking.text: `largest-number-at-least-twice-of-others/solution.py` initializes `max_val` and `second_max` to -1, which is safe only because the problem constrains values to [0, 1000] — this sentinel would break for problems allowing negative inputs

nested-helpers-are-pure-closures.text: Helper functions nested inside solution methods (e.g., `is_valid` in `countValidWords`, `diff` in `stringWithDifferentDifference`) don't capture mutable state from the enclosing scope — they are pure functions co-located for readability

net-shift-collapse.text: All individual shift operations are collapsed into a single net displacement before any string manipulation, making the solution O(n + k) rather than O(n * total_shift_amount).

next-valid-returns-surviving-character-i.text: `_next_valid` returns the index of the next surviving non-backspaced character, or a negative value if none remain.

next-valid-terminates.text: `_next_valid` in backspace-string-compare always terminates because the `index` variable strictly decreases on every iteration of its while loop, and the loop exits when `index < 0`.

nextgreatestletter-has-nine-unit-tests.text: The solution file includes nine unit tests in `TestNextGreatestLetter` covering standard, boundary, duplicate, and two-element cases.

nextgreatestletter-runs-in-log-n-time-co.text: `Solution.nextGreatestLetter` runs in O(log n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

nextgreatestletter-wrap-returns-first-le.text: When the target is greater than or equal to every letter in `letters`, `Solution.nextGreatestLetter` returns `letters[0]`.

nge-absent-from-dict-means-minus-one.text: In `next_greater_element`, values from nums2 with no next greater element are absent from the `next_greater` dict, and lookups return -1 via `dict.get(num, -1)`.

nge-linear-time.text: `next_greater_element` runs in O(n + m) time where n = len(nums2) and m = len(nums1), because each element of nums2 is pushed and popped from the stack at most once (amortized analysis).

nge-precompute-then-query.text: `next_greater_element` separates into two phases: a single O(n) pass over nums2 using a monotonic stack to build the full next-greater mapping, then O(1)-per-element dict lookups for each query in nums1.

nge-stack-monotonic-decreasing.text: The stack invariant in the Next Greater Element solution is strictly decreasing from bottom to top; the while loop pops all values smaller than the incoming element before pushing, enforcing this at every step.

nge-strict-greater-comparison.text: The monotonic stack in `next_greater_element` uses the comparison `stack[-1] < num` to determine when a smaller stack top has found its next greater element.

nge-unique-elements-assumed.text: The dict-keyed-by-value approach in `next_greater_element` is correct only because the problem guarantees all elements are unique; duplicate values would cause silent overwrites of earlier mappings.

nge-uses-o-n-space-for-dict-and-stack.text: The `next_greater_element` solution uses O(n) space for the `next_greater` dictionary and the monotonic stack, where n = len(nums2).

nibble-extraction-produces-lsb-first.text: The hex conversion loop extracts digits from least-significant to most-significant nibble, collecting them in reverse order and requiring a final `reversed()` call.

nice-substring-base-case-returns-empty.text: If the input string length is less than 2, `longestNiceSubstring` returns an empty string because no nice substring of length at least 2 can exist.

nice-substring-divide-conquer-split-corr.text: Splitting on a character whose case-counterpart is absent is sound: that character cannot appear in any nice substring, so the answer lies entirely in one of the two halves.

nice-substring-left-bias-on-tie.text: `longestNiceSubstring` uses `>=` when comparing left vs right result lengths, ensuring the earliest (leftmost) substring wins on equal length, matching LeetCode's tie-breaking requirement.

nice-substring-no-imports.text: Trivial dependency fact (no imports) — this is observable from the file itself and not an invariant that could break something if violated.

nice-substring-set-swapcase-membership-c.text: The solution builds `char_set = set(s)` once per recursive call and uses `str.swapcase()` to check each character's case-counterpart in O(1) time.

nice-substring-termination-strictly-shor.text: Each recursive call of `longestNiceSubstring` operates on a strictly shorter string because the split character is excluded from both halves, guaranteeing termination.

nice-substring-worst-case-quadratic.text: The divide-and-conquer approach is O(n^2) worst case when every split produces one empty and one n-1 partition (analogous to quicksort's worst case); best case is O(n log n) with balanced splits.

nim-game-constant-complexity.text: `canWinNim` is O(1) time and O(1) space — a single modulo operation — which is necessary because n can be up to 2^31 - 1, making DP infeasible.

nim-game-mod4-characterization.text: The first player wins Nim (1–3 stones per turn) if and only if `n % 4 != 0`; this is a complete characterization derived from the Sprague-Grundy theorem, not heuristic.

nim-game-n-zero-returns-false.text: For n=0 (outside the valid input range), `canWinNim` returns False because 0 % 4 == 0.

nim-game-no-dependencies.text: Zero imports is the default for LeetCode solutions in this repo; not a meaningful invariant to track per-problem.

nim-game-no-input-validation.text: Same as all other LeetCode solutions — no validation is the repo-wide convention, not a per-solution fact worth tracking.

nim-game-no-loops-or-allocation.text: `canWinNim` contains no loops, branching, or allocation; it performs a single modulo operation.

nim-game-solution-is-single-modulo-expre.text: The entire `canWinNim` solution is the expression `n % 4 != 0`.

no-allocation.text: O(1) space for a two-pointer palindrome check is a standard property of the algorithm, not a codebase-specific invariant.

no-auxiliary-space.text: Redundant with `three-pointer-linear-time-constant-space` which already captures the O(1) space claim.

no-bounds-violation-on-overshoot.text: When a number in `abbr` exceeds the remaining length of `word`, `i` overshoots `len(word)` and the final `i == len(word)` check catches it without raising an `IndexError`.

no-builtin-hex-used.text: to_hex manually extracts hexadecimal digits via bit manipulation instead of calling Python's built-in hex(), format(), or f-string formatting.

no-child-gets-four-dollars.text: The `others == 1 and leftover == 3` branch in distribute-money specifically prevents the remaining child from receiving exactly $4, which the problem forbids.

no-consistency-enforcement-at-any-level.text: The repo lacks any mechanism — shared imports, linters, templates, or conventions — for enforcing consistency in naming, testing, or structure across problem directories, making style drift an inevitable structural property rather than an oversight.

justifications.label: isolation removes the forcing function, duplication removes the single point of standardization, and dual-mode testing confirms that even simple conventions (where tests live) have drifted

no-cross-problem-dependencies.text: Each solution directory is fully self-contained; despite tooling artifacts showing large "Imported By" lists, no solution module imports from another problem's directory.

no-cross-problem-imports.text: Each problem's `test_solution.py` imports only its own `solution.py`; the large "Imported By" lists in code-expert output are artifacts of the tooling, not real Python import edges

no-defensive-error-handling.text: Too generic — nearly every LeetCode solution in this repo lacks defensive error handling by design. This is already captured by the repo-wide convention of trusting LeetCode input guarantees rather than being a specific invariant of the queue implementation.

no-defensive-validation.text: Nearly every LeetCode solution in this repo omits input validation — this is the universal convention, not a noteworthy property of any individual solution.

no-digit-input-returns-zero.text: A `word` containing no digits produces an empty set after replacement and splitting and returns 0.

no-external-dependencies.text: Too vague and universally true for simple LeetCode solutions — the interesting claim is which solutions *do* import stdlib modules (like `Counter`), not which don't.

no-external-dependencies-in-solutions.text: Solution files import only from the Python standard library (`unittest`, `typing`). No external packages are used anywhere in the solution code.

no-external-dependencies-reverse-only-le.text: Same as above — already covered by the cross-cutting `solutions-are-self-contained-no-imports` belief.

no-full-house-distinction.text: `best_poker_hand` uses `max_freq >= 3` which collapses Full House and Three of a Kind into the same classification, matching the problem's simplified hand ranking.

no-guard-for-empty-input.text: Subsumed by the broader `leetcode-solutions-omit-input-validation` belief — tracking each solution's specific failure mode on invalid input doesn't add value beyond the general convention.

no-guard-on-empty-input.text: Too generic and repeated across nearly every solution — the pattern that LeetCode solutions skip input validation is better captured once as a repo-wide observation than per-solution.

no-import-dependencies.text: Whether a specific solution uses imports is a trivial per-file fact, not an architectural invariant worth tracking.

no-imports-pure-string.text: Subsumed by the broader `solutions-self-contained-no-internal-deps` belief; restating it for one specific file adds no value.

no-input-validation.text: ID is too generic — would collide across solutions. This pattern is cross-cutting and better captured by a single repo-wide belief.

no-input-validation-convention.text: Solutions trust their callers to provide valid inputs within problem constraints; no range checking, type validation, or defensive error handling is performed beyond what the algorithm structurally requires.

no-input-validation-in-solutions.text: Solution methods perform no input validation or bounds checking, relying entirely on LeetCode's guaranteed constraints; invalid inputs propagate standard Python exceptions.

no-input-validation-pattern.text: Solution functions consistently omit input validation (bounds checking, type checking, error handling), relying on the LeetCode harness to satisfy problem constraints — this is deliberate, not an oversight

no-input-validation-standard.text: This is true of virtually every LeetCode solution ever written — it's too obvious to be a useful belief for this codebase.

no-input-validation-trusts-leetcode-cont.text: Solutions do not validate input preconditions (sorted arrays, valid tree nodes, binary values) — they rely on LeetCode's guarantee that inputs conform to the problem statement.

no-input-validation-uncommon.text: Duplicates the pattern already captured by per-solution beliefs; "no validation" is true of every solution in this repo and is better stated once as a repo-wide convention

no-mutation-guarantee.text: `middle_of_the_linked_list` performs a read-only traversal; no node's `val` or `next` pointer is modified.

no-mutation-make-arrays.text: Redundant with the cross-cutting `solutions-are-pure-no-mutation` belief — no need for per-solution mutation claims when the pattern holds repo-wide.

no-mutation-of-input.text: Not modifying the input list is standard practice and trivially verifiable; not a meaningful invariant to track.

no-overflow-concern.text: Python arbitrary-precision integers are a language property, not a codebase-specific invariant — any Python developer would know this.

no-padding-when-evenly-divisible.text: This is a consequence already captured by double-mod-deficit-formula (the outer mod collapses k to 0).

no-piece-usage-validation.text: While true, this is a minor implementation detail rather than an architectural invariant — the correctness argument (all piece elements are distinct subsets of arr) makes explicit validation unnecessary.

no-post-loop-fixup-needed.text: Because `checkZeroOnes` updates the max inside the loop on every iteration (not only at run transitions), the final run's length is always reflected in the result without a trailing adjustment

no-runtime-input-validation.text: Solutions do not validate input at runtime — they trust LeetCode's guaranteed constraints, and invalid input propagates native Python exceptions (`ValueError`, `TypeError`).

no-shared-node-class.text: Each solution directory defines its own `Node`/`TreeNode` class rather than importing from a shared module — tree structure definitions are duplicated per problem.

no-simulation-needed.text: The most-visited-sector function never iterates through the `rounds` array beyond reading the first and last elements, making it O(n) in sectors rather than O(len(rounds) * n).

no-sliding-window-needed.text: This is an observation about what the problem *doesn't* need — not an invariant that constrains future behavior or would break if violated.

no-solution-class-wrapper.text: Too narrow — this is true for `binary-tree-inorder-traversal` but not for the repo as a whole (binary-search and preorder-traversal use `Solution` classes). Superseded by `solution-class-vs-module-function-inconsistency` above.

no-sqrt-dependency.text: `is_perfect_square` satisfies the LeetCode constraint of not using any built-in square root or exponentiation function; it relies only on integer multiplication and comparison.

no-stdlib-date-in-date-problems.text: Date-related solutions (days-between-dates, days-in-a-month) implement Gregorian calendar arithmetic from scratch without importing `datetime` or `calendar`, since hand-rolling the math is the intended constraint

no-stdlib-date-parsing.text: The reformat-date solution avoids `datetime` entirely, relying on manual string splitting and dictionary lookup.

no-subset-enumeration.text: Redundant with `subset-xor-closed-form` — the fact that no subsets are enumerated is the direct consequence of using the closed-form formula, not a separate claim.

no-two-pair-distinction.text: `best_poker_hand` checks only `max_freq == 2`, so Two Pair and One Pair both return `"Pair "` — the problem defines no Two Pair category.

no-validation-is-deliberate-contract.text: The universal absence of input validation is a deliberate architectural choice — solutions define their correctness boundary at LeetCode's stated constraints and are not intended to handle inputs outside that boundary.

justifications.label: Validation omission is a consistent design decision, not accumulated technical debt

no-zero-integers-guaranteed-termination.text: This is a mathematical property of the problem domain, not a codebase invariant — it describes the problem's guarantee rather than an architectural or behavioral claim about the code.

no-zero-integers-linear-scan-complexity.text: no_zero_integers runs in O(n * d) worst-case time, where d is the number of digits in n, due to scanning candidate values and converting them to strings.

no-zero-integers-outputs-positive.text: no_zero_integers returns two positive integers: a starts at 1 and the loop excludes a == n, so b = n - a is also at least 1.

no-zero-integers-returns-smallest-a.text: `no_zero_integers` returns the pair with the smallest possible first element, scanning `a` upward from 1 and returning on first match, making the output deterministic.

no-zero-integers-sum-equals-input.text: no_zero_integers guarantees a + b == n by construction, computing b = n - a for each candidate a.

no-zero-invariant.text: The `min(a,b)*10 + max(a,b)` formula in `smallest_number_with_at_least_one_digit_from_each_array` assumes digits are 1-9; a zero in either array would produce an incorrect single-digit result instead of a two-digit number.

node-children-default-empty-list.text: `Node.__init__` in n-ary tree solutions avoids Python's mutable default argument pitfall by using `None` as the default parameter and replacing with `[]` inside the constructor body.

node-default-children-empty-list.text: Duplicate of `node-children-default-empty-list` from the postorder entry — same claim about the same pattern.

non-alpha-positional-invariant.text: In the Reverse Only Letters solution, non-alphabetic characters are guaranteed to remain at their original indices — the two-pointer loop only swaps when both pointers point at `isalpha()` characters.

non-binary-input-silent-miscount.text: In `checkZeroOnes`, characters other than `"1"` are silently counted toward `max_zeros`, since the only branch check is `c == "1"`

non-empty-partition-guarantee.text: The loop bound `range(len(s) - 1)` enforces that both left and right substrings are always non-empty at every split point evaluated.

none-root-is-univalued.text: Contract detail of a single problem's edge case; not an architectural invariant that affects work across the codebase.

nonlocal-accumulator-pattern.text: The diameter solution uses a nested `height` closure that captures and mutates an outer `diameter` variable via `nonlocal`, computing height as the return value while accumulating the diameter as a side effect — a pattern that also appears in other tree problems like binary-tree-tilt.

null-root-returns-empty-list.text: All tree traversal solutions return `[]` (not `None` or an error) when given a null/None root, enforced by early guard clauses or loop conditions that short-circuit naturally.

null-subroot-is-always-subtree.text: `isSubtree(any_root, None)` returns `True`, matching the LeetCode contract that an empty tree is a subtree of any tree

num-sub-does-not-mutate-input.text: `num_sub` does not mutate its input list and returns a new sorted list.

num-sub-is-pure.text: Too narrow — purity of a single trivial function is self-evident from the code and not an architectural invariant. The broader claim about mutation conventions across solutions is more useful (and is captured by per-solution mutation beliefs).

numofstrings-delegates-substring-check-t.text: numOfStrings uses Python's `in` operator on strings to test whether each pattern is a substring of `word`.

numofstrings-linear-complexity.text: The belief ID says "linear" but the actual claim is O(n * m * k) which is not linear — the ID and content contradict, making this confusing as a reference. Should be re-proposed with a corrected ID like `numofstrings-polynomial-complexity`.

numofstrings-pure-function.text: `numOfStrings` is a pure function: no side effects, no mutation of inputs, deterministic output for any given input.

numofstrings-return-range-bound.text: numOfStrings always returns an integer in the closed interval [0, len(patterns)].

numofstrings-time-complexity-n-times-m-t.text: numOfStrings has worst-case time complexity O(n * m * k), where n is len(patterns), m is the maximum pattern length, and k is len(word), because each Python `in` substring check is O(m * k) worst-case.

o-n-log-n-complexity.text: Too generic — O(n log n) due to sorting applies to most sort-based solutions and is self-evident from the code.

o1-space-via-running-accumulators.text: Multiple solutions achieve O(1) auxiliary space by maintaining scalar running-state variables (min-so-far, running-sum, running-max) instead of materializing intermediate arrays or sorted copies.

justifications.label: Running accumulators trade re-traversal impossibility for constant memory across streaming-style problems

odd-cells-counting-over-simulation.text: `oddCells` uses the counting-not-simulation pattern: since each cell's value equals `row_count[r] + col_count[c]`, it computes frequencies then uses combinatorics instead of applying increments to a matrix.

odd-cells-linear-time.text: `oddCells` runs in O(|indices| + m + n) time — one pass to count frequencies, one pass to count parities — independent of the matrix area m*n.

odd-cells-no-matrix-materialization.text: `oddCells` never allocates an m-by-n matrix; it uses O(m+n) row/column frequency arrays, reducing space from O(m*n) to O(m+n).

odd-cells-xor-parity-formula.text: A cell (r,c) has an odd value iff exactly one of `row_count[r]` and `col_count[c]` is odd; the return formula `odd_rows*(n-odd_cols) + (m-odd_rows)*odd_cols` computes this via two disjoint terms with no overlap.

odd-count-output-length-equals-n.text: Both branches of `generateTheString` produce exactly `n` characters, so the output length always equals the input `n`.

odd-count-two-branch.text: The odd-counts solution uses exactly two code paths: all-same-char for odd n, two-char split for even n

odd-count-uses-string-multiplication.text: The solution constructs its output with Python string multiplication using `a` and `b` rather than explicit iteration or backtracking.

odd-index-reads-even-no-write-hazard.text: In `replaceDigits`, each odd-index replacement reads from the preceding even index, which is never modified by the loop — so iteration order cannot affect correctness.

odd-k-residual-cost.text: When leftover k is odd after flipping all negatives, the sum penalty is exactly `2 * min(nums)` applied to the already-mutated (all-non-negative) array.

odd-string-assumes-equal-length.text: `stringWithDifferentDifference` assumes all input strings have equal length as guaranteed by the problem constraints.

odd-string-counter-frequency.text: `stringWithDifferentDifference` builds a `Counter` over the difference-array tuples to count how many words share each difference array.

odd-string-diff-consecutive-ordinal-diff.text: `diff(w)` returns a tuple of length `len(w)-1` where each element is `ord(w[i+1]) - ord(w[i])` for consecutive characters.

odd-string-diff-negative-values.text: Difference-array values can be negative; for example, `diff('ba')` produces `(-1,)`.

odd-string-exactly-one-outlier-assumed.text: `stringWithDifferentDifference` assumes exactly one word has a unique difference array; if zero are unique it returns `""`, if multiple are unique it returns only the first — the problem guarantees this won't happen

odd-string-linear-time-n-m.text: `stringWithDifferentDifference` runs in O(n * m) time, where n is the number of words and m is each word's length.

odd-subarray-count-formula.text: Element at index `i` in an array of length `n` appears in exactly `((i+1)*(n-i)+1)//2` odd-length subarrays, derived from total subarray count `(i+1)*(n-i)` with ceiling division by 2

odd-subarray-empty-array-returns-zero-wi.text: `sumOddLengthSubarrays` performs no input validation and returns 0 for an empty array without error.

odd-subarray-linear-time-constant-space.text: `sumOddLengthSubarrays` runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space, making a single pass over the array.

one-bit-characters-linear-time.text: is_one_bit_character runs in O(n) time and O(1) space, visiting each bit at most once.

one-bit-characters-loop-excludes-last-in.text: In is_one_bit_character, the while loop condition i < len(bits) - 1 guarantees the last element is never consumed during iteration; it is only checked after the loop.

one-indexed-sectors.text: Restates the problem specification rather than a codebase invariant — every LeetCode problem defines its own indexing scheme.

one-liner-pipeline-pattern.text: Easy-level solutions frequently use a composable pipeline of built-in string/list operations in a single return statement (e.g., split → transform → join) with no intermediate variables.

one-mismatch-always-false.text: Exactly one positional mismatch between two strings is never fixable by a single swap because a swap always changes two positions simultaneously

one-problem-per-directory.text: Each problem gets its own directory containing at minimum a `solution.py` and `test_solution.py`, with optional `plan.md` and `review.md` files.

op1-discriminates-all-operations.text: In `max_value`, the character at index 1 is `"+"` for both increment forms (`"++X"`, `"X++"`) and `"-"` for both decrement forms, making `op[1]` a sufficient discriminator without string matching.

opponent-order-determines-experience-res.text: The experience simulation depends on opponent array order, so reordering opponents would change the computed training hours.

optional-import-unused.text: An unused import is a code smell, not an architectural or behavioral invariant. It could be fixed at any time and has no impact on correctness or design.

ord-offset-letter-to-digit-pattern.text: The `ord(c) - ord('a')` idiom for mapping lowercase letters to integer positions recurs across multiple solutions (summation-of-two-words, decode-the-message, replace-all-digits).

ord-offset-produces-multichar-strings.text: The mapping `ord(c) - ord('a') + 1` produces values 10–26 for letters j–z, which concatenate as multi-character substrings — this is why the first phase builds a string rather than extracting digits per character.

ordered-stream-amortized-linear.text: Total pointer movement across all n `insert` calls on `OrderedStream` is O(n), making each insert O(1) amortized despite the inner while loop.

ordered-stream-duplicate-id-overwrites.text: `OrderedStream.insert` does not detect duplicate IDs; a second insert with the same `idKey` silently overwrites the stored value.

ordered-stream-fixed-buffer-size-n.text: `OrderedStream.__init__(n)` allocates a fixed-size list of `n` `None` values and initializes `self.ptr` to 0.

ordered-stream-idkey-minus-one-mapping.text: `OrderedStream.insert` writes `value` to buffer index `idKey - 1`, converting the 1-indexed ID to 0-indexed storage.

ordered-stream-none-sentinel.text: `OrderedStream` uses `None` as the sentinel for unfilled slots — inserting `None` as a value would break the contiguity scan, causing it to stop prematurely.

ordered-stream-pointer-monotonic.text: `OrderedStream.ptr` only increases; once a value is returned from an `insert` call it is never returned again, and slots below the pointer are logically consumed.

ordered-stream-returns-empty-on-gap.text: If `OrderedStream.insert` writes to a slot ahead of `self.ptr`, the while loop does not execute and the method returns an empty list.

ordinal-arithmetic-for-letter-indexing.text: Solutions use `ord(ch) - ord('a')` to map lowercase letters to indices 0–25 rather than using a dictionary, a standard LeetCode idiom used across the repo

output-dimensions-invariant.text: This is a direct restatement of the problem specification, not a codebase invariant that could be accidentally violated

output-size-equals-grid-size.text: This is a mathematical tautology of BFS on a connected grid, not a codebase invariant — it cannot be "violated" by a code change.

overflow-safe-midpoint-convention.text: Binary search solutions use `left + (right - left) // 2` instead of `(left + right) // 2` as a consistent idiom across the repo, borrowed from C/Java overflow safety even though Python has arbitrary-precision integers.

overflow-safe-midpoint-idiom.text: `guessNumber` computes midpoint as `low + (high - low) // 2` rather than `(low + high) // 2` — unnecessary in Python but signals awareness of the integer overflow pitfall and is used idiomatically across the repo.

overlap-is-conjunction-of-axis-projectio.text: 2D rectangle overlap is decomposed into the conjunction of independent 1D overlap checks on the x-axis and y-axis — a reusable geometric pattern.

overlapping-ranges-idempotent-marking.text: In the range-coverage solution, overlapping intervals simply re-mark already-True positions in the boolean array — no deduplication or merging step is needed because marking is idempotent.

pad-length-is-correct.text: Subsumed by double-mod-deficit-formula which captures the same mathematical property more precisely.

pad-then-slice-idiom.text: divide-a-string normalizes input length before slicing rather than special-casing the last group — `(k - len(s) % k) % k` computes minimal padding, and uniform stride-k slicing produces all groups.

pairs-iff-even-counts.text: An array can be divided into equal pairs if and only if every distinct element has an even frequency — the divide-array-into-equal-pairs solution checks `count % 2 == 0` for all Counter values.

pairs-leftovers-conservation.text: `count_pairs_leftovers` guarantees the invariant `pairs * 2 + leftovers == len(nums)` — every element is accounted for exactly once as either paired or left over.

pairs-leftovers-empty-input-returns-zero.text: Passing an empty list to count_pairs_leftovers returns [0, 0] without error.

pairs-leftovers-iterates-counter-values.text: count_pairs_leftovers accumulates results by looping over the frequency values produced by Counter(nums).

pairs-leftovers-returns-two-element-list.text: count_pairs_leftovers returns a two-element list containing pairs and leftovers.

pairwise-inequality-for-fixed-window.text: For the size-3 sliding window, three explicit pairwise `!=` checks are used instead of `len(set(window)) == 3` — a micro-optimization that avoids set construction

palindrome-case-sensitive.text: `longestPalindrome` treats uppercase and lowercase as distinct characters — `'A'` and `'a'` do not form pairs — matching the LeetCode problem spec.

palindrome-center-bonus-at-most-once.text: `longestPalindrome` adds at most one center character regardless of how many characters have odd frequencies, using a boolean flag converted to int via Python's `bool` subclassing `int`.

palindrome-check-uses-slice-reversal.text: Palindrome detection uses `word == word[::-1]`, creating a full reversed copy (O(m) space) rather than a two-pointer in-place comparison.

palindrome-construction-reduces-to-frequ.text: Palindrome construction and permutation problems in the repo uniformly reduce to frequency-parity analysis: a string can form a palindrome iff at most one character has odd frequency, the longest constructible palindrome sums even portions of each frequency plus at most one center character, and the actual count values are discarded in favor of their parity — the palindrome property is entirely determined by the parity signature of the character frequency distribution.

justifications.label: Depth-1 thematic grouping: four palindrome base beliefs share the same core insight that palindromicity is a parity property of frequencies

palindrome-greedy-even-portions.text: `longestPalindrome` computes the result by summing `count // 2 * 2` for each character frequency, extracting the largest even number ≤ count, plus 1 if any odd count exists.

palindrome-instantiates-hash-then-stream.text: Palindrome construction and permutation problems are specific instantiations of the hash-then-stream pipeline: Counter builds the frequency map in O(n) preprocessing, then a single-pass parity check over frequencies determines constructibility — the same two-phase structure that governs the broader pipeline taxonomy.

justifications.label: palindrome's Counter + parity-scan matches the canonical hash-then-stream decomposition

palindrome-is-canonical-counter-pipeline.text: Palindrome problems serve as the canonical exemplar of the full Counter-to-pipeline reduction chain: Counter construction from string (algebraic construction), frequency extraction (algebraic measurement), parity reduction (algebraic projection), and threshold aggregation (streaming accumulation) — exercising every layer of the hash-then-stream pipeline within a single problem class and demonstrating how Counter's algebraic completeness flows through the pipeline architecture.

justifications.label: Palindromes exercise every layer from Counter algebra through hash preprocessing to streaming output

palindrome-linear-time.text: O(n) time for a single-pass Counter solution is standard and directly readable from the code; not an invariant that warrants tracking.

palindrome-ll-empty-single-early-true.text: `isPalindrome` returns `True` immediately for an empty list or a single-node list.

palindrome-ll-linear-time.text: `isPalindrome` runs in O(n) time over the linked list's nodes.

palindrome-ll-make-list-dummy-head.text: The test helper `make_list` converts a Python list into a linked list using a dummy-head node.

palindrome-ll-mutates-input.text: `isPalindrome` reverses the second half of the linked list in-place and does not restore it — after the call returns, the original list structure is permanently altered

palindrome-ll-o1-space-via-mutation.text: `isPalindrome` achieves O(1) extra space by mutating the list in-place (fast/slow pointer to find midpoint, then in-place reversal) rather than copying values to an array

palindrome-ll-p2-terminates-comparison.text: The comparison loop iterates until `p2` (reversed second half) is `None`, not `p1`, because the reversed half is always <= the first half in length (middle node stays with first half for odd-length lists)

palindrome-ll-slow-pointer-guard.text: The `while fast.next and fast.next.next` guard places `slow` at the last node of the first half — using the alternative `while fast and fast.next` would overshoot by one node and break the split

palindrome-ll-triple-assignment-reversal.text: `isPalindrome` reverses the second half of the linked list using the triple assignment `curr.next, prev, curr = prev, curr, curr.next`, avoiding a temporary variable.

palindrome-negative-always-false.text: Negative numbers not being palindromes is definitional (the minus sign has no mirror), not a codebase-specific invariant worth tracking

palindrome-num-even-case-equality-check.text: For an even number of digits, `is_palindrome` compares `x == reversed_half` after the loop.

palindrome-num-half-reversal-technique.text: `is_palindrome` reverses only the second half of the digits and compares to the first half — the loop `while x > reversed_half` naturally stops at the midpoint, avoiding full reversal and potential overflow

palindrome-num-loop-terminates-monotonic.text: The half-reversal loop always terminates because `x` strictly decreases and `reversed_half` strictly increases each iteration.

palindrome-num-negative-immediate-false.text: `is_palindrome` returns `False` for any negative integer before entering the digit-reversal loop.

palindrome-num-no-string-conversion.text: The palindrome number solution uses only integer arithmetic (`%`, `//`, `*`) — no `str()`, slicing, or string comparison, satisfying the problem's implicit constraint

palindrome-num-o-log-n-time-o1-space.text: The palindrome number solution runs in O(log10 n) time and O(1) extra space.

palindrome-num-odd-case-discard-middle-d.text: For an odd number of digits, `is_palindrome` compares `x == reversed_half // 10` to discard the middle digit.

palindrome-num-trailing-zero-early-exit.text: Non-zero integers ending in 0 are rejected in O(1) before the reversal loop — a palindrome with trailing zeros would require leading zeros, which is impossible

palindrome-num-zero-is-palindrome.text: The input `0` correctly returns `True` — the trailing-zero guard has an explicit carve-out (`x != 0`) so zero is not falsely rejected

palindrome-perm-at-most-one-odd.text: `canPermutePalindrome` returns `True` iff at most one character in `s` has an odd frequency count

palindrome-perm-empty-string-true.text: An empty string input returns `True` (zero odd counts <= 1)

palindrome-perm-handles-any-hashable-cha.text: The solution works on any hashable characters even though the LeetCode problem scope is lowercase English letters.

palindrome-perm-linear-time.text: The solution runs in O(n) time and O(k) space where k is the alphabet size, dominated by `Counter` construction

palindrome-perm-no-validation.text: Too generic — nearly every LeetCode solution in the repo lacks input validation; this isn't a distinguishing invariant worth tracking per-problem

palindrome-perm-odd-count-parity-matches.text: The number of characters with odd frequency has the same parity as the string length, so an even-length string cannot have exactly one odd count.

palindrome-perm-parity-reduction.text: The solution reduces character frequencies to their parity (odd/even) via `c % 2`, discarding actual counts — a common idiom in palindrome problems

palindrome-perm-set-bitmask-alternative.text: An alternative O(n) approach uses a set's symmetric difference (or a bitmask) and checks whether the final set size is <= 1.

palindrome-perm-single-expression-body.text: `canPermutePalindrome` is implemented as a single expression: `sum(c % 2 for c in Counter(s).values()) <= 1`.

palindrome-reversal-adapts-across-data-d.text: Palindrome detection implements the same core insight — reverse and compare — across three data domains, each adapting the reversal mechanism to its representation: string slice reversal creates a full copy (O(n) space), integer half-reversal compares digits without string conversion (O(1) space), and linked list in-place reversal reuses existing nodes (O(1) space via mutation).

justifications.label: Three palindrome variants share reversal-comparison but adapt it to their data domain

pancakeSort-is-test-harness-alias.text: `pancakeSort = bitwiseComplement` is a class-level alias, not a separate implementation; it exists so the repo's test harness can call a consistent method name across all solution files regardless of the actual LeetCode method signature.

pangram-empty-string-returns-false.text: For an empty input string, the pangram solution computes `len(set(sentence))` as 0 and returns False.

pangram-hardcodes-alphabet-size-26.text: The pangram solution hardcodes the English lowercase alphabet size as 26 in its set-length comparison.

pangram-method-name-mismatch.text: The pangram solution (`check-if-the-sentence-is-pangram/solution.py`) names its method `min_operations` instead of `checkIfPangram` — a copy-paste artifact that doesn't break tests because the harness calls whatever method is defined on `Solution`.

pangram-set-auxiliary-space-bounded-by-2.text: Under the pangram solution's lowercase-only assumption, the set created from the sentence is bounded at 26 elements, so its auxiliary space is O(1).

parent-context-threading-via-parameter.text: `sum_of_left_leaves` passes an `is_left` boolean down the recursion so each node knows its relationship to its parent, rather than using the parent-look-ahead pattern where the parent checks `node.left.left is None`.

parity-ii-balanced-counts-guarantee-matc.text: Because exactly half the elements are even and half are odd, a misplaced odd at an even index always has a corresponding misplaced even at an odd index, so the two-pointer algorithm never gets stuck.

parity-ii-in-place-mutation.text: The `possible_bipartition` method mutates and returns the input list; callers holding a reference to the original list see the changes.

parity-ii-linear-time.text: The parity-II algorithm runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space via two stride-2 pointers that each traverse at most n/2 elements.

parity-ii-loop-invariant-even-odd-prefix.text: The loop invariant is that every even index before `i` contains an even number and every odd index before `j` contains an odd number.

parity-ii-method-name-mismatch.text: The parity-II solution method is named `possible_bipartition` rather than the LeetCode canonical `sortArrayByParityII`, likely a naming artifact from generation tooling.

parity-ii-swap-correctness.text: A swap only occurs when `nums[i]` is odd and `nums[j]` is even, guaranteeing both positions are fixed simultaneously.

parity-ii-terminates-in-at-most-n-iterat.text: Each iteration advances at least one pointer by 2, so the parity-II loop terminates in at most n iterations.

parity-ii-unbalanced-parity-counts-leave.text: If the input does not have equal even and odd counts, the algorithm can terminate while leaving some positions with the wrong parity because one pointer can go out of bounds while violations remain.

parity-slot-preservation-invariant.text: In `largest-number-after-digit-swaps-by-parity/solution.py`, the output digit at every position has the same odd/even parity as the input digit at that position — enforced by dual-pointer reconstruction from separate sorted pools

partial-week-starts-at-full-weeks-plus-1.text: The first day of the leftover partial week deposits `full_weeks + 1` (the 1-indexed week number), not `full_weeks`.

pascal-boundary-by-prefill.text: Boundary values (first and last element of each row = 1) are set by pre-filling with `[1] * (i + 1)`, not by conditional logic

pascal-generate-pure.text: `generate` is a pure function with no side effects, no imports, and no mutation of external state

pascal-generate-time-space-quadratic.text: `generate` runs in O(numRows^2) time and space, matching the size of its output list of lists.

pascal-implements-pascals-identity.text: The inner loop computes each interior element as the sum of the two elements above it, implementing `C(n,k) = C(n-1,k-1) + C(n-1,k)`.

pascal-inner-loop-safe.text: The inner loop `range(1, i)` guarantees all `triangle[i-1]` lookups are in-bounds without explicit bounds checking

pascal-iterative-bottom-up-construction.text: `generate` builds each row from the previous row iteratively rather than using recursion or the binomial coefficient formula.

pascal-negative-numrows-returns-empty.text: Calling `generate` with a negative `numRows` returns `[]` because the outer loop range is empty.

pascal-zero-rows-returns-empty.text: Calling `generate(0)` returns `[]` since the outer loop range is empty, even though this is outside the stated LeetCode constraints

pascals-triangle-ii-appends-trailing-one.text: Each outer iteration appends a trailing 1 to the row, and the leading 1 at index 0 is never modified.

pascals-triangle-ii-docstring-constraint.text: The `get_row` docstring documents the valid input range as `0 <= row_index <= 33`.

pascals-triangle-ii-inplace-dp-pattern.text: The reverse-traversal in-place mutation is the same space-optimization pattern used in 0/1 knapsack and other DP problems that reduce 2D state to 1D

pascals-triangle-ii-no-validation.text: Same rationale as palindrome-perm-no-validation — lack of validation is the norm for LeetCode solutions, not a distinguishing fact

pascals-triangle-ii-reverse-traversal.text: The inner loop must traverse right-to-left; left-to-right would use already-updated values and produce incorrect results

pascals-triangle-ii-row-zero-correct.text: For `row_index=0`, the loop body never executes and `[1]` is returned, which is correct

pascals-triangle-ii-space-linear.text: The solution uses O(row_index) space by mutating a single list in place rather than building all prior rows

pascals-triangle-ii-time-quadratic.text: `get_row` runs in O(row_index^2) time because the inner loop grows linearly with each outer iteration.

password-checker-no-short-circuit-on-fla.text: The validation loop cannot short-circuit even after all four category flags are `True`, because every adjacent pair must still be checked for duplicate characters

password-checker-special-char-independen.text: The special-character membership test is a standalone `if` (not part of the `elif` chain for lower/upper/digit), ensuring characters like space that fail all three category tests are still recognized as special

password-checker-specials-include-space.text: The special characters set is `"!@#$%^&*()-+ "` which includes the space character, matching the LeetCode problem specification

path-crossing-directions-rebuilt-per-cal.text: The directions dict mapping characters to displacement vectors is a local variable inside `path_crossing`, rebuilt on every invocation rather than hoisted to module scope.

path-crossing-early-exit.text: `path_crossing` returns `True` on the first revisited coordinate via early return, skipping the rest of the path.

path-crossing-linear-time.text: Too generic — O(n) time/space for a set-based traversal is obvious from reading the code and adds no non-trivial insight.

path-crossing-no-validation.text: Invalid direction characters (anything not in N/S/E/W) raise an uncaught `KeyError` from the directions dict lookup — no input validation exists.

path-crossing-origin-seeded.text: The visited set is seeded with (0,0) before any steps, so returning to the origin counts as a path crossing.

path-crossing-set-based-visited.text: Revisit detection uses a set of coordinate tuples for O(1) membership checks — the standard pattern for cycle/revisit detection on grids in this repo.

path-sum-base-case-ordering.text: hasPathSum handles cases in order: null node returns False, leaf node checks equality, internal node recurses on children with short-circuit or.

path-sum-leaf-only-matching.text: `hasPathSum` only returns `True` when the matching path ends at a leaf node (both children `None`); internal nodes whose cumulative sum equals the target are explicitly rejected.

path-sum-no-mutation.text: hasPathSum does not modify the tree or targetSum; each recursive call uses a new local remainder variable.

path-sum-null-always-false.text: `hasPathSum(None, targetSum)` returns `False` for any `targetSum` including 0 — an empty tree has no paths.

path-sum-self-contained-module.text: `path-sum/solution.py` defines `TreeNode`, the solution function, and the full test suite (`TestPathSum` with 9 cases) in a single file.

path-sum-short-circuit-or.text: The `or` in the recursive return skips exploration of the right subtree entirely if the left subtree already found a valid path.

path-sum-subtraction-pattern.text: The algorithm subtracts each node's value from the remaining target rather than accumulating a running sum, avoiding an extra accumulator parameter.

per-problem-data-structure-isolation.text: Each problem directory defines its own data structures (e.g., `TreeNode` in `sum-of-left-leaves`) rather than importing from a shared utility module, maintaining per-problem self-containment.

per-problem-directory-layout.text: Each LeetCode problem lives in its own directory containing `solution.py`, `test_solution.py`, `plan.md`, and `review.md` as the standard file set.

percentage-floor-integer-arithmetic.text: `percentageLetter` computes floor percentage using `count * 100 // len(s)`, avoiding floating-point entirely to prevent rounding artifacts.

percentage-letter-single-expression.text: The percentageLetter method is a single return statement with no branching, loops, or intermediate variables.

percentage-no-empty-string-guard.text: `percentageLetter` has no guard against empty-string input and will raise `ZeroDivisionError` — it relies on LeetCode's constraint that `len(s) >= 1`.

perfect-number-dedup-guard.text: The `i != num // i` check prevents double-counting the square root divisor when `num` is a perfect square.

perfect-number-excludes-self.text: The divisor sum in checkPerfectNumber never includes num itself because the loop stops at isqrt(num) and the seed is 1.

perfect-number-rejects-leq-1.text: Standard boundary handling visible from reading the code; not a surprising invariant or a constraint that would break downstream code if changed.

perfect-number-seed-one.text: The divisor sum is seeded at 1 (since 1 is always a proper divisor for `num > 1`), and the loop starts at 2, avoiding a special case inside the loop.

perfect-number-sqrt-complexity.text: `checkPerfectNumber` runs in O(sqrt(n)) time and O(1) space by harvesting paired divisors from a loop up to `isqrt(num)`.

perfect-number-uses-isqrt.text: `checkPerfectNumber` uses `math.isqrt` instead of `int(math.sqrt(n))` to avoid floating-point precision loss for large integers near 2^53.

perform-string-shifts-early-return-net-z.text: The inorder function returns early if net == 0, avoiding a wasteful string slice copy.

perform-string-shifts-empty-crash.text: Passing an empty string to `inorder` raises `ZeroDivisionError` at `net %= len(s)` — no guard exists.

perform-string-shifts-slice-rotation.text: The string rotation in inorder is implemented using the slice expression s[-net:] + s[:-net].

pigeonhole-26-letter-bound.text: The first-letter-to-appear-twice loop executes at most 27 iterations regardless of string length, since 26 lowercase letters force a collision by the 27th character via the pigeonhole principle.

pillow-holder-full-passes-floor-division.text: The solution computes `full_passes` as `time // (n - 1)` and `remainder` as `time % (n - 1)`.

pillow-holder-n1-crash.text: Calling `pillowHolder(1, t)` for any `t > 0` raises `ZeroDivisionError` because `cycle` is 0

pillow-holder-o1-time.text: `pillowHolder` runs in O(1) time and space regardless of the `time` input, using division and modulo instead of simulation

pillow-holder-parity-direction.text: Even `full_passes` means forward direction (returns `1 + remainder`), odd means backward (returns `n - remainder`)

pillow-holder-return-range-1-to-n.text: `pillowHolder` always returns a value in the inclusive range `[1, n]` for valid inputs.

pillow-holder-round-trip-period-2n-minus.text: A full round-trip from person 1 to person n and back to person 1 has period `2 * (n - 1)` seconds.

pillow-holder-zero-indexed-cycle.text: The cycle length is `n - 1` (not `n`), representing the number of hand-offs per pass, not the number of people

ping-window-boundary-inclusive.text: In the recent-calls solution (problem 933), the eviction condition `self.q[0] < t - 3000` keeps timestamps equal to `t - 3000` in the window, making both endpoints of `[t-3000, t]` inclusive

pipeline-decomposition-unifies-classific.text: The preprocess-then-stream pipeline decomposition serves a dual structural role: it is simultaneously the classification criterion that partitions the solution taxonomy into three exhaustive strategies AND the optimization mechanism that achieves correctness, time efficiency, and space efficiency — the same structural cut that classifies solutions also optimizes them.

justifications.label: Both depth-5 conclusions depend on the pipeline decomposition for different properties (taxonomy closure vs triple optimization); combining reveals a single structural principle performing dual duty

pipeline-generates-misnamed-functions.text: At least two solutions have function names from unrelated LeetCode problems due to copy-paste errors in the code generation pipeline: `longestAwesomeSubstring` solves problem 1668 (not 1542), and `busiest_servers` solves problem 1710 (not 1606).

pivot-index-accumulate-after-check.text: In `pivotIndex`, `left_sum += num` occurs *after* the equality check — this ordering is a critical invariant ensuring the pivot element is excluded from both the left and right sums.

pivot-index-boundary-no-special-case.text: Index 0 and index n-1 are valid pivot positions without special-case code because `left_sum` starts at 0 and the right sum is computed algebraically — empty-side sums are implicitly zero.

pivot-index-empty-list-returns-minus-one.text: `pivotIndex([])` returns `-1` because the loop is skipped and the default return is `-1`.

pivot-index-imports-only-typing-list.text: The pivot-index solution imports only `typing.List` and has no external or project dependencies.

pivot-index-iterates-with-enumerate.text: `pivotIndex` iterates over `nums` using `enumerate` to track the index.

pivot-index-leftmost-guarantee.text: `pivotIndex` returns the leftmost valid pivot index via early return on first match, not just any valid pivot.

pivot-index-returns-minus-one-when-no-pi.text: `pivotIndex` returns `-1` when the loop completes without finding a pivot.

pivot-index-right-sum-derived-algebraica.text: `pivotIndex` never computes the right sum directly; it derives it as `total - left_sum - nums[i]`, enabling O(n) time and O(1) space with a single pass after the initial `sum()`.

pivot-integer-closed-form-o1.text: `find_pivot` reduces the problem to checking whether `n*(n+1)/2` is a perfect square, yielding O(1) time and space with no loops or recursion.

pivot-integer-isqrt-not-sqrt.text: `find_pivot` uses `math.isqrt` (integer square root) instead of `math.sqrt` to avoid floating-point precision bugs that surface with `int(math.sqrt(n))` for large perfect squares.

pivot-integer-returns-minus-one-when-no-.text: find_pivot returns -1 when n*(n+1)//2 is not a perfect square.

pivot-integer-total-uses-floor-division.text: The triangular total in find_pivot is computed as n*(n+1)//2 using integer floor division.

pivot-integer-unique-positive-solution.text: The equation x^2 = n*(n+1)/2 has at most one positive integer solution, so find_pivot returns either that unique pivot or -1.

plate-parsing-ignores-non-alpha.text: Only alphabetic characters from `licensePlate` contribute to the required letter counts; digits and spaces are filtered by `isalpha()` and letters are lowercased at parse time, while `words` are assumed already lowercase.

pool-exactly-consumed.text: This is a correctness property of the dual-pointer algorithm, already implied by `parity-slot-preservation-invariant` — redundant

popcount-via-bin-count.text: The codebase uses `bin(n).count('1')` as its standard popcount idiom rather than Kernighan's bit-clearing loop or Python 3.10+'s `int.bit_count()`.

postorder-accumulator-pattern.text: Tree problems in this repo use a recurring idiom: a postorder DFS function returns one value (e.g., subtree sum, height) while accumulating a second aggregate (e.g., tilt, diameter) into a `nonlocal` closure variable.

postorder-uses-reverse-preorder.text: The n-ary postorder traversal computes a modified preorder (root-right-left via stack) and reverses the result, rather than using recursion or visited-node tracking.

power-of-four-constant-time.text: `isPowerOfFour` runs in O(1) time and O(1) space with no loops, recursion, or library calls.

power-of-four-mask-32bit.text: The mask `0x55555555` only covers bit positions 0–30, so the power-of-four solution assumes n fits in a 32-bit signed integer (matching the LeetCode constraint).

power-of-four-no-imports.text: Trivially observable from the file — "has no imports" is not a meaningful invariant.

power-of-four-subset-of-power-of-two.text: The first two conditions in `isPowerOfFour` (`n > 0` and `n & (n-1) == 0`) are exactly the power-of-two check; the third condition (`n & 0x55555555 != 0`) narrows from powers-of-two to powers-of-four by requiring the set bit at an even position.

power-of-three-32bit-assumption.text: The power-of-three solution is only correct for inputs in [-2^31, 2^31-1]; any power of 3 exceeding 3^19 (e.g., 3^20) would incorrectly return `False`.

power-of-three-constant-time.text: Duplicates the same claim made for power-of-two and power-of-four — better captured as a cross-cutting pattern than per-solution.

power-of-three-magic-constant.text: The constant 1162261467 equals 3^19, the largest power of 3 below 2^31, and is load-bearing for correctness — if the input domain expanded beyond 32-bit signed integers, this constant would need to change.

power-of-three-prime-dependency.text: The divisibility trick (`3^19 % n == 0` implies n is a power of 3) is valid only because 3 is prime; applying the same pattern to a composite base would produce false positives since composite powers have non-power divisors.

power-of-two-bit-trick.text: `n & (n - 1) == 0` detects positive integers with exactly one set bit (powers of two); this is a foundational kernel reused in power-of-four and referenced by number-of-1-bits (Brian Kernighan's algorithm) across the repo.

power-of-two-constant-time.text: Same as power-of-three-constant-time — O(1) is the obvious property of a branchless expression and doesn't warrant per-solution tracking.

power-of-two-no-imports.text: Trivially observable — not a meaningful codebase invariant.

power-of-two-rejects-zero.text: The `n > 0` guard in `is_power_of_two` is necessary because `0 & (0 - 1)` equals `0`, which would incorrectly pass the single-set-bit test.

power-of-x-positivity-guard.text: All three power-of-X solutions (two, three, four) share an `n > 0` guard as their first short-circuit condition, since no non-positive integer is a power of any positive base — and each would fail differently without it (false positive for zero in power-of-two, ZeroDivisionError in power-of-three).
