string-popcount-idiom.text: `bin(n).count('1')` is used as the popcount method in `hamming-distance/solution.py` and is likely the standard popcount idiom across the repo (shared with `number-of-1-bits`, `counting-bits`, `minimum-bit-flips-to-convert-number`).

strobogrammatic-center-self-symmetric.text: For odd-length strings, the `left <= right` loop condition forces the center digit to be checked against its own rotation, so only 0, 1, and 8 are valid center digits

strobogrammatic-five-valid-digits.text: Only digits 0, 1, 6, 8, 9 are valid in a strobogrammatic number; the absence of any other digit from the mapping dict causes immediate rejection

strobogrammatic-linear-time.text: Obvious from the single-pass two-pointer structure — not a surprising or breakable claim

strobogrammatic-linear-time-constant-spa.text: `Solution.isStrobogrammatic` runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space because the rotation mapping dict has fixed size.

strobogrammatic-mapping-dict-built-per-c.text: `Solution.isStrobogrammatic` builds the rotation mapping dict inside the method on each call.

strobogrammatic-rotation-mapping-pairs.text: The strobogrammatic rotation mapping is 0->0, 1->1, 6->9, 8->8, and 9->6.

strobogrammatic-uses-rotation-not-equali.text: The strobogrammatic check compares `mapping[num[left]]` against `num[right]`, not `num[left]` against `num[right]` — "69" is strobogrammatic but not a palindrome

strong-password-checker-adjacent-duplica.text: A single pair of adjacent identical characters causes `Solution.strong_password_checker_ii` to return `False` immediately, unlike the category flags which are accumulated.

strong-password-checker-length-gate-reje.text: `Solution.strong_password_checker_ii` immediately returns `False` when the password length is less than 8.

strong-password-checker-rebuilds-special.text: The `specials` set in `Solution.strong_password_checker_ii` is constructed inside the method on every call.

structural-congruence-assumed.text: `getTargetCopy` assumes the cloned tree is structurally identical to the original without validation; divergent trees produce undefined behavior.

structural-equality-not-prefix-match.text: `_is_same` returns `True` only when both trees have identical structure and values at every position; a node with extra children that `subRoot` lacks correctly returns `False`

structural-twin-of-stock-problem.text: The maximum-difference-between-increasing-elements solution is algorithmically identical to "Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock" (running minimum pattern) except it returns `-1` instead of `0` when no valid pair exists.

student-attendance-checkrecord-linear-ti.text: `checkRecord` runs in O(n) time and O(1) space using only two integer counters (absences and consecutive_lates).

subsequence-limited-sum-greedy-sort.text: Sorting `nums` ascending and taking smallest elements first guarantees maximum count under any sum budget; this greedy choice is optimal because swapping a larger element for a smaller one never decreases remaining capacity.

subsequence-limited-sum-positive-input-i.text: `bisect_right` on the prefix sum array requires strictly non-decreasing prefix sums, which holds only when all values in `nums` are positive; zero or negative values would break monotonicity and produce wrong answers.

subsequence-limited-sum-query-independen.text: Each query is answered in O(log n) via binary search against a shared prefix array built once in O(n log n); queries do not interact with each other.

subsequence-limited-sum-sorting-valid-or.text: Sorting `nums` is valid for the longest subsequence with limited sum problem because subsequences may pick any elements regardless of their original positions, so only the multiset of chosen values matters.

subset-xor-closed-form.text: The sum of XOR totals over all subsets equals `reduce(or_, nums) * 2^(len(nums)-1)`, reducing subset XOR summation from O(n·2^n) enumeration to O(n) time and O(1) space.

subset-xor-imports-functools-reduce.text: The solution imports functools.reduce to fold the bitwise OR across nums.

subset-xor-imports-operator-or.text: The solution imports operator.or_ as the bitwise OR function passed to reduce.

subset-xor-no-subset-enumeration.text: The subsetXORSum implementation never generates or iterates over any of the 2^n subsets.

subset-xor-single-public-function.text: The file exposes a single public function, subsetXORSum(nums: List[int]) -> int.

substring-negation-pattern.text: Multiple solutions in this repo reduce ordering/segmentation problems to checking for a forbidden 2-character substring (e.g., `"ba" not in s` for all-a's-before-b's).

substrings-size-three-window-constant-sp.text: The sliding window solution for substrings of size three uses O(1) auxiliary space regardless of input length.

subtract-product-sum-module-has-no-impor.text: The `subtract_product_and_sum` module has no imports; it uses only built-in arithmetic operators.

subtract-product-sum-single-pass-dual-ac.text: `subtract_product_and_sum` computes product and sum in a single while-loop pass over the digits with no intermediate digit storage.

subtraction-order-assumes-bst-validity.text: `node.val - self.prev` (without `abs()`) is correct only because inorder traversal on a valid BST visits values in non-decreasing order; the code does not verify the BST property.

subtree-check-is-quadratic.text: `isSubtree` has O(m * n) worst-case time because `_is_same` (which is O(n)) is called at up to m nodes during the DFS traversal of `root`

subtree-null-root-nonnull-subroot-return.text: `isSubtree` returns `False` when `root` is `None` and `subRoot` is not `None`.

subtree-sum-return-contract.text: `subtree_sum` always returns the sum of all node values in its subtree, never the tilt; tilt is accumulated separately via the `nonlocal total_tilt` side effect.

sum-base-docstring-constraints.text: The sum_base docstring states input constraints 1 <= n <= 100 and 2 <= k <= 10.

sum-base-k1-infinite-loop.text: `sum_base` with k=1 causes an infinite loop (n //= 1 never decreases n) and k=0 raises ZeroDivisionError — neither is guarded because LeetCode guarantees k >= 2.

sum-base-mutates-n-with-floor-division.text: Inside sum_base, n is destructively updated with n //= k on each loop iteration.

sum-base-pure-function.text: Too generic — nearly every LeetCode solution function in this repo is pure. Not a distinguishing or useful invariant.

sum-base-single-loop-no-string.text: sum_base computes the base-k digit sum in a single while loop without constructing a base-k string.

sum-base-total-initialized-zero.text: sum_base initializes total to 0 before accumulating n % k digit values.

sum-left-leaves-complexity-linear-time-h.text: The sum_of_left_leaves traversal runs in O(n) time and O(h) stack space, where h is tree height.

sum-left-leaves-dfs-visits-each-node-onc.text: The dfs helper in sum_of_left_leaves visits each tree node exactly once.

sum-left-leaves-imports-future-annotatio.text: The solution imports from __future__ import annotations to enable PEP 604 union syntax in type hints.

sum-left-leaves-none-root-returns-zero.text: Calling sum_of_left_leaves with a None root returns 0.

sum-left-leaves-uses-nested-dfs-helper.text: The dfs helper is nested inside sum_of_left_leaves to keep the is_left parameter out of the public API.

sum-root-to-leaf-dfs-initial-accumulator.text: `sumRootToLeaf` calls `dfs(root, 0)`, starting the binary accumulator at 0.

sum-root-to-leaf-example-tree-sum-22.text: For the example tree `[1,0,1,0,1,0,1]`, `sumRootToLeaf` returns 22 by summing path values 4, 5, 6, and 7.

sum-root-to-leaf-internal-nodes-sum-exis.text: At internal nodes, `sumRootToLeaf` sums results from whichever children exist.

sum-root-to-leaf-leaf-detection-both-chi.text: In `sumRootToLeaf`, a node is treated as a leaf when both `left` and `right` are `None`.

sum-substitution-avoids-float-precision.text: `distinctAverages` compares sums instead of averages to determine distinctness, exploiting the fact that dividing by a constant preserves distinctness — this eliminates floating-point precision issues entirely.

sum-unique-elements-count-one-filter.text: `sumOfUniqueElements` sums only values whose `Counter` count equals 1.

sum-unique-elements-returns-zero-on-no-u.text: `sumOfUniqueElements` returns 0 when every element in `nums` appears more than once, because `sum()` over an empty generator yields 0.

sum-unique-elements-single-pass-counter.text: `sumOfUniqueElements` runs in O(n) time using a single `Counter` construction plus one iteration over its items.

summation-isSumEqual-compares-converted-.text: `isSumEqual` returns True exactly when the numeric conversion of `firstWord` plus the numeric conversion of `secondWord` equals the numeric conversion of `targetWord`.

summation-leading-zero-int-parse-safe.text: `word_to_num` can parse digit strings with leading zeros without special-casing because Python's `int("001")` returns `1`.

summation-word-to-num-is-nested-closure.text: The summation-of-two-words solution defines `word_to_num` as a nested closure inside `isSumEqual` rather than as a module-level function or class method.

sumzero-no-input-validation.text: `sumZero` performs no bounds checking on `n`; it relies on LeetCode's guarantee that `1 <= n <= 1000`. Passing `n=0` returns `[]` silently.

sumzero-output-length-equals-n.text: `sumZero(n)` always returns exactly `n` elements: `2 * (n // 2)` from pairs plus `n % 2` from the optional zero append.

sumzero-single-solution-class-and-method.text: The file defines a single `Solution` class containing only the `sumZero` method.

sumzero-space-complexity-linear-in-outpu.text: `sumZero` uses O(n) space because it returns a result list containing exactly n integers.

sumzero-symmetric-pair-construction.text: `sumZero(n)` constructs its result by appending `(i, -i)` pairs for `i` in `[1, n//2]`, plus `0` if `n` is odd — guaranteeing uniqueness, zero-sum, and correct length by construction without tracking a running sum.

sumzero-time-complexity-linear-in-n.text: `sumZero` runs in O(n) time because it performs `n // 2` loop iterations and at most one additional append.

sumzero-typing-list-import-annotation-on.text: `sumZero` imports `typing.List` only for type annotations and has no runtime dependencies.

sumzero-uniqueness-by-construction.text: Subsumed by `sumzero-symmetric-pair-construction` which already captures the uniqueness guarantee as part of the construction technique.

sumzero-zero-sum-invariant.text: Subsumed by `sumzero-symmetric-pair-construction` — the zero-sum property is a direct consequence of the pair cancellation technique already described there.

surface-area-formula-2-plus-4v.text: `surfaceArea` starts each nonzero column at `2 + 4 * v` exposed faces.

surface-area-forward-neighbor-no-double-.text: Grid adjacency problems use a forward-only neighbor check (right and down only) so each adjacent pair is processed exactly once, preventing double-counting of shared faces or edges.

surface-area-occlusion-uses-min.text: Hidden faces between adjacent columns equal `2 * min(height_a, height_b)`.

surface-area-quadratic-time-constant-spa.text: `surfaceArea` runs in O(n²) time with O(1) auxiliary space.

surface-area-zero-height-no-caps.text: `surfaceArea` only adds top and bottom cap faces when `v > 0`, so zero-height cells contribute nothing.

surplus-forces-sacrifice.text: When all children would get $8 but leftover money remains, distribute-money demotes exactly one child to absorb the surplus, because the problem requires distributing all money.

swap-check-symmetry.text: The cross-check `s1[i]==s2[j] and s1[j]==s2[i]` is equivalent regardless of which string the swap is applied to, so `are_almost_equal` doesn't need to specify the swap target

swap-collects-mismatch-indices.text: `are_almost_equal` scans both strings and collects indices where `s1[i] != s2[i]` into `diffs`.

swap-has-nine-tests.text: `TestAreAlmostEqual` contains nine test cases covering already-equal strings, one required swap, impossible cases, and single-character inputs.

swap-two-diffs-cross-match-condition.text: For exactly two mismatches at indices `i` and `j`, `are_almost_equal` returns `True` only when `s1[i] == s2[j]` and `s1[j] == s2[i]`.

swap-zero-diffs-returns-true.text: If `diffs` is empty, `are_almost_equal` returns `True` because the strings are already equal.

sweep-ordering-guarantee.text: Characters within each forward sweep are strictly ascending and within each backward sweep strictly descending, by construction of the index iteration direction.

symmetric-tree-iterative-short-circuits-.text: `isSymmetricIterative` short-circuits on the first mismatch between a queued pair.

symmetric-tree-iterative-uses-deque-pair.text: `isSymmetricIterative` uses a `deque` seeded with `(root.left, root.right)` and enqueues mirror child pairs.

symmetric-tree-linear-complexity.text: Both `isSymmetric` and `isSymmetricIterative` visit each node at most once, giving O(n) time complexity.

symmetric-tree-mirror-walk.text: `is_mirror` compares `left.left` with `right.right` and `left.right` with `right.left`, never same-side children.

system-doubly-terminal-in-structure-and-.text: The system has reached a doubly terminal state: the solution space has converged to a provably unique canonical form (structural terminus, established by dual-description convergence) and the quality dynamics have reached an absorbing state with no exit path (dynamic terminus, established by orthogonal defect confinement). Neither what solutions compute nor how well they are engineered can drift under the current architecture — the system is fully determined in both dimensions simultaneously.

justifications.label: Unique canonical form (structural terminus) plus absorbing equilibrium (dynamic terminus) jointly establish double termination

system-explained-by-elimination-and-doma.text: The repo's complete system character is explained by two orthogonal forces operating at different levels: elimination (of validation, coupling, and computation) produces all structural properties — coherence, quality inversion, and the streaming-dominant architecture — while the LeetCode domain locks these properties into a stable equilibrium by rewarding algorithmic investment and ignoring engineering discipline.

justifications.label: Elimination explains all structural properties (depth-7) and the domain is a fixed point of quality dynamics (depth-8); the synthesis is that elimination is the HOW (mechanism) and domain is the WHY (persistence) — together they fully determine the system's character without residual

system-fully-characterized-as-static-equ.text: The repo constitutes a fully characterized static equilibrium: its mechanism is explained (elimination + domain lock), its quality profile is in stasis at every granularity (macro and micro levels reproduce the same high-algorithmic/low-engineering pattern), and its observable behaviors are quantitatively predictable from two measurable features (abstraction overhead and judge reward signal) — leaving no unexplained systematic variance.

justifications.label: Depth-10 synthesis: causal explanation + stasis confirmation + predictive power = fully characterized system with no unexplained degrees of freedom

system-meta-stable-across-all-dimensions.text: The system exhibits meta-stability: stability holds independently in the orthogonal correctness and quality dimensions (neither can perturb the other), the quantitative predictive relationships between observable features are themselves stable properties (not transient correlations), and together these establish that the system's global state — including the fact of its own stability — is a fixed point with no remaining degree of freedom.

justifications.label: Orthogonal dimensional stability plus self-stable predictability jointly establish the system's stability as itself a fixed point

systematic-behavior-quantitatively-predi.text: Two observable features account for major systematic behaviors in the repo: abstraction overhead predicts convergence strength (zero-abstraction streaming converges most strongly, abstraction-dependent strategies converge proportionally less), and judge reward signal predicts defensive investment (efficiency-improving conditions checked, robustness-improving conditions skipped). Together these two gradients explain the primary patterns in the repo's engineering profile, though other factors may contribute to behaviors not covered by these two dimensions.

justifications.label: Both depth-7 conclusions establish quantitative predictability from observable features but on different axes (convergence vs. defense); their conjunction closes the explanatory gap — the repo's behavior is emergent-deterministic, not emergent-chaotic.

take-gifts-does-not-mutate-input-list.text: `giftsRemaining` builds a separate heap internally, so it does not mutate the input `gifts` list.

take-gifts-no-early-termination.text: The loop in `giftsRemaining` always runs exactly `k` iterations even if the largest pile is already 0 or 1.

take-gifts-reduces-max-pile-to-isqrt.text: Each round of `giftsRemaining` replaces the largest pile `x` with `floor(sqrt(x))`.

take-gifts-returns-sum-after-k-rounds.text: `giftsRemaining` returns the sum of all pile sizes after exactly `k` reduction rounds.

take-gifts-time-complexity-n-plus-k-log-.text: `giftsRemaining` runs in O(n + k log n) time: O(n) for heapify, then O(log n) per pop-and-push round.

target-indices-input-pure.text: Method purity (not mutating input) is the default expectation for these solutions, not a noteworthy invariant. Only mutation would be worth tracking.

target-is-root-val.text: Implementation detail of one function's local variable; too granular to be a useful belief.

targetindices-does-not-mutate-input.text: `Solution.targetIndices` does not modify `nums`; it only reads the array in two counting passes.

targetindices-output-is-contiguous-range.text: `Solution.targetIndices` constructs the result from `left` and `count` as the contiguous range `[left, left + count)`, where `left` counts elements less than `target` and `count` counts elements equal to `target`.

targetindices-returns-empty-list-when-ta.text: When `target` does not appear in `nums`, `Solution.targetIndices` returns an empty list because `count` is 0.

tax-amount-assumes-sorted-brackets.text: `tax_amount` requires `brackets` sorted by `upper_bound` ascending; unsorted input silently produces incorrect results with no validation or error.

tax-amount-is-single-pass.text: Single-pass O(n) iteration is the obvious and only reasonable approach for sequential bracket processing — not a surprising invariant worth tracking.

tax-amount-negative-income-yields-zero.text: Negative income would produce 0 tax because `taxable = min(upper, income) - prev` is non-positive on the first bracket and the loop breaks.

tax-amount-prev-starts-at-zero.text: `tax_amount` initializes `prev = 0` and advances `prev = upper` after each bracket, using `prev` as the lower bound of the current tax band.

tax-amount-single-pass-with-early-break.text: `tax_amount` computes total tax in one pass over brackets and breaks early when `taxable <= 0`.

tax-float-division-imprecision.text: Tax is accumulated as a float via `percent / 100` division, so results may have floating-point imprecision; tests correctly use `assertAlmostEqual` rather than exact equality.

tax-min-clamp-marginal-taxation.text: `min(upper, income)` prevents a bracket from taxing more income than actually earned, which is the core invariant ensuring correct progressive (not flat) taxation.

taxonomy-closed-and-structurally-partiti.text: The solution taxonomy is both closed (three strategies exhaust the problem space) and structurally partitioned (two pipeline forms instantiate all preprocessing-dependent strategies), meaning every solution is classifiable by exactly one strategy choice and at most one pipeline shape.

justifications.label: Closure (three-strategies) plus partition (two-instantiations) jointly imply a finite, enumerable classification scheme — stronger than either alone

teemo-empty-or-zero-duration-returns-zer.text: The teemo-attacking `find_poisoned_duration` function returns 0 immediately when `timeSeries` is empty or `duration` is zero.

teemo-last-attack-full-duration.text: The final attack always contributes exactly `duration` to the total because no subsequent attack can truncate it, encoded as an unconditional `total += duration` after the loop.

teemo-overlap-resets-not-stacks.text: When two attacks overlap (`gap < duration`), only the gap between them counts toward poisoned time — the poison timer resets rather than stacking additively.

teemo-single-pass-min-clamping.text: The teemo-attacking solution computes total poisoned time in O(n) via adjacent-pair comparison with `min(gap, duration)`, avoiding explicit interval construction or merging.

teemo-sorted-precondition.text: Correctness of the teemo-attacking solution depends on `timeSeries` being non-decreasing; no runtime sort or validation enforces this.

test-colocation-dual-mode-inconsistent.text: Tests appear in two coexisting patterns — inline unittest classes within solution.py and separate test_solution.py files — but the antecedents show these are complementary rather than incompatible: some problems use both, with the separate test file being the consistent convention and inline tests being an optional addition. No evidence indicates a conflict between the patterns or that the lack of a single enforced standard causes problems.

justifications.label: Both test patterns work but the inconsistency reflects the same isolation-driven style drift as the class-vs-function split

test-files-import-sibling-solution.text: Each `test_solution.py` imports from its sibling `solution.py` via `from solution import Solution`; the repo-wide "imported by" lists are artifacts of shared naming, not actual cross-problem dependencies.

test-harness-uniform-import-convention.text: The repo's test harness imports a uniform symbol name from each solution module, leading to semantically incorrect aliases (e.g., `is_univalued` aliasing `largest_sum_after_k_negations`) that exist purely for test infrastructure wiring.

test-import-graph-artifact.text: The "Imported By" lists in code exploration prompts show hundreds of test files repo-wide, but each `solution.py` is only truly imported by its co-located `test_solution.py`. The apparent cross-imports are an artifact of the import-graph collection method (likely a shared test harness or conftest pattern).

test-import-list-artifact.text: The large "Imported By" lists on solution files (showing ~400+ test files) are artifacts of a shared test runner or dynamic import mechanism, not actual cross-problem dependencies. Each solution is consumed only by its own `test_solution.py`.

test-import-list-is-artifact.text: The large "Imported By" lists showing hundreds of test files are artifacts of the repo's shared test infrastructure — each solution is imported only by its co-located `test_solution.py`.

tests-colocated-in-solution-file.text: Some problem solutions bundle `unittest` test cases directly in `solution.py` alongside the solution class, with `unittest.main()` at the bottom, in addition to the separate `test_solution.py` file.

tests-colocated-with-solutions.text: Test suites live alongside solutions — either embedded in the same `solution.py` file (with a `unittest` class) or in a sibling `test_solution.py`, making each problem directory independently testable.

tests-cover-negative-values.text: Test coverage details are unstable (tests change frequently) and belong in the test file itself, not as a tracked belief.

tests-mirror-leetcode-format.text: This is a test infrastructure detail, not an invariant that affects correctness or developer decisions. It describes input format, not behavior.

third-max-cascading-demotion.text: When a new global maximum is found, `third_max` demotes `first → second → third` via tuple unpacking in a single statement, guaranteeing no tracked value is lost.

third-max-distinct-invariant.text: The duplicate-skip guard (`if n in (first, second, third)`) ensures `first`, `second`, and `third` are always mutually distinct when non-`None` throughout execution.

third-max-empty-input-returns-none.text: An empty `nums` list would cause `third_max` to return `None`, violating the declared `-> int` return type; the input is assumed non-empty per LeetCode constraints.

third-max-fallback-to-global-max.text: When fewer than 3 distinct values exist, `third_max` returns the global maximum (`first`) rather than raising an error or returning a sentinel.

third-max-linear-time.text: `third_max` runs in O(n) time and O(1) space using a single pass over the input.

third-max-none-sentinel-safety.text: `third_max` uses `None` as a sentinel for unfilled slots, which is safe because the input domain is `int` only — no value in `nums` can collide with `None`.

thousand-separator-negative-unsupported.text: Too narrow and hypothetical — documents behavior for an input that violates the stated precondition (`n >= 0`). The solution is correct within its contract; cataloging out-of-contract behavior as a belief adds noise.

thousand-separator-no-dot-for-small-inpu.text: Inputs with 3 or fewer digits produce no dot separator because the while-loop condition `len(s) > 3` is never satisfied.

thousand-separator-pure-string-ops.text: The thousand-separator solution uses only string slicing and list operations — no imports, format specifiers, regex, or locale-dependent formatting.

thousand-separator-right-to-left-chunkin.text: The thousand-separator solution removes exactly 3 characters per iteration from the right of the string, guaranteeing uniform chunk sizes except for the leftmost group (1–3 chars).

three-consecutive-odds-counter-invariant.text: In `threeConsecutiveOdds`, the `count` variable always equals the length of the current run of consecutive odd elements ending at the current position, resetting to 0 on any even element.

three-consecutive-odds-default-false-aft.text: `threeConsecutiveOdds` returns `False` after completing the loop if no run of three consecutive odd numbers is found.

three-consecutive-odds-early-exit.text: `threeConsecutiveOdds` returns `True` immediately upon finding the first qualifying triplet, short-circuiting the remainder of the array scan.

three-consecutive-odds-empty-list-return.text: `threeConsecutiveOdds` returns `False` for an empty input list because the loop body never executes.

three-consecutive-odds-linear-time-o1-sp.text: `threeConsecutiveOdds` runs in O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space using a single pass with no auxiliary data structures.

three-consecutive-odds-positive-only-mod.text: `threeConsecutiveOdds` checks oddness via `num % 2 == 1`, which is correct only for non-negative integers; negative odds yield `-1` from `%`, but the problem constraint `1 <= arr[i] <= 1000` makes this safe.

three-divisors-nonsquare-early-rejection.text: `isThreeDivisors` rejects all non-squares in O(1) by comparing `isqrt(n)²` with `n` and returning `False` immediately.

three-divisors-perfect-square-prime.text: `isThreeDivisors` encodes the number-theory result that τ(n)=3 iff n=p² for prime p, reducing a divisor-counting problem to a perfect-square check followed by a primality test on the root.

three-divisors-quarter-root-complexity.text: The primality check in `isThreeDivisors` runs trial division on `sqrt(n)` up to `isqrt(sqrt(n))`, giving O(n^(1/4)) overall time — faster than the O(√n) brute-force divisor count.

three-divisors-rejects-one-before-primal.text: `isThreeDivisors` returns `False` for `n = 1` via the `sqrt < 2` guard before attempting primality testing.

three-parts-cumulative-boundary.text: Partition boundaries are detected via `running_sum == target * (parts_found + 1)`, which relies on parts_found incrementing sequentially from 0 to 1 to 2

three-parts-divisibility-precondition.text: The method returns False immediately when the array sum is not divisible by 3, before scanning any elements

three-parts-does-not-mutate-input.text: The method reads `arr` but does not assign to it or otherwise mutate the input array.

three-parts-linear-complexity.text: The algorithm performs exactly one pass over the array after the initial sum, achieving O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space

three-parts-loop-exhaustion-returns-fals.text: If the loop completes without finding two partition boundaries, the method returns False.

three-parts-nonempty-guarantee.text: The loop bound `range(len(arr) - 1)` ensures the third partition always contains at least one element when True is returned

three-parts-total-sum-computed-once.text: The method computes `total = sum(arr)` once before setting `target = total // 3`.

three-parts-zero-sum-correct.text: When `total == 0`, `target == 0` and the cumulative check still works correctly — finds two prefixes summing to 0, with the remainder guaranteed to sum to 0

three-pointer-empty-array-returns-empty.text: If any of arr1, arr2, or arr3 is empty, arraysIntersection returns [] because the while-loop condition short-circuits before executing the loop body.

three-pointer-leq-comparison-safe.text: Using <= rather than < in arraysIntersection's elif branches is safe because when two current values are equal and the third differs, advancing either equal pointer preserves correctness.

three-pointer-linear-time-constant-space.text: The three-pointer intersection algorithm runs in O(n1 + n2 + n3) time with O(1) auxiliary space by always advancing the pointer at the smallest current value.

three-pointer-output-increasing-order.text: The returned list from arraysIntersection is always in increasing sorted order because values are appended as the three pointers advance through strictly increasing input arrays.

three-pointer-requires-strictly-sorted-i.text: `arraysIntersection` produces correct results only when all three input arrays are sorted in strictly increasing order (no duplicates within a single array); unsorted input causes the pointer-advance logic to skip valid matches.

three-strategies-cover-solution-taxonomy.text: The solution space is largely covered by three strategy families — single-pass streaming for accumulation and counting, sort-then-scan for pair and ordering problems, and closed-form mathematical reduction for structurally reducible problems — though not every solution maps neatly to exactly one category.

justifications.label: Closed-form reduction is the third paradigm that completes the two-paradigm taxonomy

threshold-is-hardcoded-3.text: This is a problem-specific constant, not a codebase invariant. Hardcoding problem-defined thresholds is universal across all LeetCode solutions and not worth tracking.

tickets-k-must-be-positive.text: `time_to_buy_tickets` assumes `tickets[k] >= 1`; if `tickets[k]` were 0, the expression `tickets[k] - 1` becomes -1, causing incorrect negative contributions from `min` for post-k elements.

tickets-pure-function-no-deps.text: `time_to_buy_tickets` is a standalone pure function with zero imports and no side effects, taking `(tickets, k)` and returning an integer.

tickets-returns-seconds-until-k-finishes.text: `time_to_buy_tickets(tickets, k)` returns the total number of seconds until the person at index `k` finishes buying all their tickets.

tickets-simulation-avoidance.text: `time_to_buy_tickets` replaces an O(n·max(tickets)) queue simulation with an O(n) single-pass formula that computes each person's contribution based on their position relative to index k.

tickets-split-at-k-boundary.text: In `time_to_buy_tickets`, people at indices ≤ k contribute `min(t, tickets[k])` seconds and people at indices > k contribute `min(t, tickets[k] - 1)` seconds, because post-k people do not get a turn in k's final round.

tickets-total-initialized-zero-and-singl.text: `time_to_buy_tickets` initializes `total = 0` and computes the answer by iterating once over `(i, t)` pairs in `tickets`.

tictactoe-draw-only-when-nine-moves.text: After processing all moves, the tic-tac-toe function returns "Draw " only when exactly 9 moves were made; otherwise it returns "Pending ".

tictactoe-eager-win-check-all-moves.text: Win detection runs after every move by checking all 8 winning lines, so the first player to complete a line wins immediately and later moves are never evaluated.

tictactoe-eight-winning-lines-hardcoded.text: The wins list hardcodes all 8 winning lines: 3 rows, 3 columns, and 2 diagonals.

tictactoe-function-misnamed.text: The tic-tac-toe solution exports a function named `validateBinaryTreeNodes` instead of a tic-tac-toe-related name, indicating a copy-paste naming error that tests depend on.

tictactoe-grid-values-encode-players.text: The 3x3 grid in the tic-tac-toe solution uses 0 for empty, 1 for player A, and 2 for player B.

tictactoe-player-alternation-index-parit.text: Player assignment uses index parity: player = 1 if i % 2 == 0 else 2, so A moves first and B moves on odd indices.

tictactoe-trailing-space-returns.text: All four return values from the tic-tac-toe solution include a trailing space (`"A "`, `"B "`, `"Draw "`, `"Pending "`); tests must match this exact format.

tie-breaking-earliest-year.text: `maxAliveYear` uses strict `>` in its comparison so the left-to-right scan naturally returns the earliest year when multiple years share peak population.

tie-breaking-is-insertion-order.text: The entry itself notes the problem guarantees a unique answer, making this a theoretical observation about CPython internals rather than a meaningful codebase invariant.

time-complexity-is-n-log-n.text: Complexity is a direct consequence of the algorithm (sort + linear scan) and trivially derivable from reading the code — not an invariant that could be unknowingly violated.

time-complexity-linear.text: Standard O(|s| + |target|) complexity for Counter construction; not a codebase invariant.

time-complexity-nlogn-make-arrays.text: Time complexity of `sorted()` is common knowledge and not a codebase-specific claim worth tracking.

time-complexity-sort-then-reduce.text: `maxValueAfterOperations` runs in O(m * n log n) — dominated by sorting m rows of length n — followed by an O(m * n) column-max scan.

time-is-constant-under-constraints.text: "O(1) because the domain is bounded" is a trivially true observation for any bounded-domain problem — not a useful invariant to track.

title-to-number-empty-string-returns-zer.text: An empty string input to `title_to_number` returns 0.

title-to-number-ord-offset-conversion.text: `title_to_number` converts each uppercase letter to its 1-based value using `ord(c) - ord('A') + 1`.

to-linked-list-empty-returns-none.text: `to_linked_list([])` returns `None`, matching the LeetCode convention for empty lists.

toeplitz-comparisons-bounded-by-interior.text: `isToeplitzMatrix` performs at most `(m-1)*(n-1)` comparisons, one per interior cell.

toeplitz-loops-start-at-one.text: `isToeplitzMatrix` starts its row and column loops at index 1, skipping the top row and left column because those cells have no diagonal predecessor.

toeplitz-neighbor-equivalence.text: The Toeplitz check verifies `matrix[i][j] == matrix[i-1][j-1]` for all interior cells rather than enumerating diagonals explicitly; this is equivalent by transitivity of equality along each diagonal.

toeplitz-short-circuits-on-mismatch.text: `isToeplitzMatrix` returns `False` on the first cell that differs from its diagonal predecessor, skipping all remaining comparisons.

toeplitz-single-pass-o1-space.text: `isToeplitzMatrix` uses O(1) auxiliary space and a single pass over interior cells without allocating additional data structures.

toeplitz-trivial-for-single-dimension.text: A 1×n or m×1 matrix is trivially Toeplitz because the loop ranges `range(1, 1)` are empty, so the method returns `True` without executing any comparisons.

top-projection-counts-nonzero-cells.text: The xy (top-down) projection area equals the count of cells where `grid[i][j] > 0`, not the sum of cell values — each non-empty stack casts exactly one unit square

tournament-matches-equal-n-minus-1.text: In a single-elimination tournament with `n` teams, the total number of matches played is exactly `n - 1`, regardless of how byes are distributed across rounds.

trailing-space-in-poker-output.text: All return strings in `best_poker_hand` end with a trailing space (e.g., `"Flush "`, `"Pair "`), matching LeetCode's expected output format exactly.

training-hours-non-negative-via-max-and-.text: The solution prevents negative training hours via `max(0, ...)` for the energy gap and an `if cur_exp <= exp` guard for the experience gap.

transpose-assumes-rectangular-input.text: `transpose` reads the column count from `matrix[0]` and assumes all rows have the same length; jagged input is not validated.

transpose-comprehension-loop-order.text: `transpose` builds the result with a nested list comprehension whose outer loop iterates over input columns and inner loop over input rows.

transpose-empty-input-raises.text: `transpose([])` raises `IndexError` because the code unconditionally accesses `matrix[0]` to determine the column count; this is safe under LeetCode's constraint `m >= 1`.

transpose-index-identity.text: The output of `transpose` satisfies `result[j][i] == matrix[i][j]` for all valid `(i, j)`, achieved by swapping the outer/inner loop indices in a nested list comprehension.

transpose-linear-time-space-in-output.text: `transpose` runs in O(m*n) time and allocates O(m*n) space for the new output matrix.

transpose-output-dimensions-swapped.text: `transpose` always returns an `n × m` matrix from an `m × n` input, constructing a new list-of-lists; it never modifies the input in place.

traversal-accumulation-universal-across-.text: The single-traversal accumulation paradigm — visit each element once while maintaining state via accumulators — is a recurring algorithmic shape across data structures: arrays use left-to-right streaming with scalar variables, and trees use DFS with closure-captured variables. Both achieve efficient single-pass O(n) computation, suggesting that traversal-order discipline is a primary mechanism for correctness in these patterns.

justifications.label: Generalizes the dominant streaming shape beyond linear sequences to recursive structures, with closure variables as the tree analogue of scalar accumulators

tree-node-uses-optional-forward-ref.text: TreeNode uses `Optional[TreeNode]` via `from __future__ import annotations` to allow forward-referencing in the type hint.

tree-postorder-closure-idiom.text: Tree solutions combine closure-based DFS (capturing mutable result variables from the enclosing scope for side-effect accumulation) with postorder return values (propagating subtree summaries upward for recursive composition), enabling single-pass O(n) tree computations that both accumulate a global answer and compose local results.

justifications.label: Closures handle cross-subtree accumulation while postorder handles intra-subtree composition — together they cover all tree computation needs

tree-serialization-helpers-duplicated.text: `list_to_tree` and `tree_to_list` BFS serialization helpers are duplicated per tree problem rather than shared from a common module.

tree-to-list-strips-trailing-nones.text: `tree_to_list` removes trailing `None` values from its BFS serialization, making `[1, None, 2]` and `[1, None, 2, None, None]` equivalent representations.

tree-to-list-strips-trailing-nulls.text: `tree_to_list` removes all trailing `None` entries from its BFS level-order output, matching LeetCode's canonical serialization format.

tree2str-empty-left-parens-preserved.text: `tree2str` emits `()` for a missing left child if and only if the right child exists, preserving positional unambiguity in the serialized output.

tree2str-empty-root-returns-empty-string.text: For a None root, tree2str returns the empty string.

tree2str-handles-negative-vals.text: Negative node values are serialized correctly (e.g., `-1(-2)(-3)`) with no special-case logic — `str()` handles the sign naturally.

tree2str-local-treenode.text: `tree2str` defines `TreeNode` locally rather than importing from a shared module, making the solution self-contained for LeetCode submission.

tree2str-no-unnecessary-right-parens.text: `tree2str` never emits parentheses for an absent right child, regardless of whether the left child exists — the asymmetric conditional (`if root.left or root.right` vs. `if root.right`) encodes this rule.

tree2str-preorder-string.text: Obvious from the problem name ("Construct String from Binary Tree" using preorder) — this restates the problem specification rather than documenting a non-obvious invariant.

tree2str-recursive-subtree-strings.text: tree2str recursively returns a complete string for each subtree, and the caller wraps that returned string in parentheses.

treenode-canonical-definition.text: `TreeNode` with `val`, `left`, `right` is the canonical binary tree node definition, redefined per-file to match LeetCode's interface rather than shared from a common module.

treenode-defined-in-multiple-files.text: `TreeNode` is defined locally in multiple solution files (`same-tree/solution.py`, `root-equals-sum-of-children/solution.py`, and likely others) rather than in a single shared location.

treenode-defined-locally-per-solution.text: `TreeNode` is defined locally in each tree-problem solution file rather than imported from a shared module, making each solution independently runnable.

treenode-is-de-facto-shared-via-inline-c.text: `TreeNode` is defined inline in each tree-problem solution file rather than in a shared module, yet hundreds of test files import it from individual solutions — making each copy a critical dependency despite the duplication.

treenode-is-local-not-shared.text: This contradicts `build-tree-is-shared-infra` — some solutions define TreeNode locally while others import it from `sum-of-root-to-leaf-binary-numbers/solution.py`. The reality is mixed: TreeNode exists both as shared infrastructure and as local definitions. The two beliefs `build-tree-is-shared-infra` and `treenode-defined-locally-per-solution` together capture this more accurately than a blanket "local not shared" claim.

treenode-is-shared-canonical-definition.text: `TreeNode` in `convert-sorted-array-to-binary-search-tree/solution.py` is imported by 300+ test files across the repo, serving as the de facto canonical binary tree node definition.

treenode-redefined-per-problem.text: `TreeNode` is defined locally in each tree problem's `solution.py` rather than imported from a shared module, matching LeetCode's submission format and keeping each problem directory self-contained

treenode-shared-definition-in-preorder.text: `TreeNode` defined in `binary-tree-preorder-traversal/solution.py` is imported by 400+ test files across the repo, making it the de facto shared binary tree node class — changes to its constructor signature are breaking.

treenode-shared-dependency.text: The `TreeNode` class defined in `average-of-levels-in-binary-tree/solution.py` is imported by hundreds of test files across the repo, making it a de facto shared data structure whose signature changes have high blast radius.

treenode-uses-pep604-union.text: The TreeNode class in this file uses PEP 604 union syntax (TreeNode | None) enabled by from __future__ import annotations.

trial-division-pattern-reuse.text: The strip-all-factors-then-check-residual pattern (used in `ugly-number`) recurs in `power-of-two`, `power-of-three`, `power-of-four`, and `three-divisors` solutions

triangular-number-correctness.text: A run of `n` identical characters contributes exactly `n*(n+1)/2` single-character substrings, and the integer division is always exact because one of `n` or `n+1` is even

tribonacci-base-cases-complete.text: The three Tribonacci base cases T(0)=0, T(1)=1, T(2)=1 are handled via early returns before the loop, so the loop range `3..n` never executes for n < 3.

tribonacci-iterative-o1-space.text: `tribonacci` uses O(1) auxiliary space via a three-variable sliding window `(a, b, c)`, not memoization or a DP array.

tribonacci-loop-iterations-n-minus-2.text: For n >= 3, the `tribonacci` loop runs exactly n - 2 iterations.

tribonacci-negative-n-returns-1.text: For negative n, `tribonacci` falls through both guards, executes zero loop iterations, and returns 1 silently.

tribonacci-no-validation.text: No input validation is the universal convention for LeetCode solutions in this repo; documenting it per-solution adds noise without value.

tribonacci-t37-fits-32-bit.text: T(37) = 2,082,876,103, which fits in a 32-bit signed integer.

tribonacci-tuple-swap-correctness.text: The simultaneous tuple assignment `a, b, c = b, c, a+b+c` evaluates all RHS values before any assignment, ensuring correctness without temporary variables — a Python-specific idiom critical to the sliding-window recurrence.

trim-mean-empty-input-raises-zero-divisi.text: An empty input to `trimMean` would cause a `ZeroDivisionError` at the final division because the code does not handle that case.

trim-mean-mutates-input.text: `trimMean` calls `arr.sort()` which modifies the caller's list in-place, destroying original element ordering.

trim-mean-removes-exactly-5-percent-each.text: `trimMean` removes `len(arr) // 20` elements from both the low and high ends, which equals exactly 5% when `len(arr)` is a multiple of 20; silently trims fewer than 5% otherwise.

trim-mean-safe-under-constraints.text: Division by zero cannot occur in `trimMean` when `len(arr) >= 20`, since the trimmed slice retains at least `len(arr) - 2*(len(arr)//20)` elements (minimum 18 for a 20-element input).

trim-mean-slices-sorted-array-between-k-.text: After sorting, `trimMean` slices the array as `arr[k : len(arr) - k]` where `k = len(arr) // 20`, forming the trimmed array before computing the mean.

trim-mean-test-suite-has-six-cases.text: `TestTrimMean` contains six test cases covering LeetCode examples, a uniform-value array, a 1000-element sequential array, and a boundary case with only two distinct values.

trim-mean-time-complexity-is-sort-domina.text: `trimMean` is O(n log n) dominated by the sort; the subsequent slice and sum are O(n).

trim-mean-uses-full-sort-rather-than-par.text: The `trimMean` solution fully sorts the array then slices it, rather than using a partial sort such as `heapq.nsmallest`.

triple-optimization-unified-by-pipeline-.text: The pipeline architecture simultaneously achieves three optimizations through a single structural decomposition: correctness (construction techniques prevent errors at each phase boundary), efficiency (mathematical reduction and early exit eliminate work within phases), and resource minimization (streaming minimizes time while mutation minimizes space) — these are co-products of the pipeline, not independently layered concerns.

justifications.label: Unifying three depth-4 optimization conclusions as structural co-products of the same two-phase decomposition

triple-stabilization-across-orthogonal-d.text: The system is stabilized by three independent mechanisms operating on orthogonal dimensions: correctness is dual-stabilized (paradigmatic convergence + construction techniques), the quality profile is dual-stabilized (domain attractor + self-reinforcing equilibrium), and defect tolerance is self-reinforced by the quality equilibrium itself — making the system triply resilient because any single destabilization affects only one dimension.

justifications.label: Each antecedent establishes dual stabilization in its own domain; combining them reveals a third independently stabilized dimension (immunity) that neither antecedent alone identifies as a separate axis

triplet-no-index-tracking.text: Despite the problem requiring `i < j < k` ordering, `countTriplets` never tracks indices — the product `a * b * c` (one element from each of three distinct-value groups) maps 1-to-1 to ordered index triples.

triplet-order-independence.text: The group-contribution sweep in `countTriplets` produces the same result regardless of iteration order over `Counter.values()`, because each triple of distinct groups is counted exactly once when its "middle" group (in processing order) is visited.

truncate-sentence-no-imports.text: Trivially observable from the file; not an architectural invariant worth tracking.

truncate-sentence-pure-function.text: Too granular — "method X is a pure function" is obvious from reading a one-line method with no state mutation; it doesn't encode an invariant that could break.

truncate-sentence-safe-overslice.text: `truncateSentence` safely handles `k` greater than the word count by returning the full sentence, relying on Python's slice semantics rather than explicit bounds checking.

truncate-sentence-single-expression.text: Implementation detail that's immediately visible from the code; not a constraint that guides future work.

truncate-sentence-uses-no-imports.text: The solution file imports no modules; it uses only Python builtin string and list operations.

truncate-sentence-uses-split-slice-join.text: The `truncateSentence` method implements its logic as the single expression `" ".join(s.split()[:k])`.

truncate-sentence-wraps-in-solution-clas.text: The solution wraps `truncateSentence` in a `Solution` class matching LeetCode's submission interface.

twenty-dollar-bills-never-tracked.text: The lemonade-change solution tracks only $5 and $10 bill counts; $20 bills are never stored because they can never be used as change.

two-char-alphabet-bounds-answer-to-two.text: For palindromic-subsequence removal over a 2-character alphabet, the answer is always in `{0, 1, 2}` — remove all of one character in one step, all of the other in a second step. This bound breaks with 3+ characters.

two-digit-construction-commutative.text: The `min(a,b)*10 + max(a,b)` formula produces the correct smallest two-digit number regardless of which array contributes the smaller minimum.

two-max-tracker-ge-not-gt.text: In the two-max tracking idiom (`max_product`), the primary branch uses `>=` (not `>`), which is critical for correctness: with `>`, an array of identical values would leave `max2` at the initial value of 0 instead of being promoted.

two-out-of-three-empty-inputs-safe.text: The solution correctly returns an empty list for empty input arrays because empty sets produce empty intersections.

two-out-of-three-linear-time.text: Complexity of basic set operations is a language-level fact, not a codebase claim worth tracking.

two-out-of-three-no-imports.text: The Two Out of Three solution uses no imports; it relies solely on Python builtin set operations.

two-out-of-three-no-order-guarantee.text: Standard behavior of set iteration in Python; not a codebase-specific invariant.

two-out-of-three-one-liner-body.text: The function body is a single expression computing `(s1 & s2) | (s1 & s3) | (s2 & s3)` and converting the result to a list.

two-out-of-three-output-distinct.text: The output list contains only distinct values, guaranteed by the use of set operations.

two-out-of-three-set-algebra.text: The Two Out of Three solution expresses "appears in >= 2 of 3 arrays" as the union of all pairwise set intersections: `(s1 & s2) | (s1 & s3) | (s2 & s3)`.

two-out-of-three-wrong-name.text: The function implementing LeetCode 2032 (Two Out of Three) is misnamed `largest_odd`, a copy-paste error from another solution file.

two-paradigms-cover-solution-space.text: Nearly all solutions follow one of two dominant paradigms — single-pass streaming with O(1) accumulators for counting, tracking, and accumulation problems, or sort-then-two-pointer for pair-finding, ordering, and constraint-satisfaction problems — with the choice determined by whether the problem requires aggregation or search.

justifications.label: The two depth-2 algorithmic shapes partition the solution space nearly completely; problems not fitting either are the exceptions (binary search, closed-form, divide-and-conquer)

two-pointer-backward-fill-avoids-sort.text: The squares-of-sorted-array solution fills the result array from index n-1 down to 0 using two inward-converging pointers, achieving O(n) time instead of O(n log n) square-then-sort

two-pointer-compaction-extends-streaming.text: The read/write pointer compaction idiom (used for remove-duplicates, remove-element, move-zeroes) extends single-pass streaming from pure scalar accumulation to in-place array transformation: instead of reducing the input to a scalar accumulator, the write pointer constructs the output array in-place while the read pointer streams through the input, achieving O(1) auxiliary space via mutation rather than via scalar reduction — broadening the streaming paradigm's applicability to problems whose output is a transformed array, not a single value.

justifications.label: Compaction is streaming where the accumulator is a write cursor into the input array itself

two-pointer-compaction-family.text: Problems 26 (remove duplicates), 27 (remove element), and 283 (move zeroes) all use the same read/write pointer compaction pattern with different keep-predicates; the structural code is identical, only the filter condition varies.

two-pointer-convergence-linear-time.text: The converging two-pointer pattern in `reverse-only-letters` runs in O(n) time because each pointer advances monotonically inward, collectively visiting each index at most once.

two-pointer-convergence-pattern.text: The walk-inward two-pointer technique (left pointer advances right, right pointer advances left, check convergence) recurs across mountain-array, palindrome, and sorted-array solutions.

two-pointer-inward-sweep-pattern.text: The two-pointer inward sweep (left from 0, right from end, march inward with subset-specific skip logic) is a recurring pattern used by `reverse-vowels-of-a-string` and `reverse-only-letters` for reversing a character subset in-place.

two-pointer-is-dual-cursor-streaming.text: Two-pointer techniques are a structural variant of single-pass streaming using paired cursors: they share streaming's core properties (monotonic progress, O(1) state, single traversal) but generalize the scan by allowing convergent or divergent cursor movement, making them streaming algorithms with a richer cursor model.

justifications.label: both patterns share monotonic-progress + O(1)-state invariants; two-pointer adds a second cursor axis

two-pointer-merge-scan-for-sorted-inters.text: `min_common_number` uses the two-pointer merge-scan pattern: advance the pointer on the smaller value, return on equality — the canonical O(n+m) time, O(1) space approach for finding common elements in two sorted arrays.

two-pointer-pattern-variants.text: The repo contains multiple two-pointer variants: inward sweep (valid-palindrome), lockstep with skip (valid-word-abbreviation), and matrix transpose walk (valid-word-square) — all sharing the fail-fast early-return idiom.

two-pointer-primary-linear-array-techniq.text: Converging two-pointer patterns — forward/backward fill, inward squeeze, and sorted-pair matching — are the dominant technique for achieving O(n) time on array pair and partition problems.

justifications.label: Two-pointer subsumes multiple problem families into a single O(n) framework

two-pointer-sorted-array-pattern.text: Solutions pairing min/max elements (e.g., distinct averages) sort once then walk inward with left/right pointers rather than simulating repeated removal, achieving O(n log n) overall.

two-preprocessing-paradigms-partition-pr.text: Problems partition by which preprocessing unlocks linear-time solution: hashing (Counter/set) for membership and frequency queries vs sorting for positional and pair relationships, with the core query type — lookup or comparison — determining which paradigm applies.

justifications.label: Query type (lookup vs comparison) determines the preprocessing choice

two-solution-conventions-coexist.text: The repo uses two conventions for solution entry points: `Solution` class with a method (LeetCode boilerplate style, e.g., `runningSum`) and standalone module-level functions (e.g., `is_same_tree`, `can_transform`, `roman_to_int`).

two-stack-queue-amortized-o1.text: Every element in `MyQueue` is transferred from `_in_stack` to `_out_stack` exactly once across its lifetime, so `push`, `pop`, and `peek` are all amortized O(1) despite O(n) worst-case transfers.

two-stack-queue-amortized-via-lazy-trans.text: The two-stack queue achieves correct FIFO semantics with amortized O(1) per operation through lazy bulk transfer: each element crosses from input to output stack exactly once across its lifetime, push is worst-case O(1) (never triggers transfer), and the deferred reversal preserves total ordering.

justifications.label: Three properties of the two-stack queue collectively prove amortized O(1) via the lazy-transfer mechanism

two-stack-queue-has-no-size-counter.text: `MyQueue.empty()` checks both `_in_stack` and `_out_stack` rather than maintaining a separate size counter.

two-stack-queue-lazy-transfer.text: `_transfer` only moves elements when `_out_stack` is empty — it never re-reverses elements already in `_out_stack`, which is the key invariant preserving both correctness and amortized cost.

two-stack-queue-logical-front-depends-on.text: The logical queue front is `_out_stack[-1]` when `_out_stack` is non-empty and `_in_stack[0]` otherwise.

two-stack-queue-pop-peek-raise-indexerro.text: Calling `pop()` or `peek()` on an empty `MyQueue` raises `IndexError` from the underlying list because the implementation performs no defensive empty check.

two-stack-queue-push-always-o1.text: `push` always appends to `_in_stack` and never triggers a transfer, making it worst-case O(1) — not just amortized — unlike `pop` and `peek` which may trigger O(n) transfers.

two-stack-queue-uses-two-python-lists.text: `MyQueue` implements FIFO behavior using two Python lists, `_in_stack` and `_out_stack`, with `append`, `pop`, and `[-1]` as stack primitives.

two-sum-assumes-exactly-one-solution.text: The function `twoSum` assumes the LeetCode guarantee of exactly one valid pair; it does not handle multiple pairs or zero pairs explicitly.

two-sum-complement-lookup-pattern.text: `twoSum` uses a hash map keyed by value (not index) to check whether the complement `target - num` has been seen, which is the canonical O(n) complement lookup idiom

two-sum-dict-keys-are-values-not-indices.text: The `seen` dictionary maps each previously-visited value to its index, not the other way around.

two-sum-family-spans-lookup-strategy-spa.text: The Two Sum problem family collectively spans the lookup strategy space: hash map for O(1) complement lookup with check-before-insert ordering (classic), frequency counter for duplicate-aware pairing (III), hash set for tree-traversal membership with check-before-insert preventing self-pairing (IV), and sort plus two-pointer for inequality-bounded search (less-than-k) — demonstrating that a single problem concept exercises all major lookup mechanisms in the repo's abstraction trio.

justifications.label: Four Two Sum variants exercise four distinct lookup strategies spanning the repo's full abstraction trio

two-sum-first-valid-pair-earliest-second.text: If multiple valid pairs exist (violating the contract), the function returns the pair with the earliest second index (the first index at which a valid complement is found).

two-sum-iii-add-find-asymmetry.text: `TwoSum` optimizes `add()` to O(1) at the cost of O(n) `find()`; the inverse tradeoff (precompute all sums on add, O(1) find) would be better when finds dominate.

two-sum-iii-add-is-constant.text: `TwoSum.add(number)` runs in O(1) amortized time by performing a single `Counter` increment.

two-sum-iii-counter-default-zero.text: This is a Python language fact, not a codebase invariant. Any Python developer knows `Counter` returns 0 for missing keys.

two-sum-iii-find-is-linear.text: `TwoSum.find(value)` runs in O(n) time where n is the number of distinct added values, because it scans all keys of the `Counter`.

two-sum-iii-find-is-read-only.text: Obvious from reading the method — it only reads `self.counts`. Not a surprising invariant.

two-sum-iii-self-pair-requires-count-two.text: In `TwoSum.find()`, a number can only pair with itself to reach a target if its count in the `Counter` is >= 2; this prevents `add(3); find(6)` from returning `True`.

two-sum-iii-uses-counter.text: The `TwoSum` class stores added numbers in a `collections.Counter` frequency map.

two-sum-implicit-none-on-no-solution.text: If no valid pair exists (violating the problem contract), the function silently returns `None` rather than raising

two-sum-index-ordering.text: The returned indices are always in ascending order because values enter `seen` strictly before the current index

two-sum-instantiates-hash-pipeline.text: The Two Sum family is a canonical instantiation of the hash-then-stream pipeline: the hash map serves as the O(1) preprocessing structure for complement lookup while the single-pass array scan constitutes the streaming phase, with check-before-insert ordering providing construction-based correctness — paralleling palindrome's instantiation through Counter and demonstrating the pipeline's universality across point-lookup and aggregate-frequency query modes.

justifications.label: two-sum exercises hash pipeline with point-lookup semantics complementary to palindrome's frequency semantics

two-sum-iv-bfs-iterative.text: `findTarget` uses iterative BFS with `collections.deque` rather than recursion, avoiding stack overflow on skewed trees.

two-sum-iv-check-before-insert.text: `findTarget` prevents self-pairing by checking the `seen` set *before* inserting the current node's value — the ordering of check-then-add is the critical invariant.

two-sum-iv-ignores-bst-property.text: `findTarget` uses a generic hash-set approach that works on any binary tree; it does not exploit BST ordering, trading potential O(log n) space for implementation simplicity.

two-sum-iv-includes-tests-and-build-help.text: The solution file includes a `TestFindTarget` class with seven unit tests and a `_build` helper that constructs trees from level-order lists.

two-sum-iv-linear-time-space.text: `findTarget` runs in O(n) time and O(n) space where n is the number of nodes in the tree.

two-sum-iv-uses-hashset.text: `findTarget` uses a hash set `seen` to track visited node values for O(1) complement lookup.

two-sum-less-than-k-assumes-positive-int.text: The function `max_sum_under_k` assumes `nums` contains positive integers per the LeetCode contract and does not validate for non-positive inputs.

two-sum-less-than-k-distinct-index-invar.text: The while loop condition `left < right` ensures the function never considers a pair of the same index.

two-sum-less-than-k-fewer-than-two-retur.text: For input with fewer than 2 elements, the while loop never executes and the function returns `-1`.

two-sum-less-than-k-monotonic-convergenc.text: Each loop iteration moves exactly one pointer inward, guaranteeing termination in at most n-1 steps

two-sum-less-than-k-pointer-advancement-.text: When `s < k`, moving `left` right is correct; when `s >= k`, moving `right` left is correct, based on monotonicity of sorted sums.

two-sum-less-than-k-returns-neg-one.text: The function returns `-1` (not `None` or an exception) when no pair sum is strictly less than `k`

two-sum-less-than-k-sort-mutates.text: `max_sum_under_k` mutates the input list via in-place sort; callers that need the original order must copy first

two-sum-less-than-k-strict-inequality.text: The comparison is `s < k` (strict), not `s <= k`; a pair summing exactly to `k` is excluded

two-sum-less-than-k-time-complexity.text: The algorithm runs in O(n log n) time and O(1) auxiliary space via sort + two-pointer

two-sum-no-self-pair.text: An element cannot pair with itself; the lookup-before-insert order prevents `seen[num]` from matching the current index

two-sum-single-pass-linear.text: `twoSum` runs in O(n) time and O(n) space via a single-pass hash map, never iterating the array more than once

twos-complement-mask-pattern.text: Solutions handling signed 32-bit integers use `num &= 0xFFFFFFFF` to reinterpret negative Python integers as unsigned 32-bit two's complement values, bridging Python's arbitrary-precision integers to fixed-width behavior.

typewriter-abc-example-returns-5.text: For word = 'abc', the algorithm returns 5: a→a costs 1, a→b costs 2, and b→c costs 2.

typewriter-curr-range-0-25.text: curr is always in [0, 25] because it is set directly from ord(ch) - ord('a') on valid lowercase input.

typewriter-pointer-starts-at-a.text: The typewriter pointer starts at 'a' (integer offset 0) before processing the word.

typewriter-solution-implements-leetcode-.text: The solution file implements LeetCode 1974: Minimum Time to Type Word Using Special Typewriter.

typewriter-target-offset-uses-ord-minus-.text: The target position for each character is computed as ord(ch) - ord('a'), yielding an integer offset from 0 to 25.

typing-import-for-annotations.text: The repo consistently uses `from typing import List` for type annotations rather than Python 3.9+ built-in `list[]` syntax.

typing-list-used-for-compatibility.text: Solutions consistently use `typing.List` for type annotations rather than the built-in `list[str]` syntax available in Python 3.9+, maintaining backward compatibility across the repo.

ugly-number-complexity.text: The total number of divisions across all three primes is O(log n), since each division at least halves `n`

ugly-number-definition-prime-factors-235.text: An ugly number is defined as a positive integer whose only prime factors are 2, 3, and 5.

ugly-number-factor-tuple-order-cost-hint.text: The order of factors in the tuple (2,3,5) does not affect correctness, but dividing by 2 first is cheapest due to bit shift under the hood.

ugly-number-integer-division-gated-by-mo.text: The solution uses integer division `//=` gated by a modulo check, preserving integrality throughout the factor-stripping loop.

ugly-number-one-is-ugly.text: `is_ugly(1)` returns `True` because 1 has no prime factors, so the loop body never executes and `n == 1` holds

ugly-number-pure-function-no-side-effect.text: `is_ugly` is a pure function with no side effects and no mutation of external state.

ugly-number-trial-division-pattern.text: `is_ugly` uses the strip-and-check-residual pattern: divide out all factors of 2, 3, and 5, then check if the remainder is 1

ugly-number-zero-guard.text: `is_ugly(0)` returns `False` and never enters the division loop; without the `n <= 0` guard, `0 % 2 == 0` would loop forever

uncommon-computation-is-single-expressio.text: The entire computation is a single expression chain with no intermediate state or mutation.

uncommon-concat-then-split.text: Concatenating with a space and splitting is equivalent to splitting each sentence independently and merging, because `str.split()` handles multiple consecutive spaces

uncommon-counts-globally.text: A word appearing twice in one sentence and zero times in the other is excluded; frequency is counted across the union, not per-sentence

uncommon-imports-counter-and-list.text: The solution imports `collections.Counter` for frequency counting and `typing.List` for return type annotation.

uncommon-output-order-is-insertion-order.text: The returned list preserves the left-to-right first-occurrence order of words across the combined input (Python 3.7+ dict ordering guarantee)

uncommon-returns-words-not-counts.text: The function returns a list of words whose total frequency is exactly 1, not their indices or counts.

uncommon-uses-counter-for-frequency.text: The solution uses `collections.Counter` to build a frequency map of words across both sentences combined.

uniform-frequency-set-idiom.text: `len(set(counter.values())) == 1` is used as the canonical check for whether all character frequencies are equal throughout the repo.

union-by-rank-increments-on-tie-only.text: Rank is incremented only when merging two roots of equal rank, maintaining it as an upper bound on subtree height.

union-find-uses-path-splitting.text: The `find` function in `find-if-path-exists-in-graph/solution.py` uses iterative path splitting (`parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]`), which halves path length per traversal, not full recursive path compression that flattens to the root.

unique-morse-complexity-linear-in-total-.text: The time complexity is O(S) where S is the total number of characters across all words, and space is O(N) where N is the number of distinct Morse strings.

unique-morse-morse-table-local-list.text: The Morse code lookup table is defined as a local list of 26 strings inside the method, not as a class or module constant.

unique-morse-tests-bundled-in-file.text: The file contains both the solution and a `TestSolution` class with five test cases, runnable via `unittest`.

unique-morse-uses-solution-class.text: The solution is implemented as a method `uniqueMorseCodeWords` inside a `Solution` class, not as a standalone function.

unique-occurrences-contract.text: The method returns True if and only if no two distinct values in the input list share the same frequency.

unique-occurrences-counter-values-view-p.text: Counter(arr).values() returns a dict_values view that can contain duplicate counts; converting it to a set is what collapses duplicate frequencies.

unique-occurrences-is-o-n.text: Too solution-specific; complexity of a single two-line solution is self-evident and not an architectural claim.

unique-occurrences-no-loops-or-branches.text: The solution contains no explicit loops, branching, or mutation; it is implemented as two expressions using Counter and set cardinality comparison.

unique-occurrences-o-n-time-o-n-space.text: The solution runs in O(n) time and O(n) space, where n is the length of the input array.

unique-occurrences-returns-true-for-empt.text: For an empty input array, uniqueOccurrences returns True because len(values) == len(set(values)) evaluates to 0 == 0, even though LeetCode constraints forbid empty arrays.

univalued-tree-empty-root-returns-true.text: isUnivalTree(None) returns True, treating an empty tree as vacuously uni-valued.

univalued-tree-inline-tests-eight-cases.text: The solution file includes an inline TestIsUnivalTree class with eight test cases covering single node, all-same tree, mismatches at various depths, two-node trees, and None root.

univalued-tree-read-only-no-mutation.text: The DFS never mutates the tree; the operation is purely read-only.

univalued-tree-recursive-dfs-o-n-time-o-.text: The solution performs recursive pre-order DFS in O(n) time and O(h) space, where h is the tree height.

univalued-tree-target-captured-before-tr.text: The comparison target is set to root.val before traversal begins and is the single reference value used for every node.

unknown-chars-treated-as-present.text: Characters outside `{'A', 'L', 'P'}` fall into the `else` branch and behave identically to `'P'` (resetting late counter, not incrementing absences)

unlimited-swaps-equals-independent-sort.text: For problems where unlimited swaps are allowed within a partition (e.g., same-parity digits), the optimal strategy reduces to sorting each partition group independently in descending order — this pattern appears in `largest-number-after-digit-swaps-by-parity` and likely recurs across similar problems

unreachable-return-minus-one.text: Dead code observation — useful as a code review note but not a codebase invariant that guides development decisions.

valid-boomerang-cross-product-expression.text: The solution computes (x2 - x1) * (y3 - y1) - (y2 - y1) * (x3 - x1) != 0 to decide whether three points form a valid boomerang.

valid-boomerang-destructures-points-into.text: The solution destructures the three points into six scalar coordinates using (x1, y1), (x2, y2), (x3, y3) = points before computing the cross product.

valid-boomerang-o1-time-and-space.text: isBoomerang executes in O(1) time and O(1) space with no loops or conditionals beyond the return expression.

valid-boomerang-zero-covers-duplicate-an.text: A zero cross product covers all degenerate cases — two identical points, three identical points, and three distinct collinear points — so no separate duplicate-point check is needed.

valid-mountain-array-linear-time-constan.text: The algorithm runs in O(n) time and O(1) space.

valid-mountain-array-min-length-3-reject.text: Arrays with fewer than 3 elements are rejected immediately with False before any pointer logic runs.

valid-mountain-array-multi-peak-fails-co.text: Multi-peaked arrays have i and j land on different local maxima, so i != j and the validity check fails.

valid-mountain-array-two-pointer-walk-in.text: The solution uses two pointers: i advances right while arr[i] < arr[i+1], and j advances left while arr[j] < arr[j-1], then checks whether i == j.

valid-palindrome-case-insensitive-at-com.text: Case normalization happens at comparison time via `.lower()`, not by preprocessing the entire string — the original string is never mutated or copied.

valid-palindrome-empty-is-palindrome.text: An empty string or a string with no alphanumeric characters returns `True` because the outer loop condition `left < right` is never satisfied.

valid-palindrome-ii-empty-string-returns.text: The while left < right guard causes an empty string to return True without explicit validation.

valid-palindrome-ii-is-palindrome-at-mos.text: is_palindrome is called at most twice per invocation of validPalindrome, and only when the outer loop encounters a mismatch.

valid-palindrome-ii-no-auxiliary-data-st.text: The solution uses zero auxiliary data structures; space complexity is O(1) excluding the input string.

valid-palindrome-ii-reduced-window-after.text: After a mismatch, is_palindrome checks only the remaining inner substring, not the full string, because characters validated by the outer loop are already symmetric.

valid-palindrome-ii-total-work-bounded-b.text: The total work across the outer loop and both is_palindrome calls is bounded by 2n character comparisons.

valid-palindrome-inner-loop-guards.text: The inner skip loops re-check `left < right`, which prevents index-out-of-bounds on strings containing no alphanumeric characters.

valid-palindrome-returns-false-on-first-.text: `isPalindrome` returns `False` immediately upon the first case-insensitive character mismatch between the two pointers.

valid-palindrome-skip-non-alnum-via-str-.text: The skip loops identify non-alphanumeric characters using `str.isalnum` rather than a manually maintained character set.

valid-palindrome-uses-o1-space.text: `isPalindrome` uses O(1) auxiliary space via two-pointer inward sweep; it never allocates a filtered or reversed copy of the input string.

valid-parentheses-empty-string-returns-t.text: `is_valid` returns `True` for the empty string because the loop does not execute and the final `not stack` check succeeds.

valid-parentheses-final-stack-empty-chec.text: The final `return not stack` is required to reject inputs with unmatched openers (e.g., `"("`); without it, any string whose closers all match would pass regardless of leftover openers.

valid-parentheses-implicit-else-openers.text: Any character not present in the `match` dict is treated as an opening bracket and pushed onto the stack, relying on the problem guarantee that input contains only the six bracket characters.

valid-parentheses-match-dict-dual-use.text: The `match` dict serves both as a closer-detection set (`ch in match`) and as a closer-to-opener lookup, eliminating the need for a separate set or if-chain.

valid-parentheses-match-dict-mapping.text: The `match` dict maps `')'` to `'('`, `']'` to `'['`, and `'}'` to `'{'`.

valid-parentheses-no-index-error.text: Short-circuit evaluation of `not stack or stack.pop() != match[ch]` guarantees `pop` is never called on an empty list; a lone closer like `")"` returns `False` without raising `IndexError`.

valid-parentheses-pure-function.text: Redundant — "pure function with no imports" is true of virtually every LeetCode solution in this repo and carries no distinguishing information.

valid-parentheses-single-pass-stack.text: `is_valid` uses a single-pass stack-based approach with O(n) time and O(n) worst-case space; it short-circuits on the first mismatch.

valid-perfect-square-max-mid-square-with.text: For `num = 2^31 - 1`, the largest `mid * mid` is roughly `2^62`, which is handled exactly by Python's arbitrary-precision integers.

valid-perfect-square-negative-input-retu.text: Passing a negative `num` to `is_perfect_square` silently returns `False` because `lo=1` is already greater than the negative `hi`.

valid-word-abbreviation-digit-accumulati.text: Multi-digit numbers in `abbr` are accumulated with `num = num * 10 + int(abbr[j])`, avoiding slicing or `int()` on a substring.

valid-word-abbreviation-letter-must-matc.text: When the current abbreviation character is a letter, `validWordAbbreviation` requires it to match the corresponding character in `word` exactly.

valid-word-abbreviation-loop-guard-preve.text: The main loop guard checks both `i < len(word)` and `j < len(abbr)`, and the digit-parsing inner loop checks `j < len(abbr)`, preventing out-of-bounds access without exceptions.

valid-word-bool-sum-counting.text: `countValidWords` uses `sum(is_valid(t) for t in sentence.split() if t)`, relying on Python boolean-to-integer coercion to count valid tokens.

valid-word-count-splits-whitespace.text: `Solution.countValidWords` tokenizes the sentence with `sentence.split()` and sums `is_valid` over non-empty tokens to produce the count.

valid-word-digit-immediate-reject.text: `is_valid` returns `False` immediately upon encountering any digit via `c.isdigit()`.

valid-word-hyphen-boundary-safe.text: The hyphen validation in `is_valid` checks `i == 0 or i == len(token) - 1` and returns `False` before accessing `token[i-1]` or `token[i+1]`, guaranteeing no `IndexError`

valid-word-hyphen-flanked-by-letters.text: `is_valid` accepts a hyphen only when it is not at the start or end and both `token[i-1].isalpha()` and `token[i+1].isalpha()` are true.

valid-word-nested-pure-helper.text: `is_valid` is nested inside `countValidWords` but captures no enclosing scope variables, so it behaves as a pure function.

valid-word-punctuation-only-at-end.text: `is_valid` rejects a token when it contains more than one of `!`, `.`, or `,`, or when any such punctuation appears before the final character.

valid-word-punctuation-position-before-c.text: A punctuation character not at the final position causes immediate rejection in `is_valid`, independent of `punct_count` — position is checked before count matters

valid-word-single-pass-validation.text: `is_valid` validates all character constraints (digits, hyphens, punctuation) in a single left-to-right pass with early returns — no regex or multi-pass scanning

valid-word-split-no-empties.text: This is a Python language guarantee (`str.split()` without arguments never produces empty strings), not a codebase-specific invariant — it belongs in Python docs, not the belief registry

valid-word-square-avoids-transpose-alloc.text: `valid_word_square` validates the word-square property by comparing characters in place rather than building or allocating a transposed matrix.
